You’re Not Starving" **·** Peter Singer, Hannah Arendt — The Drowning Child (obligation to aid); The Banality of Evil — Argues Louis's 'my life is evil, I drive an Infiniti' bit and 'we make them die with our cars' capture Singer's drowning-child argument that famine relief is a duty of the affluent rather than charity, since the obligation to prevent bad outcomes at little cost holds across distance. It then amplifies the harm claim with Pogge's account of a rigged global institutional order (WTO protections, sweatshop-made smartphones) and frames unthinking consumer participation in that system as Arendt's banality of evil—the 'terrifyingly normal' thoughtlessness of Eichmann repeated at the checkout.
- ch. 33 "17. Louis’s Little Believies" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Builds a three-part definition of moral failure—acting against one's own moral beliefs, freely chosen—and applies it to Louie's Infiniti bit, his stopping the country girl from helping the homeless man, and his refusal to give a soldier his first-class seat while feeling proud of merely considering it. The chapter concludes Louie acts unselfishly only when someone might judge him (the sheriff's kiss, the limousines for his daughter's stranded field trip), so without the threat of judgment his 'little believies' stay inert, and a world where such hypocrisy goes unremarked would lose the power of moral criticism altogether.
- ch. 34 "18. Believies are Not Motivaties" **·** David Hume — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Uses the 'believies' bit, the 'I think it's wrong to eat meat... I eat them all' confession, and 'of course, but maybe' to place Louis in the meta-ethics of moral motivation: he is a cognitivist and partial success theorist, but a Humean who treats beliefs as causally inert without desire and an externalist who denies a necessary link between moral judgment and motivation. That combination, the chapter argues, lets Louis sincerely judge and not be moved without incoherence—making the amoralist conceivable and avoiding 'the moral problem.'
- ch. 35 "VII. Take Some Responsibility for the Shitty Words You Want to Say" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "19. The Playful Thought Experiments of Louis C.K" **·** Plato, Daniel Dennett — Allegory of the Cave — Argues Louis's bits function as playful philosophical thought experiments in Ernst Mach's and Tamar Gendler's sense: the white-people time machine, sitting 'in a chair in the sky,' and the 'Indians' naming skit are make-believe scenarios that reconfigure our frames and draw out truths we already knew, just as Plato's cave and Nathan's parable to King David do. Pairing the cognitive 'Aha!' with the mirthful 'Ha-ha' (via Hurley, Dennett, and Adams's Inside Jokes) makes his humor an error-detection reward loop that takes audiences to upsetting territory and makes them glad they went.
- ch. 37 "20. Feminists Can Take a Joke" **·** Feminism — Argues Louis performs feminist philosophy by writing marginalized voices into his work: Rick's poker speech about what 'faggot' means to gay men who hear it during beatings, Vanessa's seven-minute 'So Did the Fat Lady' confrontation that leaves Louie silenced, and his Daily Show reflection on learning that rape polices women's lives. The chapter does not excuse his slurs ('cunt,' 'nigger,' 'faggot'), but contends his admitted fallibility is what keeps a broad, mixed audience listening—the guy who came for masturbation jokes leaves having heard about rape culture—so feminism and comedy are not natural enemies.
- ch. 38 "21. If You’re Not White, You’re Missing Out" **·** Kimberlé Crenshaw — Intersectionality — Treats Louis as a 'comedic philosopher of race' whose time-machine, 'white people problems,' and 'if you're white and you don't admit that it's great, then you are an asshole' bits teach identity privilege as unearned, systemic advantage. It credits him with an intersectional grasp of white-plus-male benefit, contrasts his 'but for now, Weeeeeee!' complicity over smartphone suffering with Barbara Applebaum's argument that the privileged cannot simply opt out and should mobilize against systems rather than police individual guilt, and concludes his job is descriptive: showing us privilege and leaving the remedy to us.
- ch. 39 "VIII. Of Course but Maybe . ." *(front)*
- ch. 40 "22. Sometimes Cartesian" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito — Takes the character name 'Never Cartesian' as a clue for reading Louie through Descartes's Meditations: the show's dream sequences, hallucinations, and continuity-breaking strangeness (Jane stepping off the subway to test whether she is still in her 'nice dream,' the model's 'maybe it is not really happening,' Liz's possibly dreamed death) make it a sustained exercise in the dream argument and distrust of the senses. The chapter concludes Louis C.K. breaks with Descartes at the rebuild—with no God to anchor the cogito, Louie's world stays suspended between waking and dream, a doubt Louie can live with.
- ch. 41 "23. Louis C.K. Meets the Unconscious" **·** Jacques Lacan, Sigmund Freud — The Unconscious; The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real — Reads the 'of course, but maybe' bit as a wrestling match between Lacan's big Other—society's unwritten rule book of queues, taboos, and approval—and the Freudian unconscious that betrays itself in the therapist's 'the climax results in the death of the woman' slip and other parapraxes. Jokes then work as sublimation and a release valve: Louis's nut-allergy and slavery bits ('you all clapped for dead kids... you don't get to cherry-pick') let audiences laugh at their disavowed 'I know very well, but...' contradictions, though comedy remains confession without absolution.
- ch. 42 "24. An Hour" **·** Jacques Lacan, Jacques Derrida, Sigmund Freud — The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real; Deconstruction — Argues Louis's shift to an hour-a-year of digressive storytelling—spurred by George Carlin's 'dig deeper' tribute speech and forced by fatherhood—is 'secular revelation' in Adam Phillips's sense: his wandering bits work like the free play of the signifier and free association, so the stage becomes staged therapy in Lacan's return-to-Freud mode. The chapter reads the trumpet purchase as anxiety speaking through parapraxis, the street-sign and 'suck a bag of dicks' bits through Saussure's arbitrary sign and Derrida's catachresis, and Louie following Tarese home as desire that self-consciousness cannot account for.
- ch. 43 "References" *(notes)*

## Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*

- ch. 7 "Introduction Doing Philosophy in the Wasteland" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction argues that Max's journeys across the Wasteland mirror the activity of philosophy itself — frustrating, difficult, often painful, but eventually enlightening — as the man who 'runs from the living and the dead' is drawn into savior roles he tries to evade in every film. It frames the book's guiding questions (what politics could we build, what ethics could we salvage for parts after the fall) and previews essays on the franchise's politics, heroics, ethics, and aesthetics, closing on George Miller's chord of hope.
- ch. 8 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Part I POLITICS AFTER THE POX‐ECLIPSE ANARCHY, STATE, AND DYSTOPIA" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Notes" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke — Anarchism; The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Skoble argues the Mad Max world is misread as anarchy: Immortan Joe, Aunty Entity, and Humungus are genuine rulers, so the Wasteland depicts tyrannical bad government, not 'no rulers'. Against Hobbes's claim that only fear of a sovereign produces order, he cites organically evolved order (medieval merchant law, the common law, private arbitration firms) and Locke's mere 'inconveniences' of statelessness to argue peaceful anarchism is possible and stable. Thunderdome's 'two men enter, one man leaves' shows the films' dispute resolution is power-based trial by combat, not the consent-based voluntary order anarchism envisions.
- ch. 11 "Notes" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Niccolò Machiavelli, Hannah Arendt — The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Spanakos and Drake argue that although the films look Hobbesian — life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' on roads without guardrails — rule in the Wasteland is never sustained by violence alone. Humungus needs the Toadie's epithets ('Lord Humungus... the Ayatollah of Rock and Rolla') and Immortan Joe rules through water rituals and the Valhalla myth that send War Boys kamakrazee willingly, believing they pursue their own glory. Drawing Weber's power/authority distinction, Arendt on power as people acting in concert, and above all Byung-Chul Han, they argue power takes its place 'in the soul of the other' through ritual, habit, and titles, turning into violence only when mediation fails.
- ch. 12 "Notes" **·** Thomas Hobbes — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; Ethical Egoism — Littmann treats Hobbes's Leviathan as a survival manual for post-apocalyptic Australia: the films illustrate his three causes of conflict — resource wars over guzzoline and water, preemptive strikes, and glory (the Nightrider's radio rant, Wez's stunts, the War Boys' 'Witness me!'). Bartertown's Thunderdome covenant and 'bust a deal, face the wheel' exemplify the social contract enforced by an absolute sovereign like Aunty Entity, while divided power (Master Blaster versus Aunty) courts civil war. He concludes Hobbes errs twice: Max's selfless acts (sparing Blaster, transfusing Furiosa) refute psychological egoism, and concentrating power in an Immortan Joe invites the very violence it fears — democracy removes leaders without blood.
- ch. 13 "Notes" **·** Karl Marx, G.W.F. Hegel, Mahatma Gandhi, Adam Smith — Class Struggle; The Dialectic; The Invisible Hand; Climate Ethics — Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.
- ch. 14 "Notes" **·** Utopia and Dystopia — Jones argues the franchise is neither post-apocalyptic nor dystopian: fuel keeps being produced, blood can still be typed, livestock and camel trains survive the pox-eclipse, and Max can rebuild his Interceptor, so the catastrophe was devastating but never global — Perth may be untouched. Nor is it a dystopia in the sense of Mill's coining (the opposite of More's utopia), because people demonstrably choose to live there: Bartertown boasts brothels, barbers, doctors, and a working methane plant, and Aunty Entity is a soft-hearted despot who spares Max against her own decree. A world can contain dystopian communities — the Citadel, Bartertown — without being a dystopia.
- ch. 15 "Part II THE MAN WITH NO NAME HEROES AND FINDING ONESELF POST‐APOCALYPSE STYLE" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Notes" **·** Albert Camus — The Myth of Sisyphus; The Absurd — Kohoutek tests Max against two models of heroism: Joseph Campbell's 'hero with a thousand faces' and Camus's absurd hero from The Myth of Sisyphus. Max never completes the Campbellian cycle — no apotheosis, no decisive victory, no return and reintegration — because the refinery tribe and the Waiting Ones mythologize him from outside (as Messiah, as Captain Walker) while he himself returns each film to the same desert. Like Sisyphus, for whom 'the whole being is exerted toward accomplishing nothing,' Max helps people build pockets of civilization he is always shut out of, making his heroism absurd rather than archetypal.
- ch. 17 "Notes" **·** John Locke, Aristotle — Tepley uses Fury Road's body modifications — Max's muzzle and forced tattoo, his use as Nux's Bloodbag, Immortan Joe's breathing mask, the wives' chastity belts, Furiosa's prosthetic arm — to test five criteria for what makes something part of a human body: adhesion, bonding, life, function, and integration. He rejects adhesion, bonding, and function (boots and breathing masks have functions too), then defends integration — a part performs a function whose removal harms the body beyond the loss of that function — via a thought experiment about gradually replacing a brain with artificial parts. Verdict: Max's tattoo and Furiosa's detachable arm are not body parts, but a prosthesis wired into the nervous system would be.
- ch. 18 "Notes" **·** Susan Wolf, Thomas Nagel — Meaning in Life; The Meaning of Life — Berk maps Fury Road onto contemporary theories of meaning in life through three characters. Nux begins a Supernaturalist — Immortan Joe is his god and Valhalla his afterlife — collapses into nihilism after the humiliating 'Mediocre!', and ends a Naturalist who gives his life meaning by sacrificing himself to collapse the thruway and block Immortan Joe's armada. Max moves from pure survival to Susan Wolf's Hybrid Naturalism (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) when he commits to retaking the Citadel, and Furiosa, already there, embodies the film's own Objective List theory: virtue, autonomy, and relationships.
- ch. 19 "Part III BUILDING A BETTER TOMORROW! ETHICS IN MAD MAX" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Notes" **·** Carol Gilligan — The Ethics of Care; Ecofeminism; Objectification — Kolb reads the whole franchise through Carol Gilligan's ethics of care and the ecofeminism of Ariel Salleh and Mary Mellor: Max begins as a caregiver in an egalitarian marriage, Toecutter's gang and the Citadel embody toxic masculinity, and Aunty Entity shows women can administer patriarchal capitalism too. In Fury Road, 'We are not things,' the milking mothers, and water branded as Aqua Cola literalize Salleh's claim that capitalist patriarchy treats women and nature as resources. The Vuvalini, the Keeper of the Seeds, Max washing in mother's milk, and his voluntary blood transfusion to Furiosa enact the ethic of care as the film's saving alternative to domination.
- ch. 21 "Notes" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche, Thomas Hobbes — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Virtue Ethics; The Übermensch; The State of Nature — Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.
- ch. 22 "Notes" **·** Thomas Nagel, Harry Frankfurt, Susan Wolf — Moral Luck; Second-Order Desires (personhood) — Kitchen asks who is to blame in a Wasteland where Nux's 'We're not to blame!' is the standing excuse. Blaster's death in Thunderdome illustrates the problem of many hands — no one, from Max to Ironbar, was sufficient and maybe no one necessary — while Nagel's resultant, circumstantial, and constitutive luck seem to excuse War Boys indoctrinated from puphood. Applying Frankfurt's freedom of action and freedom of the will together with Susan Wolf's Real Self view through three hypothetical War Boys (Maniac, Fanatic, Addict), he argues Nux becomes praiseworthy when Capable prompts him to reflect on and revise his desires, while Immortan Joe, Slit, and the other leaders are fully responsible.
- ch. 23 "Notes" **·** Michel Foucault, Immanuel Kant — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Meyer reads the franchise through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: Max's terror of becoming a 'terminal crazy' replays madness-as-contagion, the great confinement of the mad alongside rabid animals recurs in Max's leashing and Humungus 'unleash[ing] my dogs of war,' and delirium as one step out of reason's furrow frames Johnny the Boy's 'I was sick!' plea. Applying the M'Naghten cognitive test and the wild-beast standard to Johnny the Boy, Blaster, Wez, and Nux, he concludes most followers can still tell right from wrong and remain responsible. The ultimate blame therefore falls on the cult leaders — Toecutter, Humungus, and Immortan Joe — who manufacture and exploit a shared psychosis.
- ch. 24 "Notes" **·** Plato, John Stuart Mill — Justice in the Republic; Tripartite Soul; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; The Harm Principle — Writing as a mechanic, Gordon argues Max embodies Plato's Republic: like the ship-of-state navigator, only someone who knows justice may rule, and the Myth of the Charioteer — reason holding the reins over spirit and appetite — explains why the Nightrider's unchecked spirit crashes while the cool-headed, deliberative Max endures. On punishment, Plato's rejection of retaliation (the unjust should be made just, not harmed) interrogates Max's execution of Johnny the Boy, while Polemarchus's 'render to each his due' frames the just-deserts debate. Mill's harm principle then justifies Max's force against the gangs once the state and its courts have vanished, leaving Max an administrator of street justice.
- ch. 25 "Part IV MOTHER'S MILK GENDER AND INTERSECTIONALITY" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, G.W.F. Hegel — Amor Fati (love of fate); Master–Slave Dialectic — Conway reads Fury Road as a homecoming (nostos) story that overturns Homer's patriarchal template of Odysseus: Furiosa's trusted Green Place proves as idealistic as the War Boys' Valhalla, and both are diagnosed by Nietzsche's critique of idealism as 'mendaciousness in the face of what is necessary.' The cure is amor fati joined to Max's flinty realism — turn around and make a home by retaking the Citadel — while Hegel's master-slave dialectic explains Immortan Joe's unacknowledged dependency on the women he enslaves for milk, heirs, and recognition. The film ends with Furiosa raised up as a matriarchal ruler and Max departing as the self-exiled wounded healer, barred by his own guilt from the green place he helped make.
- ch. 27 "Notes" **·** Val Plumwood — Ecofeminism; Objectification; Anthropocentrism — Quick applies Cary Wolfe's humaninized/animalized humans and Carol Adams's animalized women to the Citadel: Max is hunted, caged, and muzzled as an unnamed 'it', War Pups serve like littermates, and the milking mothers produce Adams's 'feminized protein' while the 'breeders' are groomed like show animals. Following Val Plumwood's ecofeminist critique of the masculinity that conquers mother nature — and Joe's branding of water as Aqua Cola — the chapter reads Furiosa's return to the Citadel as an ecofeminist revolution in which 'We are not things' restores women, men like Nux and Max, and nature itself from property to personhood.
- ch. 28 "Notes" **·** Kimberlé Crenshaw, bell hooks — Intersectionality; Feminism — Pérez and Jackson use Crenshaw's intersectionality to demarginalize Aunty Entity: a Black woman (Tina Turner) in an all-white franchise, she occupies the race-gender intersection invisible both to white feminism and to Black male-centered politics, and her 'Aunty' title and high cage evoke Black women's commodified emotional labor and Angelou's caged bird. Reading her through Moreton-Robinson's white possessive doctrine, hooks's 'white supremacist capitalist patriarchy,' and the Combahee River Collective — and then through hip-hop's Thunderdome trope from 2Pac's 'California Love' to Kendrick Lamar — they argue that Max's white male gaze retroactively makes her a villain, when she is in fact the franchise's most just hero.
- ch. 29 "Notes" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Judith Butler, Thomas Hobbes — One Is Not Born a Woman; Heteronormativity; The State of Nature — Held uses the Wasteland as a Hobbesian state-of-nature reset to pry apart biological sex and socially constructed gender: Aunty Entity and Furiosa show that sex is not destiny — one is not born, but becomes, a woman, as Beauvoir says — while the apocalypse scrambles gendered conventions yet leaves reproductive biology untouched. Butler's sex/gender distinction frames how a real difference like gestation gets weaponized into Immortan Joe's breeder system: the biology is a fact, the enslavement a choice. Finally, the casually acknowledged bond between Wez and the Golden Youth looks 'homoerotic' only through the viewer's heteronormativity — in the Wasteland, orientation categories simply stop mattering.
- ch. 30 "Part V WASTELAND AESTHETICS MUSIC, FASHION, AUSTRALIA, AND NATURE" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Arthur Schopenhauer — The World as Will — Belluomini analyzes how Junkie XL's score drives Fury Road aesthetically. Aristotle's Politics Book 8 and his theory of catharsis explain why the 'Bloodbag' cue's war-drum rhythms imitate the War Boys' anger and fear while purging ours, and 'emotions of appreciation' at the beauty of 'Brothers in Arms' and 'Storm Is Coming' deepen our admiration of the film. Max's cello motif — one, two, or three repeated notes — telegraphs his panic, safety, or menace and advances the plot with almost no dialogue, and Schopenhauer's claim that the right music is a scene's 'most accurate and distinct commentary' fits the hopeful 'Claw Trucks' cue as Max chooses redemption.
- ch. 32 "Notes" **·** Martin Heidegger — The Question Concerning Technology; Philosophy of Disability; Embodiment (the lived body) — Di Summa reads Jenny Beavan's costume design as philosophy of technology: Immortan Joe's oxygen-fed carapace and the chrome-spraying War Boys visualize Heidegger's warning that technology converts nature and bodies into resources, while Max's blood-drip tether to Nux literalizes our co-dependence on machines — and on each other's flesh and blood. Through Rosemarie Garland-Thomson's staring, Sherri Irvin's body aesthetics, and Tobin Siebers's disability aesthetics, Furiosa's uncovered stump becomes an act of aesthetic exploration that defeats ableism: in this film, disability is a thing for heroes, and vulnerability is itself a human strength.
- ch. 33 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Littmann asks whether the Mad Max films owe Australians an Australian feel, weighing accents (Theron's Midwestern Furiosa, Hardy's English Max), the Namibian locations of Fury Road, and the franchise's mixed debts to Australian road movies and bushranger lore versus American action cinema. Applying Aristotle's Poetics standard that characters act 'by the rule either of necessity or of probability,' he judges the improbable accents artistic faults that may still be worth their box-office payoff, and notes the saga's international gross grew as its Australianness faded. On representation, he argues that if seeing Australians matters for building sympathy, the same must hold for Indonesians, Pakistanis, and Brazilians — and leaves the question open.
- ch. 34 "Notes" **·** Nick Bostrom, Immanuel Kant — Respect for Persons — Koepsell argues the franchise stages the bioconservatism-versus-transhumanism debate: the villains are machine-altered (Immortan Joe's breathing gear, the People Eater's prosthetic nose, Master Blaster's contraption) while the saved live green and unmodified, so George Miller's films side with Leon Kass's bioconservatism against Nick Bostrom's transhumanist embrace of enhancement. Dignity — derived from Kant and contested between Kass and Bostrom — is the hinge, and the recurring green places (the family farm, the Sunshine Coast, the Crack in the Earth, the Green Place) mark the dignity of nature the Wasteland destroyed. The bioconservative lesson holds even though Max and Furiosa, patched with prosthetics, must partially embrace their posthuman condition to survive.
- ch. 35 "Index" *(notes)*

## Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Mad Men and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright Page" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Introduction" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors introduce the volume by framing Mad Men as a show that immerses viewers in the morally ambiguous world of 1960 Madison Avenue, where we find ourselves rooting for Don Draper to sell cigarettes, hide affairs, and conceal his stolen identity while cringing at the office's treatment of women. They argue the series teaches uncomfortable truths about the early 1960s (drinking, smoking, systemic sexism, racism, homophobia) while dramatizing how people experienced era-defining events as they happened, and so helps us understand both past and present. The chapters that follow, they say, are written by fans for fans who want to think further about the role of women, the morality of advertising, and how to lead a meaningful life.
- ch. 8 "PART ONE - “PEOPLE MAY SEE THINGS DIFFERENTLY, BUT THEY DON’T REALLY WANT TO”" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "“It’s Like Watching a Dog Play the Piano”" *(no index entry yet)* — Schurtz argues the Mad Men characters are not stupid but epistemically bounded by what their era counts as a reason: Don dismisses Dr. Guttman's 'death wish' research (and the proto-Marlboro-Man danger angle) because a research psychologist's testimony does not register as expertise for him, and the senior partners ignore Pete's correctly pro-Kennedy insight because a junior account executive's word is not a justifier. Working through knowledge as justified true belief (Betty is justified but wrong to believe her husband is Don Draper), the chapter moves from epistemic individualism to social epistemology (testimony, expert disagreement) and finally standpoint epistemology, illustrated by the Belle Jolie secretaries whose 'moron' insight Peggy vindicates with the winning pitch. The upshot: sexism, closeted gay life (Salvatore in 'The Hobo Code'), and Betty's dry-cleaning-bag ignorance persist because 1960 society does not distribute justifying testimony to women, the young, or the marginalized.
- ch. 10 "“All That Is Solid Melts into Air”" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Karl Marx — Tripartite Soul; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Dunn reads Mad Men through Plato's Republic: the passions are the 'mad masters' Cephalus describes, embodied in Pete Campbell's au pair indiscretion and remorse, and because passions cannot tell staged appearance from reality, the mimetic perfection of Don's 'You're a whore' scene with Betty grips viewers exactly as Plato feared televised drama would, watering the parts of the soul that should be ruled. He extends the point to advertising: Don's 'I make pictures where people appear to be in love' and 'love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' work because mimesis bypasses reason and attaches feeling to images, while Aristotle's account of imitation shows drama can also train virtue by making us delight in what we should. Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air' frames the title sequence, where Don's office dissolves past advertising images revealed as empty simulacra, until the final shot restores the convincing façade of his confidence.
- ch. 11 "Bringing Corporations and Government Together" **·** Compatibilism; Free Will vs Determinism — Guilfoy stages Galbraith's The Affluent Society against Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom through the Heineken case: Don's end-aisle display made Betty serve the beer at her dinner party, and when she found out she had been the target demographic she accused him ('You embarrassed me'). Galbraith's deep-self compatibilism holds that advertising-created desires are not genuinely ours, so Betty's choice was unfree, and that consumerism produces private wealth amid public squalor (the Cadillac picnic litter scene, the Madison Square Garden account Lane kills for lack of profit); Friedman's libertarian free will answers that Betty simply chose, desires are reasons rather than causes, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch shows the market punishing racist irrationality. Both economists converge on the danger dramatized in 'The Inheritance': when Sterling Cooper sells corporations to congressmen and congressmen to corporations, consumers lose under either theory.
- ch. 12 "PART TWO - “THERE IS NO BIG LIE, THERE IS NO SYSTEM, THE UNIVERSE IS" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "“Have Done” with the Past" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Ressentiment — Fritz applies Nietzsche's On the Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life and the Genealogy to the dialectic of remembering and forgetting: Pete cannot 'have done' with anything, so Ken Cosgrove's Atlantic Monthly story and Peggy's promotion become 'vermin' that eat into him, his reactive rancor and entitlement driving him to make Trudy broker his bad talking-bear story. Peggy is the opposite extreme of active forgetting, from not registering her own pregnancy to telling Pete flatly 'I had your baby and I gave it away. I wanted other things,' after Don's hospital advice that 'This never happened. It'll shock you how much this never happened.' Don knows forgetting is the strength of strong natures (the $5,000 offer to Adam, 'my life only goes in one direction, forward'), yet the Carousel's home-movie slides and other external triggers keep forcing the past back on him, so only Peggy fully inhabits the Nietzschean ideal.
- ch. 14 "Existential Values" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Martin Heidegger — The Stages on Life's Way; Authenticity; The Last Man; Will to Power — Belliotti tests Roger Sterling against three existential standards. Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage fits him 'crisply': his quips about the chase, drinking 'because it's what men do,' and the penny-jar view of marriage reveal flight from commitment and terror of boredom, and even his twenty-year marriage to Mona lacked Kierkegaard's passionate inwardness, making it objectively true but existentially inauthentic. Measured by Nietzsche he falls between the last man who wants an agency 'where everybody has a summer house' and the will-to-power grand transcender he never becomes, oscillating between frustration and boredom; measured by Heidegger he settles for chatter, clings to fixity, and reflects on mortality only briefly after his heart attacks. The verdict: significantly inauthentic, capped by the blackface 'My Old Kentucky Home' serenade that makes Don whisper 'Can we go?'
- ch. 15 "The Universe Is Not Indifferent" **·** Ethical Egoism; Virtue Ethics — White takes Bert Cooper's shelf display of Atlas Shrugged seriously and argues, against Cooper's claim that Don is 'completely self-interested,' that Don is the conventional image of the egoist rather than a Randian one: he is a second-hander whose stolen identity makes his life a lie, so Betty is married to a man who does not exist and only Anna Draper, who sees Dick Whitman, gives him psychological visibility. Objectivism's primacy of existence explains why every lie collides with facts (the train recognition, Adam's newspaper photo, the misplaced dog-tag parcel) and why Don's 'ruthlessness' and the 'indifferent universe' he complains of are products of his own vices, since what is, is. The chapter walks through Rand's virtues (rationality, independence, honesty, productiveness, pride, self-esteem grounded in objective self-appraisal, not the 'whore-child' label) to show Don sought spiritual gain through deceit and so placed his self-esteem against reality.
- ch. 16 "Television and Existential Awakening" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Jean-Paul Sartre, Herbert Marcuse, Immanuel Kant — Bad Faith; Woman as the Other; One-Dimensional Man; Objectification — Jaarsma argues Mad Men dramatizes an existential rather than Kantian-enlightenment model of advertising: Don's 'freedom from fear' pitch ('Whatever you are doing is okay. You are okay') sells escape from the anxiety of real choice, which is precisely Sartrean bad faith and what de Beauvoir calls the stagnant 'happiness' of women rewarded for being the other. Betty on her psychiatrist's couch, Peggy measured by Joan's paper-bag mirror and the Playtex bullet-bra silhouette, and the closeted Salvatore all internalize the dominant values Marcuse describes, finding meaning in conformity to the objectifying gaze ('bras are for men; women want to see themselves the way men see them'). Rachel Menken, who refuses to 'put on an apron' and calls out the contingency of gendered embodiment, models authenticity as choosing to choose, and the chapter closes with the hope that television itself can occasion the viewer's existential awakening.
- ch. 17 "PART THREE - “AND YOU KNOW WHAT HAPPINESS IS ” MAD MEN AND ETHICS" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "The Question of Ethical Advertising" **·** Immanuel Kant — Respect for Persons; Humanity as an End in Itself; The Categorical Imperative — Novakovic and Whitney use the Heineken incident, where Betty discovers she was the target demographic for her husband's campaign ('Must be so funny, being in on it'), to test advertising against Kantian honesty and respect. Kant's humanity formula and the lying-promise example show that manipulation wrongs the consumer as a rational agent, and Don's defense that advertising sells 'happiness' fails because Kant allows making others' happiness an end but never at the cost of truth, whether the consumer is a stranger or a wife. The chapter sets this against the era's brainwashing anxieties (Hunter's Brainwashing in Red China, Packard's The Hidden Persuaders, Precon subliminal projection) and concludes that honest advertising must survive disclosure of its methods, noting that real sponsors like Canada Dry and BMW responded to the show with stripped-down 'transparent' ads that let viewers be 'in on it.'
- ch. 19 "Each of Us Would See Ourselves" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Martin Heidegger, Karl Marx — The Übermensch; The Question Concerning Technology; Master and Slave Morality; The Apollonian and the Dionysian — The Teschners cast Don as a Nietzschean creator of value in technological culture: his nihilism ('There is no big lie. There is no system. The universe is indifferent') and 'What you call love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' embody anti-foundationalism, while the beatnik Roy plays the resentful slave mentality whose passion lives only off what it despises. Don's creative process (sleep on it, 'forget it, and an idea will jump in your face') mirrors the camel-lion-child metamorphoses of Zarathustra, and the collapse of the principium individuationis explains his fluid identities from Dick Whitman to the 'Adam and Eve' fantasy with Rachel. Heidegger's techné frames the Kodak Carousel as genuine art, a revealing that transfigures 'a hell of a gadget' into 'a place where we know we are loved,' at the tragic price of a man outside community, and the falling figure of the credits is one 'we would each see ourselves' in.
- ch. 20 "“The Wrong Direction”" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Deontology — Barkman builds a definition of lying (communicating what one believes false while hiding that fact, with intent to hurt or disrespect, which distinguishes mere deception and parts ways with Aquinas's blanket ban) and applies it to five advertising worries, from bags of chips designed to invite false inference to the Belle Jolie 'promise' no one actually believes and the Israeli Tourism ad that omits danger. Persuasion is legitimate because rational souls are equals to be treated as ends (Aristotle's justice), but manipulation (ads aimed at preschoolers that use children to pressure parents) and fear-preying coercion (Clearasil on insecure teenagers, nylons to unmarried women like Rachel Menken) treat people as means, while government must regulate factually (FDA 'smoking kills' labels) without overriding adult choice. Responsibility is then distributed across producer, agency, media, public, and state, and Don was indeed 'looking in the wrong direction' in this sense: being able to talk anyone into anything does not mean he should.
- ch. 21 "Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel" **·** Plato, Aristotle, David Hume — Virtue Ethics; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Terjesen asks whether Don is a good man, testing his mixed record (egalitarian instincts, loyalty to Mohawk Airlines, protecting Horace Jr., against habitual adultery and the stolen identity) through Aristotle's habituation, Plato's Protagoras unity-of-virtues theses, Hume's sensible knave, and John Doris's situationist attack on global character traits. The unity theses imply Don's vices undermine his virtues (affairs make him unavailable when Betty crashes; evasions about his past block honesty), and Doris's dime-in-the-payphone literature suggests even Don's reliability may be circumstance-bound, as with Pete's weddings-and-vacations-only philandering. Against full situationism, Don's consistent rules (never forcing women, valuing women he genuinely finds interesting) point to 'regional' traits, yet Roger's verdict stands: 'You're no good with relationships because you don't value them,' since Don runs family on a business code, from Adam's bribe to 'that's what people do' consolation for Pete.
- ch. 22 "Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle" **·** Albert Camus, Alasdair MacIntyre, Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Virtue Ethics; The Absurd — Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.
- ch. 23 "PART FOUR - “NO ONE ELSE IS SAYING THE RIGHT THING ABOUT THIS” MAD MEN AND" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "“To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”" **·** Aristotle, Carol Gilligan — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The Ethics of Care; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Myers grades the moral development of the Sterling Cooper cast with Kohlberg's justice stages and Gilligan's ethics of care in order to find Aristotelian friendships, which require equals in moral development who wish each other good for the other's sake. Don and Peggy emerge as moral equivalents, each hiding a dark secret (the stolen identity; the baby given away) and each having done for the other what no one else could, from the hospital visit ('Move forward') to Don's 'nobody understands that, but you do' recruitment pitch; Joan and Roger form a second pair whose mutual esteem survives his marriage to Jane and her departure, shown when he trusts her to build Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce. Closing with Aristotle's claim that friendship holds states together, the chapter gives the new agency a better-than-average chance because these friendships are 'not for sale.'
- ch. 25 "Don’t Go Mad" **·** Aristotle — Objectification; Feminism — Barkman applies a qualified Aristotelian standard of justice, that women possessing rational souls must be treated as equals, to Peggy, Betty, and Joan as second-wave feminism dawns. Peggy is the 'mad woman' in the best sense: she demands a desk, equal pay ('You have everything and so much of it'), and Don's apology while never resorting to blackmail like Pete, whereas Betty is repressed at home by a husband who shows her off ('I want to show you off, Betts') and Joan suppresses herself, measuring worth by appearance and enduring Greg's violation until the vase incident. The sexual objectification Peggy faces from her first day (Ken's elevator leers, Joan's paper-bag advice, the panty-hunt in 'Nixon vs. Kennedy') is the chapter's core injustice, and the warning is that women who cannot stand up to it may simply go mad.
- ch. 26 "What’s on the Horizon" *(no index entry yet)* — Carveth traces race across three seasons: Carla and Hollis are seen but not heard in season one, Paul's Mississippi Freedom Ride with Sheila plays out in season two, and season three brings Roger's blackface 'My Old Kentucky Home' and Pete's Admiral 'Negro market' pitch, which the client kills with 'monkey see, monkey do' and Cooper with 'no interest in becoming a colored television company.' The chapter argues the show practices differential racialization, black characters existing to support white ones without backstories (Carla silenced with 'This is not a conversation I am going to have with you,' Sheila reduced to proof Paul is interesting), while anti-Semitism gets more multidimensional treatment through Rachel Menken's 'we thrive at doing business with people who hate us.' Hollis mourning Marilyn Monroe yet silent on Medgar Evers illustrates race as a social construction and his silence as hiding in plain sight, and the chapter faults Mad Men for softening Northern racism while hoping season four moves forward.
- ch. 27 "“I’m Enjoying the Story So Far, but I Have a Feeling It’s Not Going to End Well”" **·** Plato — Justice in the Republic; Tripartite Soul — South uses 'New Amsterdam' to examine how social convention, not personal authority, constrains agency: Bert Cooper's 'New York City is a marvelous machine' and 'There are other rules... His mother is Dorothy Dyckman Campbell' reveal that Pete's value lies in a name he doesn't understand, just as Don's authority dissolves before forces neither he nor Pete consented to. Reading through Plato's Republic city-soul analogy and Adeimantus's warning that changes in music insinuate themselves 'little by little' into character and laws, the chapter shows Pete missing the worth of his old-family name, the Bethlehem Steel man missing that steel cannot be advertised like flour, and Don, despite seizing a fresh identity, quietly conforming to the suburban corporate script he claims never to have envisioned. The Kennedy-assassination pitch to Peggy ('The way that they saw themselves is gone') and Conrad Hilton's 'It's business' close on Plato's caution: the city's gears keep turning, and 'people don't change' may be the show's last word.
- ch. 28 "Appendix It’s Not a List of Titles and Air Dates; It’s An Episode Guide" *(front)*

## Mark Twain and Philosophy

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "17_177_00a_HT" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "17_177_00a_Srs" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "17_177_00b_Ttl" *(not yet read)*

- ch. 6 "17_177_00d_Ded" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 7 "Contents" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 8 "Introduction" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); The Problem of Evil — Alan Goldman's editorial introduction previews the volume's essays, framing Twain as a serious philosopher hidden behind humor and irony. It lays out the Huckleberry Finn debate over whether Huck's refusal to turn in Jim is weak-willed conscience versus reason-bearing sympathy (Bennett, Goldman, Fudge, Lyons, Gehrman), then Twain's late attacks on religion via Letters from the Earth and the problem of evil, plus essays on lying, animal rights, humor, and comparisons to Diogenes, the Epicureans, Nietzsche, and Hume. It treats these as genuine philosophical stakes drawn from Twain's fiction and late writings.
- ch. 9 "Part I Morality in Huckleberry Finn" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Chapter 1 The Conscience of Huckleberry Finn" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Moral Relativism — Jonathan Bennett reads the chapter 16 raft episode as a clash between 'bad morality' and sympathy: Huck's conscience (slave-owning principles telling him to return Jim to Miss Watson) supplies all the reasons, while his sympathy for Jim is a bare, reasonless feeling that wins by weakness of will, so Huck does right while believing he does wrong. He contrasts Huck with Himmler, whose bad morality overrode his surviving sympathy, and Jonathan Edwards, whose Calvinist approval of eternal damnation left no sympathy to conflict. The lesson is that principles should be kept open to revision under pressure from sympathy, since one cannot declare one's own morality bad but should stay open to correction.
- ch. 11 "Chapter 2 Huckleberry Finn and Moral Motivation" **·** Immanuel Kant — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Reason Is the Slave of the Passions — Alan Goldman argues against Bennett and against Arpaly and Schroeder that Huck is not weak-willed or irrational: his sympathy for Jim is an intentional emotion containing implicit judgments and awareness of the genuine moral reasons to help Jim, so Huck acts on his strongest reasons and is courageous rather than akratic. Because Huck is rational yet not motivated by his explicit (corrupt) moral judgments, and his real motivation comes only through emotional attachment, Goldman concludes against Kant that moral motivation is not rationally required. He uses Huck's failure to extend concern to other slaves, and analogies to meat-eaters and arbitrary aesthetic taste, to show moral inconsistency is not practical irrationality.
- ch. 12 "Chapter 3 Sympathy, Principles, and Conscience" **·** Adam Smith — The Impartial Spectator; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Robert Fudge uses Adam Smith to reinterpret Huck's conscience and praiseworthiness. Against Bennett (conscience as accepted principles) and Arpaly-Schroeder (inverse akrasia via a whole-self theory), Fudge argues, following Smith, that conscience is the sentiment-based judgment of the 'man within the breast,' the impartial spectator, and that propriety rests on sympathetic 'feeling with' others rather than abstract principle. Huck's sympathy for Jim in the chapter 16 raft scene is a reason-bearing emotion, so he is not acting akratically or against his true conscience; instead he is growing morally, molding his conscience toward the loyalty and friendship that already constitute his core self.
- ch. 13 "Chapter 4 Huckleberry Finn’s Struggle between Sympathy and Moral Principle Reconsidered" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Consequentialism — Michael Lyons defends the 'pedestal' of moral principles against Bennett's chapter 16 reading. He accepts that sympathy rightly saved Jim and that Edwards's principled cruelty and Himmler's suppressed sympathy show principles must be revisable, but rejects the stronger claim that sympathy should override conduct while leaving conflicting principles intact. Reconstructing Bennett's argument into 'stronger' and 'adjusted' versions, Lyons argues principles remain the best primary guide once corrected by sympathy, and that Twain shows Huck retaining a natural, humanity-grounded morality even after rejecting society's 'deformed conscience.' He prizes incorruptibility, sticking to correct principles, as the mark of the highest heroism Huck could aspire to.
- ch. 14 "Chapter 5 Twain’s Last Laugh" **·** Aristotle, Socrates, Arne Naess — Socratic Method (elenchus); Virtue Ethics (arete); Double Consciousness — Kristina Gehrman argues that reading Huck as a moral hero who overcomes racism is Twain's ironic trap. Using Arne Naess's idea of identification, Aristotle on habituation of character, and Iris Murdoch's 'just and loving attention,' she gives a developmentally attuned reading of Huck as a traumatized, morally immature, still-racist child whose regard for Jim never generalizes ('I knowed he was white inside'). Twain lures his white readers into identifying with Huck's supposed triumph, then exposes their own stunted moral growth about race; Jim is the only mature adult yet is barred from identification by the novel's racist caricature. The novel's greatness is Socratic and gadfly-like rather than triumphant.
- ch. 15 "Part II Twain on Religion" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates, David Hume — Faith and Reason; The Unexamined Life; The Problem of Evil — Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.
- ch. 17 "Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil" **·** Albert Camus, Augustine of Hippo, David Hume, Plotinus — The Problem of Evil; Rebellion and Revolt; Fate and Foreknowledge — James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.
- ch. 18 "Part III Moral Issues" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Chapter 8 The Noble Art of Lying" **·** John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — James Edwin Mahon reconstructs Twain's two essays on lying ('On the Decay of the Art of Lying' and 'My First Lie') into a philosophy of lying. Twain holds that everyone lies constantly, that lying need not be spoken or deceptive (the 'silent lie,' nondeceptive polite lies, acts as lies, and 'modified' lies/palters), and that the gravest lies are the 'silent National Lies' such as the collective silence that slavery was not unjust. Mahon shows Twain's ethics of lying is broadly utilitarian and Rossian: guided by nonmaleficence and beneficence, an injurious truth is no better than an injurious lie, and self-sacrificing lies that help others are virtuous, so lying should be practiced as a cultivated art.
- ch. 20 "Chapter 9 Twain’s Critique of Human Exceptionalism" **·** Peter Singer, Jeremy Bentham, René Descartes, Michel de Montaigne, Tom Regan — Speciesism; Anthropocentrism; Animal Liberation; Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life) — VanDette argues that Twain's late anti-vivisection writings anticipate posthumanist animal ethics by inverting the Darwinian species hierarchy. Through 'Letters from a Dog,' the essay 'Man's Place in the Animal World,' his 1899 London Anti-Vivisection Society letter, and the mother-dog narrator Aileen in 'A Dog's Tale,' Twain gives animals voice and subjectivity to attack human exceptionalism. His refusal to weigh vivisection's benefit against animal pain echoes Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', while his target is the Cartesian view of animals as insensible machines and the evolutionary logic used to justify experiments; Dr. Gray's cold killing of Aileen's puppy indicts a science that deadens compassion.
- ch. 21 "Part IV Literary Devices" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, Arthur Schopenhauer, David Hume, Socrates, Democritus, Bertrand Russell — Existentialism; Bad Faith; The Problem of Evil; Philosophical Skepticism — Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.
- ch. 23 "Chapter 11 Socratic Irony in Twain’s Skeptical Religious Jeremiads" **·** Socrates — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Socratic Method (elenchus); Philosophical Skepticism — Jacquette demands a precise definition of Twain's much-invoked irony, adopting Vlastos's/Quintilian's formula that irony says the contrary of what is meant while letting the real meaning be recovered. He classifies Twain's irony as local vs. global and comic vs. sober (tragic/historical): 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc' is globally ironic (falsely presented as de Conte's eyewitness manuscript), while the relic-mocking passages of 'The Innocents Abroad' (St. Luke's Madonna, kegs of true-cross nails, three skulls of John the Baptist) are local comic irony. Jacquette concludes Twain's irony is distinctively Socratic: like Socrates interpreting the Delphic oracle, Twain makes a moral and epistemic virtue of ridiculing experts who claim to know what no one can know about God, sin, and the afterlife.
- ch. 24 "Part V Comparison to Other Philosophers" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Chapter 12 The American Diogenes" **·** Diogenes the Cynic, Epicurus, Socrates — Cynicism (living according to nature); Death Is Nothing to Us; Stoic Cosmopolitanism (citizens of the world) — Johnson argues Twain is best understood not as a religious skeptic but as an 'American Diogenes'—a Cynic of Christianity-as-practiced. As Diogenes 'defaced the coinage' to remove counterfeit customs, Twain uses 'sacred profanity' (honest, even profane speech that exposes phony piety, e.g. the swearing butcher, Satanic narrators in 'The Mysterious Stranger' and 'Letters from the Earth') to strike four counterfeit coins: superstition/special providence, hypocrisy, artificial 'Moral Sense'/conscience, and heavenly rewards. On death Twain matches Diogenes and Epicurus (annihilation is nothing to fear), and his self-description as 'Member at Large for the Human Race' mirrors Diogenes the cosmopolitan; Diogenes carries a lantern to find a real human, Twain a mirror to show we are worse than we think.
- ch. 26 "Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life" **·** Epicurus, Lucretius, Martha Nussbaum — Death Is Nothing to Us; Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Virtue Ethics; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.
- ch. 27 "Chapter 14 Moral Value and Moral Psychology in Twain’s “Carnival of Crime”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, David Hume — Master and Slave Morality; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); The Übermensch — Boardman treats Twain's 'The Facts Concerning the Recent Carnival of Crime in Connecticut'—in which a narrator kills his personified conscience (a shabby dwarf) and gleefully commits a spree of crimes—as staging an 'exasperating metaphysical question' about the value and psychology of morality. On a Nietzschean reading the narrator becomes an Overman revaluing values, seeing conscience as the internalized lie of slave morality; on a Humean reading conscience is moral feeling (not reason), so once it is destroyed the narrator can still reason about right yet has no motive to act morally, illustrating the oak-tree and willful-murder arguments that vice lies in sentiment, not relations or facts. Boardman concludes both interpretations fit yet neither settles whether Twain endorses or lampoons the result—our horror at the crimes is what makes the story funny.
- ch. 28 "Chapter 15 Making the Heart Grow Fonder" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Subjectivity Is Truth — Dueck reads Twain's 'Life on the Mississippi'—where mastering the river as a pilot drains away its beauty, like a doctor who sees a face as a medical case—through Edward Bullough's aesthetic principle of 'psychical distance,' the balance between under-distancing (practical absorption) and over-distancing (cold abstraction) that makes experience aesthetic. He argues knowledge need not kill wonder if we re-establish distance, and that Twain's fiction ('Tom Sawyer,' 'Huckleberry Finn,' 'The Prince and the Pauper,' 'A Connecticut Yankee') itself creates the right distance. He links this to Kierkegaard's 'indirect communication': humor, irony and story convey existential, subjective truth that the reader must 'undo the knot' to grasp, so that distance makes the heart grow fonder and the mind wiser.
- ch. 29 "Notes" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "About the Editor and Contributors" *(notes)*

## Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Martial Arts and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" **·** Socrates, Plato, Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Buddhism; Stoicism; Utilitarianism — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- ch. 6 "Enter the Dragon - Traditional Asian Martial Arts" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" **·** Aristotle, Confucius, The Buddha — Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Li (ritual propriety); Virtue Ethics (arete); Zen Buddhism — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" **·** The Buddha — Zen Buddhism; Non-Self (anatman); Emptiness (sunyata); Compassion (karuna) — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- ch. 9 "A Koan" **·** Zen Buddhism — Finnigan and Tanaka use the kendo student Kenzo, struck down whenever he thinks 'Now is the time to strike!', to pose the puzzle of intentional action without thought. They set Donald Davidson's causal theory of action (intentions as belief-desire causes) against Takuan Soho's mushin, which warns that wherever you put your mind it stops, then resolve it: training lets a master act 'as Yagyu would', and giving reasons afterwards is how one accepts responsibility for an action no reason was 'in mind' for. The koan dissolves once how-questions (how could I act without thinking?) are distinguished from why-questions (why did you do that?).
- ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" **·** Plato, The Buddha — Tripartite Soul; Non-Self (anatman); The Philosopher King; Zen Buddhism — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- ch. 11 "Knowledge and Mastery" *(no index entry yet)* — Schubert asks what his own master's certificate actually certified and dismantles two accounts of martial mastery: the 'Secret Knowledge' account (hidden teachings like Crouching Tiger's stolen Wu Dan manual) and the 'Complete Knowledge' account, which absurdly implies mastery is suspended when a new takedown joins the syllabus or his forgetful Iaido master omits a step of a form. Using the distinction between knowing-that, knowing-how and physical ability (he knew how to jump-spin heel-kick with his foot in a cast), he argues mastery is knowing that and how across the essential techniques, principles and strategies a style could have consisted of, by analogy with fluency in a language. Rank, politics and even the ability to perform are at best signs of mastery, not the thing itself.
- ch. 12 "The Karate Kid - Character and Education" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "An Enemy Lying in Ambush" **·** Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Zeno of Citium, Seneca — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control — Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.
- ch. 14 "Don’t Carry the World upon Your Shoulders. Only Your Opponent" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle; The Hedonic Calculus — Cooper and Taylor argue that Kano's judo principles, seiryokuzenyou (maximum efficiency) and jitakyouei (mutual welfare and benefit), echo Bentham's principle of utility: both men swept away archaic rules to reach one efficient ethical goal, and Kano accepted the comparison. They run the hedonic calculus over training bruises versus the joy of a clean throw, use Mill's secondary principles as rule-utilitarian guidelines (release the armbar at the tap rather than calculating each time), and answer the objection that utilitarianism demands too much with Kano's own ethos: like judo, it is about continual improvement, not impossible maximization.
- ch. 15 "Living the Absurd Life" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche — Existentialism; Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd; Authenticity — Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.
- ch. 16 "The Last Resort" **·** Michel Foucault — Feminism; Power/Knowledge — Petersen recounts fighting off a man who threatened to rape and kill her, and argues that karate, not feminist doctrine or therapy, made her a real feminist by rewiring her self-concept, fear responses and relationships. Against the Lara Croft fantasy she sets practical self-defense doctrine ('don't be there'; assertiveness, not aggression, with the bus pest), Australian, US and UN statistics on violence against women, and the Guthrie study of Chicago's feminist Thousand Waves dojo. She frames the transformation with Foucault's 'care of the self': karate's practices of the self give women power through knowledge, so that by black-belt time enduring harassment simply 'isn't who she is'.
- ch. 17 "The Way of the Place" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete) — Beattie uses Henri Lefebvre's account of the production of space to read the dojo as a 'differential space' practitioners actively create against abstract, conformist space. He shows how bow-ins, founder portraits, Japanese counting, mats, dogi and belt hierarchies mark ownership, bind the school to a lineage, separate 'dojo' from 'street', and shape bodies and safety (with Kendo's door-side seating and MMA's display of physique as hierarchy written into space). Play matters too: Aristotle's point that virtues are built by habit explains how playing at combat in a safe place breeds real courage, and the whole exercise teaches a moving balance between inside and outside.
- ch. 18 "The Perfect Weapon - Ethics and Value" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Back at the Bins, or Loving Your Enemy Like Your Neighbor" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Hannah Arendt, Immanuel Kant — The Face of the Other; The Categorical Imperative — Kohn begins with her own response to a serial bin-tipper: practicing iaido sword draws in full view of the neighbours to intimidate an imagined Other. Contrasting iaido's virtual opponent (a mere tool for the self) with aikido's real partners, she deploys Levinas's face of the Other, responsibility without waiting for reciprocity and philosophy as 'the Wisdom of Love', alongside Arendt's shared responsibility for the world's conflicts, to argue that care for even one's attacker comes first, with Kant's categorical imperative as the generalizable counterpart to Levinas's ethics. Her confession: she treated the imagined culprit as an object of hate, when meeting 'the Face' would have demanded an apology and maybe a hug.
- ch. 20 "Why It Matters" **·** The Buddha — Russell, who at eleven believed practice would let her kill a bull with one blow, argues that martial arts culture systematically breeds epistemic vices: gullibility (ki knockouts, chocolate milk for recovery), closed-mindedness, dojos treated like churches, sunk-cost defence of the side-kick-knifes-from-hands story, and deference to sensei and founders (Funakoshi curing fevers with karate). She diagnoses data-poverty, since lethal techniques cannot be ethically tested, as the enabling condition, and prescribes cautious belief, closing with the Buddha's counsel from Harry Cook's dojo wall: believe nothing on the authority of masters alone. It matters because these are beliefs about what can injure and kill.
- ch. 21 "The Moving Shadow of Truth" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Aristotle, Michel Foucault, René Descartes — The Dialectic; Mind–Body Dualism; Embodiment (the lived body); Discipline and Docile Bodies — Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.
- ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" **·** The Buddha — Buddhism; Zen Buddhism; Karma and Rebirth — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- ch. 23 "Living Beauty" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Pythagoras — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Yin and Yang — Saltzman explains why a flowing Shaolin Kenpo form is beautiful by way of Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: the Apollonian geometry of square, triangle and circle fuses with Dionysian power and intention, just as yang hardness needs yin softness. She grounds the body's fitness for this in the Golden Ratio known to Pythagoras, answers 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' with Clive Bell's 'significant form' as an objective structure that trained judges can recognize, and locates 'living beauty' in the practitioner's own breakthrough, the moment when, as Nietzsche and Yeats agree, the dancer and the dance dissolve into pure mindless movement.
- ch. 24 "Excalibur - Western Martial Arts" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Jousting for Virtue" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.
- ch. 26 "Boxing, a School for Virtues" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean — Marino answers colleagues who call college boxing 'teaching violence' with an Aristotelian defense: courage is the mean between fearlessness and excessive fear, and the ring is one of the few workshops where fear is actually practiced. He cites Wacquant's boxing gym as 'a school of morality' in Durkheim's sense, Rotella's 'education at the fights', and boxers like Maja Cavlovic and George Foreman on how training takes over when fear hits, to argue boxing forges emotional self-command. His challenge to his own students: 'How can you be consistently honest or just if you don't have the mettle to take a hit?'
- ch. 27 "Is Fencing a Dishonorable Art" **·** Thomas Hobbes — Ethical Egoism; The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Michaud argues that fencing is the loneliest and most egoistic martial art: alone on the strip, you seek to understand your opponent only in order to deceive them through disengages and parry-feints. He maps the bout onto Hobbes: psychological egoism, the dueling ground as a state of nature of 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', and the referee as the Leviathan whose rules keep the bloodshed out while licensing normative egoism inside them. Testing defenses from Rand, Friedman and Carr's business 'rules of the game', he concludes that fencing kept its soldier's anything-goes ethos after the lethal stakes vanished, making it a 'dishonorable' art: a Hobbesian feast of solitude, egoism and deception.
- ch. 28 "The Personality of the Épée" *(no index entry yet)* — Lawrence asks why anyone practices the épée, an 'unmartial martial art' with no self-defense payoff, one-sided exercise value, and only stylized descent from dueling to first blood (unlike foil and saber's artificial targets and right-of-attack rules). His three answers: fencing uniquely rewards psychology, timing and dexterity over strength and pain-endurance (he prefers Odysseus's guile to Ajax's force); it continues a Bronze-Age tradition ('the history of the sword is the history of mankind'); and the named swords of epic, from Excalibur to Sting, point to the weapon's distinctive personality of courage, honor, deadliness, aesthetic fitness for purpose, and an intimacy with the opponent that Housman's saber-duel poem captures.
- ch. 29 "Back to Square One" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham — Moss concedes fencing's romantic dueling aura, noting that Kant classed a killing in a duel as mere manslaughter, Bentham proposed giving duelists the protection of self-defense for the sake of honor, and Rousseau and Schopenhauer sneered at the whole business. But he argues the sport's uniqueness lies not in honor, psychology or combat origins, which it shares with other martial arts, but in a combination of rules: the blade-set distance between fencers, protective gear that makes them effectively invulnerable, right-of-way, and the return to a neutral start after each point. That combination allows the complex 'phrases' of feint and disengage that make fencing 'physical chess'; what is unique, he concludes, is a matter of rules, not romance.
- ch. 30 "And in the Blue Corner, Wearing the White Pants" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "The University of Hard Knocks" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Fighting Index" *(notes)*
