- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Once More into the Time Vortex" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction: it surveys what changed since the first Doctor Who and Philosophy volume (the War Doctor, the Trenzalore death and survival, the Impossible Girl, Dalek divine hatred, the Master becoming 'the Mistress') and previews the volume's questions—whether Clara is possible, whether the Doctor may lie, whether he could have avoided Trenzalore, and whether the Ninth Doctor's 'coward, any day' pacifism gave way to the Twelfth's less-pacifistic cowboy streak. It also introduces the fandom insiders (podcasters, convention runners, a Time Lord Rock musician) who serve as 'Time Lord Presiding' over each Serial, framing the book around the show's emphasis on personal identity and time paradoxes.
- ch. 8 "Serial 1 The Real Never-Ending Story" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Magnetic North" **·** Virtue Ethics; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.
- ch. 10 "1. A Good Man Goes to War" **·** Virtue Ethics; The Ethics of Political Violence — Pless argues the Doctor's shift from the Ninth's self-avowed 'coward, any day' to the Eleventh's gun-toting action hero tracks real-world politics and markets rather than internal story logic: after the 7/7 London bombings and amid the War on Terror, and as the show's global export grew, a war-weary British ideal gave way to the decisive 'Oncoming Storm.' She traces the arc through the Tenth's gleeful xenocide of the Racnoss in 'The Runaway Bride,' the eternal punishment of the Family of Blood, the Eleventh brainwashing humanity to exterminate the Silence in 'Day of the Moon,' and the assault of 'A Good Man Goes to War,' before 'The Day of the Doctor' retcons the Time War so the Doctor never destroyed the Time Lords, validating the action-hero persona. Her conclusion: in a crisis culture demanding proactive heroes, cowardice—once the Doctor's honest self-assessment—was rebranded as vice.
- ch. 11 "2. How Time Lords Invented TV" *(no index entry yet)* — Dray reads Doctor Who as a metaphor for television itself: the Doctor and his box emerge from a junkyard just after FCC chairman Newton Minow called TV a 'vast wasteland,' and the show turns the medium's supposed weaknesses—shaky effects, departing actors, budget limits—into its fiction, most famously converting William Hartnell's failing health into regeneration. Following 'An Unearthly Child' through the cancellation-era New Adventures novels, the flawed 1996 TV movie, and the Davies and Moffat eras (including Amy literally believing the erased Doctor back into existence in 'The Big Bang'), he argues television's iterative, audience-entangled, endlessly rewritable nature is the show's real subject. The TARDIS, 'bigger on the inside,' is television itself, and 'The Day of the Doctor' celebrates a medium that can remake the old anew—self-interrogating its own dangers in stories like 'The Idiot's Lantern' and 'Bad Wolf.'
- ch. 12 "3. The Mystical Alchemy of “Midnight”" *(no index entry yet)* — Sas uses literary alchemy's three-stage magnum opus to read 'Midnight' as the nigredo—the black stage of dissolution that begins the Tenth Doctor's arc of purification, death, and rebirth ending in his regeneration in 'The End of Time.' She shows Russell T Davies loading the episode with nigredo imagery: the deadly Xtonic sunlight that calcinates bodies to ash, the planet of endless 'midnight' and witching-hour folklore, the Salem-style mob panic modeled on The Crucible as the mimicking Sky drives the passengers to demand a sacrificial victim, and the Doctor stripped of TARDIS, companion Donna, authority, and finally his voice. The Doctor's humbling—he solves nothing and is saved only by the Hostess's self-sacrifice—purges the ego that later swells into 'Time Lord Victorious,' while his reunion with the fiery Donna foreshadows the alchemical fusion of the DoctorDonna and eventual rebirth.
- ch. 13 "4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl" **·** Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Aristotle, Plato — Personal Identity; The Unconscious; Archetypes; The Collective Unconscious — Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.
- ch. 14 "5. Every Lonely Monster Needs a Companion" **·** Aristotle, Plato, David Hume — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Is–Ought Problem; The Ethics of Care — Gadsden asks why a near-omnipotent Time Lord needs companions at all and tests four hypotheses against his solo meltdowns—executing Solomon in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship,' nearly murdering Jex in 'A Town Called Mercy,' and declaring himself 'Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars.' He rejects the Lord Acton power-corrupts hypothesis via Glaucon's ring story in Plato's Republic, since powerless companions offer no threat of reprisal or dishonor, and qualifies J.J. Sylvia's care-ethics 'empathetic link' because the Doctor cares for non-human species like the Star Whale too. He favors two answers: Hume's fact/value gap as a millennium-long moral myopia ('I can't see it anymore,' the deleted 'Flesh and Stone' confession), and Aristotle's point in the Nicomachean Ethics that only virtuous friends—moral peers who mirror us—can expose the Doctor's blind spots, like his 'God Complex.'
- ch. 15 "Serial 2 Mind-Bending Impossibility-Shattering Jammie Dodgers" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "You’re Fantastic!" **·** Potentiality and Actuality — Viguié's Serial 2 preface argues the show's ultimate philosophy is 'you're fantastic': the Doctor takes people yearning for something more—Rose the shop girl becoming Bad Wolf, Rory becoming the Last Centurion, Donna the temp becoming in a way the Doctor herself—and actualizes potential they never believed they had. He applies the lesson to his own life, describing how the show's belief in untapped human potential pushed him from a soul-sucking job to creating his Doctor Geek's Laboratory STEM-outreach audio show and Science Fair, urging readers to answer the Doctor's call and live up to what the Fourth Doctor called our 'inventive, invincible, indomitable' species' promise.
- ch. 17 "6. Weeping Angels and Many Worlds" **·** Aristotle — Free Will vs Determinism; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds — Sutton argues the causal loops of 'Blink' and 'The Angels Take Manhattan' need not destroy libertarian free will: the Doctor's claim that a known future is 'written in stone' conflates ordinary foreknowledge, which leaves agents free to make the knower wrong, with infallible knowledge that only exists because the act occurs. Adapting Hugh Everett's many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to free choices, he shows how branching timelines let the Doctor read Melody Malone, decline to break River's wrist, and still close the loop—some parallel Doctor does what the book records—while Aristotle's future contingents in De Interpretatione secure the indeterminacy of what 'will' happen. Answering the objection that branch-splitting is really fatalism, he appeals to the subjective viewpoint (what matters is 'my me'), explains how Kathy and Billy's messages in 'Blink' reach Sally on at least one branch, and solves why the Doctor is always so lucky: we follow the one branch where he survives.
- ch. 18 "7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Compatibilism; Fate and Foreknowledge — Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'
- ch. 19 "8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds; Fate and Foreknowledge — Pigliucci treats the two Trenzalore timelines of 'The Name of the Doctor' and 'The Time of the Doctor' as allohistory—an if-then counterfactual in Livy's tradition about Alexander the Great—and argues Everettian many-worlds quantum mechanics best explains how the Time Lords' one decision (granting or withholding a new regeneration cycle) can go both ways across parallel worlds. Rejecting contra-causal free will as a theological leftover, he prefers the cognitive scientist's 'volition' and defends compatibilism: the split stems from ordinary quantum-random interaction during deliberation, not magic, so the Doctor's choices are real without violating physics. Distinguishing fate from free will via Oedipus and the Doctor's 'Destiny Trap,' he concludes the Doctor was fated to make his last stand on Trenzalore as a fixed point in time, while the outcome of the siege depended on a genuine choice that, as David Deutsch puts it, thickened the stack of universes where good things happen.
- ch. 20 "9. How the Doctor Knows" **·** René Descartes, Alvin Goldman, Charles Sanders Peirce, Plato — Brain in a Vat; Reliabilism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito — Smithka argues the Doctor is a reliabilist about knowledge rather than a Cartesian strong foundationalist: using 'Amy's Choice,' 'The Beast Below' (the glass of water, the engine room, Amy's inference that the Star Whale came willingly), 'Silence in the Library' (the chicken-leg experiment implicating the Vashta Nerada), and Davros's Dalek trials in 'Genesis of the Daleks,' she shows him trusting perception in the right causal chain and reasoning inductively and abductively—Peirce's inference to the best explanation—instead of demanding Cartesian certainty. Against Descartes's dream and evil-genius skepticism, updated as Putnam-style brain-in-a-vat scenarios via the Dream Crabs of 'Last Christmas' and the Dream Lord's two-worlds game, she deploys Goldman's three criteria for perceptual knowledge: justification is packed into reliable belief-forming processes, and doubt is warranted only in known abnormal contexts like funhouses or Dream Lord games.
- ch. 21 "10. One Good, Solid Hope—the Impossible Girl" **·** John Locke, Plutarch — Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — Elsby and Luzecky ask what stays constant across Clara's echoes and argue traditional identity theories fail her: Locke's memory-continuity and same-life account cannot apply because no echo remembers the others, and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus—invoked by the Doctor's broom speech in 'Deep Breath'—rules out bodily continuity, since the echoes have different bodies and minds. Their positive view is that Clara is less a particular than a universal, a 'recipe' or species whose instances share an essence ('the soufflé isn't the soufflé; the soufflé is the recipe'), with the modern-day Clara 'real' as the origin of the echoes. That essence, shown in climbing the ladder to the clouds in 'The Snowmen,' facing the parasite-god with the most important leaf in human history in 'The Rings of Akhaten,' stepping into the Doctor's torn timeline in 'The Name of the Doctor,' and persuading the Time Lords in 'The Time of the Doctor,' is hope itself.
- ch. 22 "11. What the Soufflé Girl Could Teach Descartes" **·** René Descartes, Sigmund Freud, Hilary Putnam, Alan Turing, Gilbert Ryle — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Mind–Body Dualism; Brain in a Vat; The Turing Test — Becker-Lindenthal uses 'Amy's Choice' to revise Descartes's dream skepticism: the Dream Lord is not an external evil demon but the Doctor's own repressed alter ego fed by psychic pollen, so the self-delusion Descartes dismissed becomes the real deceiver, read through Freud's Interpretation of Dreams (Rory's death as the Doctor's wish, Amy's choice as Thanatos). She then reads Oswin in 'Asylum of the Daleks' as a brain-in-a-vat variant (Putnam's Reason, Truth and History) with a crucial difference—Oswin hacks the Dalek program and follows her own agenda—so her self-deceptive soufflé-baking fantasy is a self-formation that preserves her 'I' inside Dalek hardware, complicating Ryle's rejection of the ghost in the machine. Finally, the Doctor judges Oswin by a Turing test plus Putnam's test of reference (the impossible milk and eggs), but her self-deception is vindicated when it lets her save the Doctor and the universe.
- ch. 23 "12. How to Build a TARDIS" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Physicists Tippett and Tsang lay out a real general-relativistic 'TARDIS'—a Traversable Achronal Retrograde Domain in Spacetime: a bubble of curvature carrying occupants around a closed loop through space and time, with outside observers seeing two bubbles, one evolving forwards and one backwards, and interior events bound by Novikov's self-consistency condition. After touring the Alcubierre warp drive, Morris-Thorne wormholes with their twin-paradox time offset, the Tipler cylinder's frame dragging, and the Grandfather Paradox (with 'Father's Day' and 'Genesis of the Daleks' as illustrations), they show their geometry requires exotic, gravitationally repulsive faster-than-light matter violating the classical energy conditions. Splicing cut TARDIS segments could connect any two events in space and time, and a half-TARDIS would send its traveler emerging backwards in time as antimatter, as when Omega converts the Doctors in 'The Three Doctors.'
- ch. 24 "Serial 3 Values in the Time Vortex" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "The Doctor Who Masculine Romantic Ideal" *(no index entry yet)* — Spivey's Serial 3 preface proposes 'The Doctor Who Masculine Romantic Ideal': female fans are drawn to the Doctor's humor under fire (the banana daiquiri, the tie wrapped round his head), his lively intellect, and his 'broken while unattainable' past—the post-Time-War scars that kept him aloof from Rose, and the sense that he is a damaged man worth saving. Writing from his background in interpersonal communication and his experience as a Gallifrey-inspired rock musician dubbed 'Sexiest Man in Tampa Bay,' he argues the Doctor's appeal transfers by association to fandom men who share these traits, and that bookish 'cool savants' overlooked by traditional masculinity can cultivate this ideal—humor, intellect, and honorable wounds—as a genuine romantic alternative.
- ch. 26 "13. Should the Doctor Eat His Companions" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; Speciesism; Food Ethics — Littmann turns the Doctor-companion relationship into a mirror for animal ethics: since the Doctor stands to humans as we stand to animals—deciding for Rose without asking in 'The End of the World,' implanting nanorecorders unconsented in 'Day of the Moon'—every standard justification for our treatment of animals (might makes right, superior intelligence, natural predation) would equally license him to eat Clara cutlets, yet he instead defends humanity from Daleks, Cybermen, and naturally predatory species like the Weeping Angels, the Minotaur, and the Swarm. Finding no non-arbitrary place to draw the intelligence line—what of the human-level gangers, the enslaved Ood, or mentally disabled humans?—he endorses Bentham's utilitarian suffering standard from 'Can they suffer?', concluding that eating humans fails the utilitarian test because the pleasure cannot outweigh a whole life's happiness, and that whether eating meat passes that same test is the question our own treatment of animals must answer.
- ch. 27 "14. The Doctor’s Desire for Human Suffering" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, John Stuart Mill — Amor Fati (love of fate); Will to Power; The Last Man — Cooper reads 'Rise of the Cybermen' and 'The Age of Steel' as staging Nietzsche against Mill's pain-eradicating utilitarianism: John Lumic, who builds the Cybermen to abolish his sickness, exemplifies the life-denying herd—losing his creativity, craving 'unity and uniformity,' becoming 'a living brain with a heart of steel'—while the Doctor, answering that a life without pain would be 'you might as well kill me,' affirms suffering as the source of creativity, striving, and strength. She extends the Nietzschean reading to the Doctor's character: his guilt over the Time War double-genocide and his loneliness ('the only certainty left is that you'll end up alone') become the pain that makes him merciful, from offering Dalek Caan compassion after 'Evolution of the Daleks' to forgiving the Master in 'Last of the Time Lords,' so that mercy is, as the Genealogy of Morals says, 'the privilege of the most powerful man.'
- ch. 28 "15. The Way of the Doctor Is Deception" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham, Plato, Bernard Williams, Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Noble Lie; The Categorical Imperative; Respect for Persons; Utilitarianism — Dodge takes Rule #1 - the Doctor lies - through the major theories of lying: Bernard Williams's definition (asserting what you believe false with intent to deceive), Aristotle's claim that all lies are base, Kant's categorical imperative and respect for persons (even the Vinvocci's shimmer disguises in 'The End of Time' abuse trust), and Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus, which condemns the faked death at Lake Silencio ('The Impossible Astronaut') for the grief it caused Amy and Rory yet rewards the greater happiness it made possible. Against the absolutists he sets Plato's Noble Lie from the Republic - the elite falsehood that keeps society functioning - as what the Doctor emulates by deceiving the universe into thinking him dead ('The Wedding of River Song'), and Nietzsche's point in Human, All Too Human that lying is ethically neutral when the pretense is sustainable, as when the Doctor hides the ganger-Amy switch from Rory ('The Almost People'). The upshot: the Doctor's lies are wrong in themselves but routinely justified by the good they do, which is why sometimes the hero lies.
- ch. 29 "16. Divine Hatred—Dalek Beauty" **·** Immanuel Kant, Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche, David Hume, Arthur Schopenhauer — Theory of Forms; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Bowman uses 'Asylum of the Daleks' - where the Daleks preserve broken, insane Daleks as embodiments of 'divine hatred' - to test whether beauty is objective or subjective. Plato's Theory of Forms explains how hatred could be beautiful (the more a thing instantiates its Form, the more beautiful it is), while the Hume-Kant antinomy of beauty, Kant's disinterested judgment of taste (illustrated by Rory and Amy's invested judgments of each other versus the TARDIS's detached 'pretty'), and Nietzsche's account of beauty leading to divinity frame the Dalek hive mind's shared conceptual scheme. Since Kant says beauty is a symbol of morality, the Asylum-as-museum reveals Dalek values - which is why human-on-the-inside Clara is enshrined under maximum security, and why the Doctor is sickened to learn that he is himself an object of Dalek beauty.
- ch. 30 "17. The Friends of a Time Lord" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Littmann applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship - pleasure, usefulness, and mutual goodness - to fifty years of Doctor-companion pairings, from the Hartnell Doctor's glee touring Vortis with Ian to New Series companions chosen as friends who routinely save the day, from Barbara's Dalek revolt to Clara saving every incarnation of the Doctor. He argues Aristotle would still judge the Doctor's friendships defective: they are short-lived, unequal in station, intellect, and morality, and the companions cannot know him well enough (not even his name) for the perfect friendship of the good. Littmann then corrects Aristotle on two counts: friends need not be moral experts to serve as moral critics (Rose in 'Dalek,' Amy in 'A Town Called Mercy'), and the Doctor's favoritism toward his companions - risking worlds to save them, as when Rory weighs Amy's life against the universe in 'The Big Bang' - shows that preferring friends over strangers is itself his most frequent moral failing.
- ch. 31 "18. Sex for Dummies, Humans, and Time Lords" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Lewis argues the New Series' sexual revolution (Captain Jack, Vastra and Jenny, the Doctor's multiple marriages) teaches that any relationship between rational, autonomous, consenting adults is morally permissible. Building on John Corvino's defense of homosexual sex, he dismantles the 'unnatural means immoral' argument definition by definition (unusual, not practiced by animals, contrary to innate desire, contrary to natural purpose or divine intent, disgusting), rejects the empirical slippery slope as a fallacy, and uses Whoniverse cases - young Amelia Pond's non-autonomous choice to leave with the Doctor, the Slitheen pig as mere causal agent, manipulation that would undermine informed consent - to show that only autonomy grounds sexual morality. Objections to same-sex or human-alien relationships turn out to confuse the aesthetic ('ugly') with the ethical ('wrong').
- ch. 32 "19. The Doctor is a (Wo)Man!" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Judith Butler — One Is Not Born a Woman; Gender Performativity — Kellen asks whether the Doctor could regenerate as a woman, marshaling the canon evidence (the Corsair's lives as both sexes, the Sisterhood of Karn offering 'man or woman,' Missy) to show biology poses no obstacle - clownfish and rare human sex changes make the point mundane. Against Peter Davison's claim that a female Doctor 'doesn't work,' he deploys Simone de Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Judith Butler's account in Gender Trouble of gender as a stylized repetition of acts performed over time, arguing the Doctor already performs care-ethicist, 'feminine' roles and could just as well perform female ones. Since regeneration routinely transforms personality without ending the Doctor, the only remaining objection is bias toward a supposedly male core identity.
- ch. 33 "Serial 4 Gallifrey Falls No More" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "Terrifying, and Mad, and Bloody Brilliant" *(no index entry yet)* — Hennessee's interlude is a fan memoir told in cuts between 1984, 1994, 2004, and 2014: discovering Tom Baker's Doctor at twelve, dropping fandom as a New York undergraduate, and finding community again through a bookstore corkboard meeting and the 2005 revival. It shows rather than argues that Doctor Who is life-shaping - informing its fan's morality, tastes, friendships, and speculations about time, free will, and the self - while asking whether the boy of 1984 would recognize the man of 2014. It closes by refusing to separate the show from life: both are 'terrifying, and mad, and bloody brilliant.'
- ch. 35 "20. The Doctor Lies" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo, Plato, Henry Sidgwick — The Noble Lie; The Categorical Imperative; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — McCain distinguishes lying (directly asserting what you believe false to make another believe it) from mere deception - the Sixth Doctor feeding Jamie false information for Sontaran Stike to overhear in 'The Two Doctors' deceives without lying - then asks whether the Doctor can lie to himself, answering that incarnations can lie to later selves (the Eleventh's suspicious 'I have absolutely no idea' about the children on Gallifrey in 'The Day of the Doctor') but a current self cannot. The stakes are moral: against Kant's and Augustine's absolute prohibition of lying, Plato's Republic and Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics defend noble lies, and Robert C. Solomon's view of self-deception as coping with the unbearable suggests that if the Doctor did engineer himself to forget the Time War genocide - as Ten and Wilf did to Donna in 'Journey's End' - it might be a good man's forgivable way of going on.
- ch. 36 "21. Forgetting Is the Human Superpower" **·** Sigmund Freud — The Unconscious; Personal Identity — Seymour reads the War-through-Eleventh Doctors through Freud's notion of Afterwardness (Nachtraeglichkeit) from Studies on Hysteria - memory is continually reforged as new information recontextualizes the past - so that learning Gallifrey was saved in 'The Day of the Doctor' changes not the Doctor but his memories of himself, turning penance into hope. She traces each Self constructed from Time War memory: Nine's guilt exploited by the Gelth and voiced in 'Boom Town' ('Only a killer would know that'), Ten's hubris once he forgets what he is capable of ('Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars'), and Eleven's danger when the memory fades and companions must remind him who he is ('A Town Called Mercy'). The chapter concludes the Doctor must keep the memory of his regret to keep being the Doctor - Clara's 'What you've always done. Be a doctor.'
- ch. 37 "22. The Mnemotechnics of Amy Pond" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Holdier explains how Amy remembering the Doctor back into existence at her wedding ('The Big Bang') could work, combining Nietzsche's mnemotechnics from the second essay of On the Genealogy of Morals - only that which never ceases to hurt stays in the memory - with J.R.R. Tolkien's 'On Fairy-Stories,' whose internally coherent secondary worlds sustain cultural memory and 'recover' a clear view of reality. On this reading the Doctor deliberately plants his painful loss in Amy's subconscious wrapped in a fairy tale; Amy is the ideal medium because she lacked the willpower to hold onto Rory when the cracks rewrote her ('Cold Blood'), yet her fairy-tale-soaked childhood beside the Crack in her wall let the Doctor's last story germinate into the words that returned the TARDIS to the universe.
- ch. 38 "23. Failing and Forgiving in the Name of the Doctor" **·** Forgiveness; Personal Identity; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Hoffman reads the Doctor's banishment of the War Doctor ('Doctor no more,' his actions 'not done in the name of the Doctor') as a failure of self-forgiveness driven by what Jeffrie Murphy calls the moral hatred of self and Robin Dillon the 'self-as-feared,' rather than mere guilt over the genocide of Gallifrey. Drawing on the self-forgiveness literature (Blustein, Griswold, Westlund), he argues that 'The Day of the Doctor' shows forgiveness neither excuses nor extinguishes blame: the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors forgive their past self by recognizing he shared their Doctorly motives and was forced into an impossible choice. Clara's outsider faith ('be a doctor') supplies the third-party affirmation that dissolves the identity-destroying dilemma and frees the Doctor to find the third option that saves Gallifrey.
- ch. 39 "24. Who’s Duty to Whom" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Hobbes, David Hume — The Categorical Imperative; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; The Social Contract; The State of Nature — Dawson asks why the Doctor sides with humans and humanoids against rational non-humanoids, testing Kant first: a logic-grounded categorical morality can count the Daleks as immoral rather than amoral (universalized slavery is incoherent), but pure reason cannot motivate Daleks or the Master, and Kant's theory absurdly condemns the Doctor's lies and his theft of the TARDIS. Hobbesian psychological egoism and the social contract fare worse - the Daleks are no co-signatories, and self-sacrifices from Katarina to the Doctor's seemingly final years on Trenzalore resist the egoist's retelling - so the chapter lands with Hume: sympathy and benevolence found morality on feeling, which explains and partly excuses the Doctor's parochial partiality for beings who resemble him, making him 'at least half-Humean.'
- ch. 40 "25. Meeting Up with Your Self" **·** Gilles Deleuze, John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Existentialism — Sylvia and Stevens use Doctor Who's crossover episodes to complicate the Self-Other distinction: existentially (via Yalom and Maslow), the Doctor's name-promise - 'never cruel or cowardly... never give up, never give in' - supplies meaning, while Ten and Eleven must stop treating the War Doctor as Other. Deleuze's account of learning through the shock of encountering the Other structures the reading of 'The Girl Who Waited,' where young Amy and her thirty-six-years-older self form an assemblage in which the older Amy relearns her love for Rory and chooses annihilation for his sake. Locke's memory theory of personal identity frames the puzzle that a version of you with different memories may be an Other, which the authors extend to confronting our recorded past selves on social media and learning empathy from the shock.
- ch. 41 "26. Time Lords Are Us" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology; Embodiment (the lived body) — Elder argues the 'back to front' love story of the Doctor and River Song - her past is his future, as at Lake Silencio - refutes both the objective 'river' model of time and the subjective 'song' model on which the mind assembles moments like notes into a flow. Following Merleau-Ponty, he grounds the experience of flow in pre-reflective embodied perception: Clara's walk around the TARDIS and her 'it's smaller on the outside' show a finite body gripping a multifaceted world, so that 'time is the subject and the subject is time.' Because temporalities, unlike private consciousnesses, can intertwine in a shared present, the Doctor and River can build a relationship out of each other's pasts and futures - and in this sense we are all Time Lords.
- ch. 42 "More Matrix of Time-Lord Bibliographic Sources" *(notes)*
- ch. 43 "The Second Great Gallifreyan High Council" *(notes)*
- ch. 44 "Higher-Order Logical Index for the Cyberman and Dalek in All of Us" *(notes)*

- ch. 10 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Immanuel Kant — Lintott's editor's introduction argues that motherhood is a site of serious philosophical significance rather than 'navel-gazing,' organizing the anthology's essays around Kant's three questions from the Critique of Pure Reason – what can I know, what ought I to do, what may I hope. She recasts these as the daily questions of contemporary mothers (about knowledge, ethical choices like breastfeeding or lying, and existential/spiritual meaning) and draws on Sara Ruddick's 'maternal thinking' to insist mothers are thinking beings. It is a framing essay connecting lived mothering to canonical philosophy rather than to a single pop-culture work.
- ch. 11 "MOTHERHOOD" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** John Dewey — Pragmatism; Experience and Education — Sue Ellen Henry uses John Dewey's pragmatism, especially The Quest for Certainty and Democracy and Education, to diagnose her own 'quest for certainty' as a new mother mediating expert parenting books against her own instincts. She argues Dewey's rejection of the false dichotomy between knowledge and belief shows that a mother's home is her 'laboratory,' where experience is itself a form of knowledge; her La Leche League experience models Dewey's integrated, feedback-driven inquiry against the isolating authority of 'scientific motherhood' texts.
- ch. 13 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Augustine of Hippo — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism — Amy Kind examines the pervasiveness of parents lying to children (her own 'Bad Dream Spray') against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibition of lying, Mill's utilitarian permissiveness, and Sissela Bok's principle of veracity. She applies Kant's categorical imperative and formula of humanity – treating persons never merely as means – to argue that because young children have not fully developed their rational natures, the Kantian wrong of lying is mitigated, while illustrating the debate with South Park's Kyle reading Descartes, A Few Good Men's 'you can't handle the truth,' and Seinfeld's George Costanza ('it's not a lie if you believe it').
- ch. 14 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Judith Jarvis Thomson, Immanuel Kant — The Violinist Argument; Humanity as an End in Itself — Bertha Alvarez Manninen reconciles her deepened respect for fetal life (after seeing her daughter on ultrasound) with a pro-choice stance by deploying Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment and the real McFall v. Shimp bodily-integrity ruling. She argues that even granting the fetus full personhood, no one's right to life entitles them to another's body, buttressing this with Kant's formula of humanity that a woman must not be reduced to a mere incubating means, and calls for American mizuko-kuyo-style grieving rituals so 'pro-choice' is not conflated with 'pro-abortion.'
- ch. 15 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Judith Butler, bell hooks — Gender Performativity — Kim Anno recounts raising an intensely masculine adopted African-American son, Zack, as a lesbian mother, using Judith Butler's account of gender and desire (from Undoing Gender) and bell hooks's We Real Cool on black masculinity to interrogate the social construction of gender against Zack's seemingly 'hardwired' boyness. She reads his gendered choices in toys, clothes, and music (Black Eyed Peas hip-hop, Black Sabbath's 'Iron Man,' the Rocky theme) and his racialized treatment through these lenses, contrasting his family with the rigid gender scripts of I Love Lucy and The Jetsons and her own parents' Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf dynamic.
- ch. 16 "MOTHERHOOD" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Ethics of Ambiguity; Existentialism; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Elizabeth Butterfield reads her exhausting early motherhood through Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity and The Second Sex, arguing that 'the ideal mother,' like 'true womanhood,' is a social construction and that a mother is 'freedom in situation,' never a mother 'the way a stone is a stone.' She recasts Beauvoir's 'serious man' as the 'serious mother' who flees her freedom into the Motherhood Religion, and invokes Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and 'Hell is other people' (No Exit) to advocate the honest, self-aware 'genuine mother' over inauthentic self-sacrifice.
- ch. 18 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** The Buddha, Jeremy Bentham — The Four Noble Truths; Impermanence (anicca); Non-Self (anatman) — Sheryl Tuttle Ross applies three of the Buddhist noble truths – pain is inevitable, pain arises from attachment, suffering can end – to contemporary mothering, contrasting the Buddhist acceptance of pain with Bentham's utilitarian pleasure-maximizing. Drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's mindfulness and the doctrines of impermanence and no-self, she offers 'mommy meditations' (breathe, become aware, recognize social scripts, respond kindly) and reads the novel I Don't Know How She Does It, whose 'Court of Motherhood' dramatizes the guilt-inducing scripts mindfulness helps mothers see through to experience beauty in ordinary moments.
- ch. 19 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** David Hume — Glenn Parsons asks whether mothers really perceive their own infants as more beautiful (cuter) than others do, and if so whether that taste is defective. He applies David Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' – the five marks of the 'true judge,' especially freedom from prejudice – to argue that a mother's love makes her a biased, poor critic like the egotistical artist or an author's friend. But drawing on Jerrold Levinson's account of why good taste matters, he concludes that since a mother cannot 'drop her homely baby like a bad paperback,' she has no aesthetic reason to correct her loving 'distortion,' unlike someone choosing Shakespeare over Danielle Steel.
- ch. 20 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Plato, Socrates — Theory of Forms — Laura Newhart narrates coming to know Kevin, her son adopted from Guatemala, first through monthly photographs and then in person, repeatedly finding her interpretations 'fuzzy and incomplete.' She frames this epistemic problem with Plato's Republic – Socrates' hierarchy in which a two-dimensional image is inferior in being and truth to the physical object, which is inferior to the eternal Form or soul – concluding that because we are bound to changing physical bodies, the soul is hardest to know, so she and Kevin may never fully know each other, a shared condition rather than a failure.
- ch. 21 "MOTHERHOOD" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** The Ethics of Care; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Chris Mulford, a nurse and lactation consultant, analyzes infant feeding as an ethical question of rights, duties, and responsibilities, drawing on a feminist ethic of care and the claim that women learn empathy through caregiving (linked to oxytocin's role in birth and nursing). She argues that the right at stake is the mother-child dyad's 'protection from interference' with breastfeeding, that no mother is saddled with a solitary duty to breastfeed, and that the duty toward breastfeeding falls on the whole community; she frames the mother's dependency on 'the kindness of strangers' via A Streetcar Named Desire and the innate 'breast crawl.'
- ch. 23 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Carol Gilligan — The Ethics of Care; Objectification — Maureen Sander-Staudt uses a feminist ethic of care – especially Carol Gilligan's mole-and-porcupine fable of reciprocal accommodation – to argue that pressuring women to nurse privately or covered imposes 'lactational burkas.' She runs public breastfeeding through the Miller obscenity test to show it is not obscene, opening with Gloria Steinem's 'If men could menstruate' to imagine 'milkmen,' and cites the Emily Gillette Freedom-flight ejection, Facebook's photo removal, the Janet Jackson Superbowl scandal, and PETA's human-milk proposal to expose hypocritical, biologically reductive double standards about the female breast.
- ch. 24 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Utilitarianism; Deontology; Virtue Ethics — Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.
- ch. 25 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Michel de Montaigne, Seneca — Stoicism; Virtue Ethics; Social Darwinism — Jen Baker interrogates why unmedicated 'natural' childbirth is treated as morally superior, dissecting five senses of 'natural' and rejecting each, including a social-Darwinist appeal to evolution she deems dangerous. She engages Montaigne (via Cicero) on philosophizing as learning to die and cites Dylan Thomas and Neil Young on facing pain soberly, then turns to the Stoics' claim that pain 'is nothing to us' – arguing from a neo-Aristotelian/Stoic virtue ethics that pain has no moral value and that keeping one's wits with an epidural can preserve moral agency, so natural birth is an 'optional and amoral' thrill, not a virtue; she frames it with Bill Cosby's and Carol Burnett's labor jokes.
- ch. 26 "MOTHERHOOD" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Plato, John Rawls — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Brain in a Vat; The Veil of Ignorance — Sara Goering uses the fantasy of a child 'off button' as a thought experiment, situating it alongside Plato's Ring of Gyges, the brain-in-a-vat, and personal-identity puzzles to argue that such control would be overused and would treat children as objects rather than developing subjects. She then turns reflexive, critiquing thought experiments themselves – including Rawls's veil of ignorance (via Okin and Benhabib) and Susan Brison's critique of personal-identity cases – for diverting from the messy real world, arguing that the off-button fantasy really signals the need for 'distributed mothering' and structural support; she illustrates with The Matrix, Multiplicity, Harry Potter, and Woolf's 'room of one's own.'
- ch. 28 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics; Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Golden Mean — Nin Kirkham applies neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics to define the 'virtues of motherhood' as character dispositions that let a mother flourish (achieve eudaimonia) qua mother. She elaborates three virtues – endurance (commitment, selflessness, and long-view 'vision,' likened to endurance running), liberality (knowing when to let a child go), and moral exemplarity – each analyzed as an Aristotelian mean between vices of excess and deficit, and argues good mothering is learned by example and does not license judging other mothers against one's own ideal.
- ch. 29 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Feminism — Clemence Due and Damien Riggs analyze how media images of celebrity mothers reproduce Sharon Hays's 'intensive mothering' ideology, reporting a study in which students judged Jodie Foster a 'good/normal' (if 'boring') mother for domestic self-sacrifice, Angelina Jolie a 'savior' but not fully 'good' because of her career, Nicole Richie a reformed 'bad-girl-come-good-mom,' and Britney Spears ('Toxic Mummy') a 'bad' mother. They argue readers uncritically absorb and extend these gendered norms – fathers escaping such scrutiny – and call, from a feminist standpoint, for mothers to be allowed to be 'good' in many ways while pursuing other interests.
- ch. 30 "MOTHERHOOD" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Anselm of Canterbury, Aristotle — The Problem of Evil; Caring as the Ground of Ethics — George Dunn asks whether classical theism can call God 'Mother,' beginning with the Book of Job (taught in his Problem of Evil course) and the divine name Shadday's link to womb-love and 'blessings of breasts and womb.' He works through Anselm's 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' the attributes of impassibility and incorporeality, and Aquinas's doctrine of analogy, arguing Aquinas wrongly rejected maternal God-language because he swallowed Aristotle's biology of woman as 'defective and misbegotten'; drawing on Nel Noddings's caring 'receptivity' and Julian of Norwich, Dunn contends divine impassibility should yield to a maternal, receptive God, with a nod to Homer Simpson's burrito paradox.
- ch. 31 "MOTHERHOOD" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "MOTHERHOOD" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "MOTHERHOOD" *(notes)*

## Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Mr. Monk and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Mr. Monk Meets Alexander the Great" **·** Albert Camus, Diogenes the Cynic — The Myth of Sisyphus; The Absurd; Cynicism (living according to nature); Rebellion and Revolt — Wittkower argues that Monk's daily, unwinnable war on dirt and disorder is Camus's happy Sisyphus made concrete: Monk vacuums ceilings, touches lampposts, and solves murders knowing the dirt and the murderers will always return ('There's never hope... Hope. I hate hope's guts' in 'Mr. Monk Can't See a Thing'), yet he still finds enough satisfaction to take up the wipe again. Reading Ecclesiastes' vanity alongside the uncaring wasp of the opening, the chapter claims Monk shows us how to live wisely without resignation in an absurd world that does not care. He is paired with Diogenes the Cynic, whose barrel, raw onions, and midday lantern mirror Monk's pot-pie-Tuesdays and his refusal to overlook what everyone else ignores; like Diogenes telling Alexander the Great 'get out of my sun,' Monk lives by his own ideals no matter how society judges him. The essay closes that, like Camus addressing the Dominican monks, we should refuse to 'be reasonable' about evil and disorder and keep struggling without hope, wipe in hand.
- ch. 7 "I Just Solved the Case - How Monk Think" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "It’s a Gift ... and a Curse" **·** Edmund Husserl, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology — Welsh argues Monk's 'gift and curse' is being permanently stuck in Husserl's phenomenological attitude. Selective-attention experiments (the swapped interviewer behind the door, the gorilla-suit walker) show that the rest of us see only what expectation renders possible, while Monk, like Poe's Dupin finding the Purloined Letter in plain sight, brackets his assumptions and actually perceives: the moved decorative rock in Dr. Kroger's courtyard, the wing-back chair and wiped bullets proving the 'suicide' in 'Mr. Monk and the Garbage Strike' is murder, and the illiterate suspect's English-sign slip in 'Mr. Monk Goes to a Fashion Show' — all through his hand-framing 'Zen Sherlock Holmes thing.' But because he cannot exit back into the natural attitude, the same perception is pathological. Drawing on Damasio's Descartes' Error and Merleau-Ponty's patient Schneider, the chapter argues that emotion is what structures relevance and action, so Monk's refusal to let emotional bonds organize his life leaves him isolated and unhappy — though curing the curse might cost him the gift that solves the cases.
- ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" **·** Karl Popper, René Descartes — Falsificationism; The Best of All Possible Worlds; Ockham's Razor — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- ch. 10 "Step Back" **·** David Hume — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Problem of Induction — Gallagher uses Monk's phobias to test Hume's claim that believing is itself a kind of feeling. The chapter asks whether a fear conflicting with a rational belief (Monk paralyzed by the possibly-on stove during a murder investigation) feels any different from a conflict between two fears ('Snakes trump heights' in 'Mr. Monk and the Very, Very Old Man') or two beliefs, and answers with Hume that beliefs are forceful-feeling representations — there is a 'what it's like' to believing the German shepherd is dangerous. On Hume's account the force of a belief comes from repetition of experience, which explains both why Monk's fears should fade (countless safely landed flights, millions of milk drinkers) and why they persist: his mind dwells repeatedly on the rare catastrophe, giving fearful representations extra force, as when his repeated experience that 'she's always cheating' makes him wrongly believe Brody's wife in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully.' The practical lesson is to step back and widen attention to all the possibilities, as Monk intermittently manages with the help of Natalie and Stottlemeyer.
- ch. 11 "He’s the Guy - What Monk Is Made Of" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); The Golden Mean; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.
- ch. 13 "It’s Time for the Other Walkie-Talkie" **·** Aristotle, Plato, Seneca, Michel de Montaigne — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Philosophy of Love; Stoicism — Dodge puts Monk on the case of friendship's nature, structured by Aristotle's three kinds from the Nicomachean Ethics: Hal Tucker's fake buddy act in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend' is pure utility, while Natalie's is virtue-friendship — she is his friend 'in spite of' the job since 'he doesn't pay her that much.' The friend as mirror and 'second self' grounds the claim that Stottlemeyer, Sharona, Natalie and Randy reflect Monk's excellence back to him, and Bacon's point that a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in half is shown when they stay up all night during his suicide watch. Seneca's Stoic counsel — judge a person long before admitting him, then hold nothing back — is exemplified by Natalie's fish-over-moon-rock test of Monk's character, while Montaigne's once-in-centuries friendship in which two selves blur fits only Trudy, whose dying words 'bread and butter' tell Monk they belong together. Plato's Lysis (the 'great cosmic swirly' Monk cites in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully') opens the puzzle Socrates could not solve, and the single walkie-talkie his father gave him shows why the chapter's verdict — Monk now has friends — matters.
- ch. 14 "Mr. Monk’s Greatness" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Plato — The Übermensch; Existence Precedes Essence — Lewis argues Monk is Nietzsche's Übermensch. Sketching Sartre's existence-precedes-essence through the contrast between the designed wipe and self-defining humans, the chapter claims Monk creates his own essence through choices — keeping the coffee table askew in memory of Trudy, 'dirtying' his house in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend,' drinking stream water in 'Mr. Monk Gets Cabin Fever' — and lives by self-prescribed values (hourly flossing, bagged tissues, relentless truth-seeking) that separate him from the herd of the Court of Public Opinion. The comparison with Stottlemeyer — Nietzsche's lookalike with the mustache, 'the quintessential man' of the herd — inverts the expected hierarchy: 'He was a yardstick for me, of both detection and character' ('Mr. Monk Goes to Mexico') shows the badge-carrying everyman is the inferior one. Monk therefore challenges the macho sci-fi stereotype of the superman: the Übermensch can be gentle and kind, fight for truth and a cleaner world, and still have room to improve ('What does not kill me makes me stronger').
- ch. 15 "Unless I’m Wrong, and I’m Not... - Monk’s Logic" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Mr. Monk Is Mr. Monk" **·** John Locke, David Hume, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Bundle Theory of Self — Malloy runs the classic theories of personal identity through Monk episodes. Bodily (really brain) identity fails when 'the Monk' — the reckless medicated alter of 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' — shares Monk's body and brain yet is not held responsible, and Stanley Tucci's method actor in 'Mr. Monk and the Actor' shows that copying Monk's looks and behavior does not transfer identity. Locke's memory theory breaks on the amnesia of 'Mr. Monk Bumps His Head' (Monk becomes roofer 'Jerry') and the blackout in 'Mr. Monk and the Rapper,' and Reid's brave-officer paradox yields contradiction once recovered Monk remembers being both Monk and Jerry. Hume's bundle theory — 'I never can catch myself,' the self as theatre of successive perceptions — grounds psychological continuity's graded identity, but then cult-swayed Monk in 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' might count as a different person, making his deprogramming a kind of murder; the chapter closes by rejecting Reid and Butler's 'simple and unassayable' escape, insisting a philosopher, like a detective, must keep theorizing how Monk stays Monk.
- ch. 17 "Here’s How It Happened and Didn’t Happen" *(no index entry yet)* — Michaud asks how TV's most logical detective can assert contradictions: Monk says 'I know it's impossible, but he's the guy' about Derek Philby murdering while proctoring an exam ('Mr. Monk Goes Back to School') and about astronaut Steve Wagner killing while in orbit ('Mr. Monk and the Astronaut'), seeming violations of the Law of Non-Contradiction that his own valid arguments (the missing glass of water ruling out suicide) depend on. The chapter stages Graham Priest's dialetheism — the Liar Sentence as a true contradiction — as a possible defense, even borrowing Gricean maxims to argue Monk would announce a dialetheia if he believed one, but concludes Monk never actually accepts true contradictions: the impossible accusation creates a tension that drives him to find the hidden mechanism (Wagner's pre-rigged garage door), so the 'contradiction' dissolves once a false assumption is exposed. Michaud's closing suggestion is that the Liar Sentence itself should be treated as a crime to be solved rather than a dialetheia to be accepted.
- ch. 18 "Here’s What Happened" **·** The Myth of Sisyphus — Kane, a catalog librarian, argues that Monk's detecting mirrors library cataloging. Monk 'collocates' — identical boxes on one wall, a row of matching Trudy photos on another — and reasons user-first, exactly as Cutter's rule says to choose the entry a library's users will look under first: in 'Mr. Monk and the Bad Girlfriend' he sees the suspect with no alibi must be innocent because a killer who hides in the bathroom already has an alibi secured. Like the invisible cataloger, Monk imposes the order others see without knowing someone arranged it, and both face Sisyphus's rock: Monk's control ends at his apartment door ('Mr. Monk Makes the Playoffs' tailgate chaos), and Universal Bibliographic Control — one standard for describing every work ever created — will never stay at the top of the hill. The Cutter-versus-Dewey rivalry parallels Monk versus Harold Krenshaw, the flashy thunder-stealer who gets famous first, and the chapter ends by pronouncing Monk a natural-born cataloger.
- ch. 19 "He’s a Iteal Character - Monk Competition" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Identity" *(no index entry yet)* — Zaffran reads Monk and Dr. House as twin heirs of Sherlock Holmes — impossible crimes versus impossible diseases — both 'marked' like Oedipus, the first fictional detective, whose truth-seeking destroyed him: Monk's OCD begins with the unsolved murder of Trudy, which he feels implicated in, while House's limp, addiction and misanthropy trace to a misdiagnosis and childhood abuse. The chapter's core argument uses Bachelard's Prometheus complex, 'the Oedipus complex of intellectual life': both sleuths are punished for their insight, chained like Prometheus to their disorders (OCD; Vicodin and the bad leg), yet keep stealing the fire of explanation — their real goal is not justice or cure but disclosing the hidden how of each murder and disease. Monk and House are ultimately mirrors of their writers and audience: fiction (via Brian Boyd's evolutionary account) lets us rehearse moral situations and appease our fear of boredom, which is why we love these gift-and-curse characters and keep coming back for the next episode.
- ch. 21 "The Emotion-Reason Dilemma, Part II" **·** Michel Foucault — Feminism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Pribram places Monk and Dr. House in the tradition of the brilliantly rational but emotionally plagued detective (Dragnet's emotionless Joe Friday vs Cracker's Fitz), arguing both shows treat excessive emotion as the price of genius: Monk's OCD is tied to his pattern-spotting ('You're a freak of nature'), and when medication cures the OCD in 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' his detective genius vanishes. She applies Foucault's Birth of the Clinic to House's subtracting of the patient, but shows both series critique that modernist rationality through Eve in 'One Day, One Room', who forces House to face the rationally inexplicable. Using feminist scholarship (Jaggar, Alberti, Battersby), she argues the opposition of male reason to female emotion is a historically specific construction, and offers the best friends Stottlemeyer and Wilson as integrated alternatives who pay for their balance with ordinariness: polarization equals greatness, integration signals the mundane.
- ch. 22 "Herr Leibniz Consoles Mr. Monk" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, Ludwig Wittgenstein — The Best of All Possible Worlds; Principle of Sufficient Reason; Monadology — Kavas distinguishes Monk's method from Holmes's modus ponens, Poirot's elimination, and Goren's profiling: Monk accepts only what completes a coherent total narrative, so 'Here's what happened' re-tells the order of the whole world, as in the chess-game solution of 'Mr. Monk and the Genius'. The chapter uses the Tractatus's world of contingent, logically independent facts to model Monk's picture-completion, then brings in Leibniz: the principle of sufficient reason, the best of all possible worlds, and preestablished harmony justify Monk's faith that even Trudy's death must have a reason. Monk emerges as a pessimistic Leibniz who takes the world to be the worst possible precisely because, since learning the bomb was meant for Trudy in 'Mr. Monk Goes to Jail', he cannot see any sufficient reason for her death ('Why her?').
- ch. 23 "He’s ... Not Like Everyone Else - The Spiritual Side of Adrian Monk" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Does the Habit Make the Monk" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Anselm of Canterbury, Aristotle — The Ontological Argument; The Five Ways — Elliott maps the recurring Monk stalemate onto medieval theology: in 'Mr. Monk Goes to the Circus', Stottlemeyer and Disher reason forward from a hunch and the evidence, exactly like Anselm's ontological argument, which assumes what it sets out to prove, while Monk, like Aquinas against Anselm, refuses assumptions and reasons backward from verifiable facts, asking why an assassin would somersault except to advertise the acrobatic alibi. Aquinas's First Cause argument (Aristotle's unmoved mover) supplies the model of proving a certainty from observable things, paralleling Monk's 'I don't know how he did it, but he did it' backward deduction. The chapter's closing move likens Monk to the medieval monks themselves: his OCD-driven ascetic withdrawal from the dirty, chaotic world (contemptus mundi) is what lets him notice the imperfection in scenes like the locker room of 'Mr. Monk and the Big Game' that reveals sabotage.
- ch. 25 "Shaman, Heal Thyself" *(no index entry yet)* — Culver reads Monk as a shamanic figure in Arnold van Gennep's and Victor Turner's sense: a liminal man, neither cop nor civilian, fixed in the transitional stage of mourning Trudy, who heals society's disorder from its margins as Holmes and Poirot did. Drawing on Mary Douglas's Purity and Danger (dirt as defilement and disorder), she interprets Monk's ritualized gestures and utterances, framing the scene with his hands, the rare solving-smile, 'he's the guy' and 'Here's what happened', as the ceremonial performance by which disorder is overcome. Episodes like 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' and 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' then show the shaman's bind: whenever Monk attains purity or happiness he loses his sacred gift, so he must refuse to heal himself and remain 'a blessing and a curse'.
- ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" **·** The Buddha — Compassion (karuna); Emptiness (sunyata); Non-Self (anatman) — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- ch. 27 "Our Hour Isn’t Over Yet, It’s Only Been Fifty-Eight Minutes - Monk in Therapy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "16 - Mr. Mead Starts Couples Therapy" *(no index entry yet)* — Clinical psychologist Sylvia Randall writes a thinly fictionalized case study in which 'Andrew Mead' (Monk: wife Terry killed violently, severe OCD, assistants Sheila/Sharona and Naomi/Natalie) brings his working relationships to couples therapy. Through 'I statements' and gentle confrontation, the sessions surface unconscious associations: Mead's fear that his father left because of him, his mother's OCD, Sheila's 'suck it up' childhood, and his survivor's guilt over joy since Terry's death, which an imagined conversation with Terry releases. The chapter's argument is the psychodynamic one that making unconscious material conscious lowers its emotional charge, widening the client's behavioral repertoire and restoring empathy and intimacy in the couple.
- ch. 29 "Mr. Monk, Jungle Guide" **·** Aristotle, The Buddha — Kagan reads Monk through Ernest Becker's Denial of Death: everyone is born hyper-aware like Monk and learns 'how not to see', managing the terror of the jungle out there through denial, shopping, and hero systems, which is why Randy Disher can ride in a cab driven by a corpse without noticing. Monk, who cannot forget (his nudity phobia traced to the trauma of his own birth in 'Mr. Monk and the Naked Man'), is our funhouse mirror and, like the Buddha seeing the four sights of sickness, old age, death, and the renunciant, he re-enters the world after Trudy's death to guide us through it. Aristotle's catharsis explains the pleasure of watching: pity and fear are burned off as Monk, more afraid than we are, still pursues truth and justice.
- ch. 30 "The Strength to Mourn" **·** Jacques Derrida — Tarantino and Wittkower read Monk through Freud's Beyond the Pleasure Principle: repetition compulsion (the fort/da child, the anxiety dream of running toward Trudy's car in 'Mr. Monk Is on the Run, Part 1') is the mind's attempt to retroactively prepare for trauma, which explains both the nudity phobia traced to Monk's birth and his endless return to Trudy's case. Monk's compulsions are also displacement behavior, standing in for the one disorder he cannot put in order, Trudy's death itself, which resists mourning because the beloved object cannot be de-cathected, a Derridean impossible mourning that leaves him haunted. Only when solving the crime proves empty does Monk reach the chapter's conclusion: happiness lies not in possessing lost objects of desire but in new emotional investment in a changing, uncertain world, which the authors name hope.

## Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
