- ch. 10 "Real, This Book" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — The volume's introduction is written in Elliot's paranoid voice, doubting whether the book, the reader, or reality itself exist. It lays out the questions the essays will tackle: fsociety's hack of the Evil Corporation, whether it was political ideology or revenge for the corporation killing Elliot's and Darlene's father, whether either motive (or hacking in general) can be justified, and what order could survive after the financial system falls.
- ch. 11 "I. We’re All Living in Each Other’s Paranoia" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "1. The Deed of F’ing Society" **·** Mahatma Gandhi — Anarchism; Just War Theory; The Ethics of Political Violence — Rocha reads fsociety's 5/9 logic-bomb attack on E Corp as anarchist 'propaganda of the deed' - a shocking act meant to wake people from their comfortable slumber inside hierarchy - and positions it between Alexander Berkman's violent anarchism (mirroring Phillip Price's 'bullet in the right place') and Gandhi's nonviolent self-suffering, quoting satyagraha and the older Goldman's rejection of violence. He then runs the hack through just war theory's four questions (necessity, proportionality, justification, effectiveness), noting that wiping the debt records also destroyed savings and indirectly got people like Gideon killed, and that fsociety, as Trenton says, never paints the alternative society - so the reader is left to answer whether the deed was justified.
- ch. 13 "2. If I Don’t Listen to My Imaginary Friend, Why the Fuck Should I Listen to Yours" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Theory of Forms; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Kreider stages a chat between Plato and Aristotle about the show. On Plato's account, mimesis is an imitation of an imitation of the Forms, so Elliot's imaginary friend, his fake persona with Krista, and the Mr. Robot personality are intellectually and morally dangerous deceptions that let him commit terrorism without his rational self's consent; yet the Republic's censored poetry for the auxiliaries explains how fsociety's masked videos teach true beliefs, and how Elliot uses the fictional Mr. Robot to educate himself toward ideas he already knew were right. Aristotle's Poetics then defends imitation as natural and instructive - the show is a cautionary tragedy, and the Mr. Robot crutch is how Elliot eventually steps up to claim responsibility.
- ch. 14 "3. Click Bait for Black Fish" **·** Isaiah Berlin, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Two Concepts of Liberty; The General Will; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Porot reads Elliot through Berlin's positive liberty: people are enslaved to their lower selves - the 'daemons' of addiction and primal urge Elliot describes in 'eps1.3_da3m0ns.mp4' - and freedom requires a contract in which an external force holds you to your higher self. Elliot writes such contracts with Shayla over his drugs and imagines Mr. Robot as the paternalistic enforcer who pushes him off the pier when he breaks his word, while corporations run the reverse contract, 'hacking' people from within through addictive sugar, clickbait, and advertising. The black fish dream crystallizes this: everyone at the office devours the confined fish of reverse-contract slavery while Elliot alone eats Pop's pie - freedom through the father figure of Mr. Robot.
- ch. 15 "II. Control Is an Illusion" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "4. The End of Privacy" **·** Utopia and Dystopia — Brake reads Mr. Robot through Thomas More's Utopia: Hythloday's 'conspiracy of the rich' matches E Corp's Washington Township cover-up, his attacks on private property echo Elliot's monologue about property and money, and the island with 'nothing private anywhere' frames the provocative idea that the veil of privacy shelters corporate injustice that only lawbreaking - fsociety's hacks, Manning, Snowden, Assange - can lift into daylight. Yet More splits himself between idealist Hythloday and pragmatic More, and the messy aftermath of the 5/9 hack shows that utopian dreams implemented without caution can become nightmares.
- ch. 17 "5. We Become the Grid" **·** Thomas Hobbes, René Descartes, Martin Heidegger — The State of Nature; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Extended Mind — Ketcham updates Hobbes for the network age: the grid born of ARPANET and Cold War mutual destruction has devolved into a new state of nature, out of which a coming 'Leviathan' - the one percent of the one percent - will rule invisibly by curating your memories, your purchases, your spouse, and whole countries like the diamond-republic fable. Invoking Descartes's evil demon and Heidegger's ready-to-hand, he asks whether we have become the grid, an external brain we can no longer control, and concludes that Elliot, the rogue 'Ebola' who hacks for justice rather than profit, is exactly the loose cannon Leviathan would quarantine.
- ch. 18 "6. Who Has the Power" **·** Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — The Panopticon (surveillance); Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Samuelson uses Foucault to dismantle Phillip Price's creed of being 'the most powerful person in the room': power is not a possession but an operation. Elliot's men in black and the FBI's surveillance are disciplinary power - Bentham's panopticon realized in Allsafe's cube farm and the internet itself - while Angela's fight over the Washington Township leak is a struggle with biopower that no sovereign can be punished for, and Whiterose's knowledge is power-knowledge that operates anonymously no matter who holds it. If Foucault is right, Price, Mr. Robot, and Zheng are mere conduits, and no one will ever be the most powerful person in the room.
- ch. 19 "III. They All Think I’m the Ringleader" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "7. What Kind of Revolutionary Is Mr. Robot" **·** John Dewey — Anarchism; Pragmatism; Democracy as a Way of Life — Ralston traces Mr. Robot's hacktivist philosophy to David Graeber's anarchism behind Occupy Wall Street and to Anonymous's 'moralfags' who hack for a higher cause (Project Chanology as the template for fsociety), then stages the Dewey-Trotsky debate on means and ends: Trotsky's 'Their Morals and Ours' lets the end justify any means, while Dewey's means-end continuum demands experimental, democratic means suited to the end. The verdict: Mr. Robot's ends are anarchist and his means pragmatist - he will frame Terry Colby and risk lives at Steel Mountain, but rejects means like actual slavery that would betray the movement's own ideal of liberation.
- ch. 21 "8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Death of God; Existentialism; Authenticity — Hoyt places Mr. Robot in the film noir tradition born when world war proved Nietzsche's point that God is dead: as with Bogart's Spade turning in Brigid in The Maltese Falcon, the noir hero's task is existential self-definition - guarding integrity in a world without truth, justice, or absolute meaning. But where classic noir blamed gangsters, neo-noir from Chinatown through Fight Club to Mr. Robot points at capitalism and unbeatable conspiracies (Price apparently able to bend the federal government itself), and the show's cold blue offices and 'shortsighting' framings show characters breaking under the pressure of choices no space protects.
- ch. 22 "9. What Elliot Doesn’t Know Won’t Hurt You (Or Will It )" **·** René Descartes, Socrates — Philosophical Skepticism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito — Greene argues Elliot is in the worst possible position for a knower: Descartes's skeptical scenarios of madness, dreams, and the evil demon apply to everyone, but hit Elliot harder through morphine and ecstasy hallucinations, lucid dreams indistinguishable from waking (as Whiterose suggests), and a dissociative disorder so severe he spends months in prison believing he lives at his mother's house - with Mr. Robot even hiding facts from him, blocking the Socratic 'know thyself.' Yet by the Meno's knowledge problem he may be no worse off: he still catches the pedophile ring and brings down E Corp, so the hero of the show succeeds without knowledge.
- ch. 23 "IV. Politics Is for Puppets" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "10. If It Isn’t Justified Is It Still My Revolution" **·** Karl Marx — Class Struggle; Historical Materialism; The Ethics of Political Violence — Writing as a guilt-ridden fsociety member haunted by James Plouffe's on-air suicide, Altmann tests the 5/9 revolution against three theorists: Burke's conservatism condemns all revolution as destruction of social tradition (and fsociety's blackout chaos and Susan Jacobs's death seem to prove him right), while Marx's class struggle between E Corp's bourgeoisie and the indebted proletariat makes revolution the only exit from history's cycle. Kai Nielsen's condition - revolution is justified only when no other recourse exists - settles it: Angela's failed attempt to reform E Corp from within shows non-revolutionary change is impossible, so the author keeps fighting 'with a keyboard whose clacking is endless.'
- ch. 25 "11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Problem of Evil; The Death of God; Master and Slave Morality; The Übermensch — Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.
- ch. 26 "12. Why Angela Drops the Whistle" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Jones asks why Angela flees the Nuclear Regulatory Commission at the exact moment she could expose the Washington Township cover-up, and answers with the real world of whistleblowing: Chelsea Manning's thirty-five-year sentence shows the legal peril, and the Rasmussen poll branding Manning a traitor plus the Enron fallout show the court of public opinion demonizes whistleblowers. Tribal survival instincts make insiders punish anyone who drops the tribe's secrets, and coworkers must condemn the whistleblower to preserve their own self-worth against the mirror of their silence - so even a legally protected, morally sound Angela backs away.
- ch. 27 "V. Power Belongs to the People Who Take It" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "13. How to Become a Revolutionary" **·** Gilles Deleuze — Luzecky and Elsby argue traditional political philosophy cannot describe Mr. Robot's revolution - a leader who calls himself a computer virus - and turn to Deleuze and Guattari: capitalism runs on coded flows of money, labor, and desire (taxation existing to insert the state into our lives), and hackers become revolutionaries by interrupting those flows. Elliot is a 'nomadic war-machine' whose non-segmented space makes his power literally beyond measure, and the true revolution turns out to be personal and affirmative: embracing the countless fucked-up desires you are instead of accepting the coded range of acceptable behavior.
- ch. 29 "14. Is E Corp an Evil Person" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Theory of Forms; Humanity as an End in Itself — Wood asks what E Corp ontologically is: on Plato's theory, it would participate in a Form of Corporation, while Aristotle's primary substances show E Corp is not an individual at all - just a name for ways people interact. Corporate personhood (from 1819 contract rights through Citizens United and Hobby Lobby) makes it a legal person whose responsibility diffuses 'almost to the point of evaporation,' and Kant's humanity formula explains the unease: a legal fiction with no intentions or dignity can never respect persons as ends, which is why Angela's quest for a moral 'who' behind Washington Township ends only with the two ordinary executives Price hands her.
- ch. 30 "15. Reset Virtues" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Doll argues Elliot approximates Aristotelian virtue despite his vices: he craves eudaimonia, uses practical wisdom to recognize the harm the 5/9 hack caused innocent people ('I'll own it all'), and habituates himself against vice by confessing, exposing Ray's website, and restraining Mr. Robot even at the cost of Adderall binges and prison. Leon's 'existence could be beautiful, or it could be ugly, but that's on you' frames the choice of a life to fight for, and Krista's counsel leads Elliot to the golden mean of a 'handshake' with Mr. Robot - integrating the two identities rather than annihilating one - while the viewer serves as the if/then programming keeping him virtuous.
- ch. 31 "VI. Is Any of It Real" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "16. 0n-keeping-everyb0dy-1n-the-d4rk.docx" **·** René Descartes — Fallis treats Mr. Robot as a hidden war of epistemic adversaries - not Descartes's deceiving demon mostly, but combatants who keep each other in the dark. Testing Sissela Bok's definition of secret-keeping against counterexamples (Elliot keeps Krista in the dark just by holding his tongue; not reporting breakfast is not keeping people in the dark), he adopts Chisholm's 'negative deception' - intentionally causing a lack of true belief - and resolves the paradox of self-deception through the show's split centers of agency: the Mr. Robot part of Elliot's mind deceives the Elliot part about Tyrell, Stage Two, and prison itself.
- ch. 33 "17. Our Lying Eyes" **·** John Locke, George Berkeley — Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Tabula Rasa; Philosophical Skepticism — Wood asks how Elliot - and we, who see only what he sees - can know anything, and contrasts two empiricisms: Locke's white-paper mind furnished by ideas copied from mind-independent objects, which explains Mr. Robot as perceptual error, and Berkeley's idealism, on which only ideas and their divine cause exist, which makes Elliot's unshared hallucination of Mr. Robot dangerously hard to distinguish from reality. Consistency of perception is the only test left, and it fails Elliot until the pier video proves no one pushed him - and fails us again when his cozy Season Two routine turns out to be prison.
- ch. 34 "18. Psycho-Politics in a Burnout Society" **·** Michel Foucault — The Panopticon (surveillance); The Culture Industry — Pagnoni Berns and Aguilar read the show through Byung-Chul Han's philosophy: in the transparency society everyone stacks their life online - Krista is transparent to Elliot because her password is Dylan and her birthday, while he stays opaque - and psycho-politics replaces Foucauldian punishment with seduction, a digital panopticon (Operation Berenstain, Minister Zhang) whose inmates voluntarily build it. Elliot's attention deficits, Tyrell's breakdown over Sharon Knowles's corpse, and Gideon's fatigue embody the burnout society's neuronal violence, and even fsociety reproduces the systemic coercion it fights, leaving 'real life' only outside the system.
- ch. 35 "19. Please Tell Me You’re Seeing This Too" **·** Theodor Adorno — The Culture Industry — Ehrnberger argues Mr. Robot hooks us like a Trojan horse: Todorov's 'ambiguity of the fantastic' - the irresolvable hesitation over whether Elliot's world is real or imagined - makes his unreliable narration endlessly rewatchable, which is how a mainstream network show smuggles in Adorno's critique of the very culture industry that airs it. Adorno explains the sedation Elliot decries ('we wanna be sedated') and why enlightenment reverts to mythology - meritocracy, consumerism, digital connection as modern myths we no longer recognize as myths - while Ehrenberg's 'illness of responsibility' explains why freed people retreat into the comfort of those myths rather than bear freedom's weight.

## Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

- ch. 1 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors introduce the volume by reading Gaiman's fiction as travel literature: heroes like Richard Mayhew in Neverwhere, Coraline, and Shadow in American Gods are forced or seduced into enchanted worlds that press against the mundane, and must map and decode those worlds to survive, transforming themselves in the process. They contrast tourists, who stay detached behind camera and guidebook, with travelers, who engage and are changed, and argue that reading Gaiman philosophically turns readers into travelers. They close with Gaiman's Newbery speech about stories as 'good lies that say true things' that leave readers changed forever.
- ch. 8 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Seneca — Philosophical Skepticism; Free Will vs Determinism — Elizabeth Swanstrom reads Mr. Wednesday's recruitment of Shadow in American Gods as a two-man con that exploits Hume's account of causation: because the mind projects causal links from constant conjunction, Odin and Loki stage a chain of 'coincidences' (Laura's death, rerouted flights, the first-class seat) and use classic misdirection, from Sweeney's warning at Jack's Crocodile Bar to the Herodotus tale of Croesus, so that the mark never looks at the hand with the coin in it. Setting Hume's billiard-ball analysis against Seneca and the Stoic idea of derivative causality, she argues Wednesday manipulates association rather than chance itself. Shadow's counter-training in coin sleights, especially the Sucker Vanish, and Sweeney's gift of the resurrection coin that revives Laura introduce genuine chance, letting Shadow see the set-up, stop the sacrificial battle, and demonstrate that a causally saturated world still leaves room to break the game.
- ch. 10 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Tripartite Soul; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Greg Littmann stages Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under the Republic's charges against poetry: the novel is full of 'greatest of all lies' about gods behaving badly, from Odin and Loki's sacrificial plot to Czernobog's head-smashing, gods degrading themselves into lesser forms like Horus the road-kill-eating hawk and Media as Lucille Ball, and characters ruled by passion rather than reason, from Mad Sweeney drinking himself to death to Thor's suicide, corrupting a soul that should be governed by rationality. Against this he sets Aristotle's Poetics: listening to music and intellectual leisure are valuable in themselves, fiction is more philosophic than history because it shows what could happen, the impossible is justified when it astounds, and catharsis through pity for figures like the weeping Mad Sweeney purges rather than corrupts. Because American Gods' absurd premise unfolds with internally probable, character-consistent events (loyal Shadow, loving Laura, grifter Odin), it satisfies Aristotle's requirement that fantasy make artistic sense.
- ch. 11 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** John Dewey — Pragmatism; Truth as What Works — Ray Bossert reads American Gods as an allegory of American philosophy: like Gaiman's gods, American philosophers labor invisibly in the background while European publics canonize their thinkers, and Shadow's prison exchanges show the point, since Loki must beg him to read Herodotus ('It's cool') while Johnnie Larch's 'don't piss off people who work in airports' beats Shadow's abstract generalization in usefulness. Following Hickman's Deweyan instrumentalism, he argues the gods are survival tools humans craft from need and discard when obsolete, so Czernobog's hammer gives way to Media's television, Wednesday treats even his own son as an instrument, and the buffalo man's 'believe everything' is advice about keeping one's tools of survival working. The chapter ends on liberty: Shadow refuses to be a god because 'we don't need anyone to believe in us,' and in the Egyptian death trial he claims the most American reward, the freedom to choose his own afterlife.
- ch. 12 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Gottfried Leibniz, David Chalmers, René Descartes — Theory of Forms; Monadology; The Hard Problem of Consciousness; Allegory of the Cave — Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America. Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.
- ch. 13 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, George Berkeley, Zhuangzi, Bertrand Russell, David Chalmers — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream); Philosophical Zombies — T. Bradley Richards takes The Sandman's Dreamworld seriously as a hypothesis: could our nightly dreams be travels to a mind-independent place like Morpheus's realm? Starting from Zhuangzi's butterfly dream and Descartes's dream argument, he uses Berkeley's God-sustained idealism as a model for how Morpheus's mind could uphold the Dreamworld's order, and a thought experiment about glitchy dream-travel defuses Descartes's appeal to the discontinuity of dreams. Against the objection that dreams are blatantly contradictory ('it was Dave, but it also wasn't Dave'), he deploys Russell's theory of descriptions against Meinongian subsistence, Chalmers-style conceivability-implies-possibility reasoning from philosophical zombies, and Graham Priest's dialetheism, concluding that dreams could be experiences of an objective world, with waking and dreaming on a par.
- ch. 15 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Hannah Arendt, Richard Rorty — The Banality of Evil; The Ethics of Care; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry reads Neverwhere's magic invisibility as a model of real social invisibility: after Richard helps the injured Door he loses his job, his fiancee Jessica, and even the ability to be perceived, joining the homeless, slaves, and Jews under Nazism as people excluded from the moral community whose needs no longer register. Using Arendt's banality of evil to explain everyday indifference and Richard Rorty on torturers who fail to see a 'real' human, he distinguishes radical from partial invisibility, shown in Jessica stepping over the bleeding Door and misreading her need as 'sleep it off.' The remedy is Iris Murdoch's 'loving gaze' of just and careful attention, which seizes Richard before he can rationalize, backed by a practical wisdom about whose needs matter, so that acknowledging the invisible, down to apologizing to a rat in London Below, is what makes both them and us better.
- ch. 16 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito — Kandace Lytle maps Coraline's other mother onto Descartes's evil genius: a world-manipulating deceiver whose seductive sensory pleasures, from the gravy-train dinner to the adoring other father's songs, must be doubted in favor of the intellect, exactly as the wax argument shows that understanding comes from the mind and not the senses. Because Coraline enters the portal awake, Gaiman sidesteps the dream-skepticism worry and makes the other mother's world a parallel reality built to entrance, seduce, and possess her. Coraline's refusal to sew buttons in place of her eyes protects her autonomy and free will, the ghost children who lost their names and memories show what surrender costs, and the nameless cat's 'we know who we are, so we don't need names' guides her to the cogito, so that she defeats the deceiver by finding the 'I' in Coraline, a self-sufficiency the 2009 film version, the author argues, fails to capture.
- ch. 17 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Frank Jackson, Thomas Nagel — The Knowledge Argument (Mary's Room); What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Being-Toward-Death — Andrew Terjesen asks what Death could learn from living one mortal day per century in Sandman's Death: The High Cost of Living, after a little girl's 'How would you like it?' shamed the once icy Death into the practice. Using Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Nagel's bat to probe whether knowing what mortality is like requires first-person experience, he raises the 'Soul Man Effect' objection that Didi, like the fake black student in the 1986 film, always knows she will revert to being Death, and argues that simulation, not verbal description, is the efficient way to convey life's texture (Didi's hot-dog aftertaste). The real lesson, he concludes, is the existentialist one that each of us stands alone at death and that life's meaning lies in the unnoticed 'little moments' the dying regret missing, which only immersion in the distractions of living can teach Death, which is why the one-day-a-century program must continue.
- ch. 19 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jean-François Lyotard — The End of Grand Narratives — Wade Newhouse reads The Graveyard Book as a fusion of the coming-of-age tale and the Gothic ghost story, from The Turn of the Screw to Stephen King's haunted narcissists, and uses Lyotard's postmodern condition to explain the hybrid: Bod's self forms not by accepting one governing metanarrative but at Lyotardian 'nodal points' among many ghosts, each a fragment of history with its own partial morality, from the Roman Caius Pompeius to the witch Liza Hempstock. The Danse Macabre, where living and dead mix under rules neither remembers choosing, dramatizes borders that feel absolute, yet Bod's development consists in violating boundaries, befriending the outcast witch and hunting the Jacks on his own terms. The ending, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' offers a postmodern self most itself by being no one, with the acceptance of death as the one metanarrative even postmoderns keep, for Bod it is the first lesson rather than the last.
- ch. 20 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; The Panopticon (surveillance) — Najwa Al-Tabaa reads Sandman: Season of Mists through Derrida's paradox that only the unforgivable can truly be forgiven: Morpheus's freeing of Nada works as forgiveness precisely because condemning his lover to Hell was unforgivable, while Lucifer, who was never wronged by the damned, can give them only a devalued semblance of pardon, and they cling to punishment they feel they deserve. She then brings in Foucault's Discipline and Punish and Bentham's Panopticon to read the angels' rebuilt Hell of redemption as the modern rehabilitative prison, where watched souls are expected to reform themselves. The experiment fails, she argues, because redemption is imposed without hearing the prisoners, violating Derrida's condition that forgiveness needs a shared language, so the inmates prefer Lucifer's honest eternity of despair to a salvation they never asked for, a lesson about real prisons that seek rehabilitation through punishment.
- ch. 21 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Jean-Paul Sartre, Søren Kierkegaard — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Authenticity; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Wayne Yuen uses The Graveyard Book to teach the good life: Bod's family's murder, like students owing their existence to the Holocaust, is an unalloyed moral evil that still enables a better life, and Saul Smilansky's distinction between being 'sorry for' and 'sorry that' lets Bod benefit without endorsing the tragedy. His graveyard education is Aristotelian, virtues acquired through practice and models, from the Owenses' duty and Silas's wisdom to 'righteous indignation' against school bullies and friendship with Scarlett as intrinsically valuable, all building toward eudaimonia. The existentialist virtue of authenticity (attributed to Sartre and Kierkegaard) explains why Bod must be 'nobody but himself' rather than a copy of the vampire Silas, why the scavenged identities of the ghouls mark inauthenticity, and why wiping Scarlett's memory threatens her authenticity, resolving the apparent conflict between virtue and being oneself because bravery or wisdom is relative to the individual.
- ch. 22 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate); The Übermensch; The Death of God — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- ch. 24 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** David Lewis, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Bertrand Russell, Plato — Language Games — Tuomas Manninen asks how Gaiman's recycled mythological figures can be the same characters as their originals when Revelation's male, sword-wielding War becomes Good Omens' arms-dealing Carmine 'Red' Zuigiber and Pestilence retires in 1936 for Pollution, with the problem of talking truthfully about non-existent entities reaching back to Plato's Sophist. David Lewis's 'Truth in Fiction' makes the original author the arbiter of a character's properties, and Amie Thomasson's artifact theory makes fictional characters abstract artifacts created by authors, but only adding the type/token distinction and Wittgenstein's family resemblances, the same criss-crossing network of overlapping similarities by which we count games, lets Revelation's Four Horsemen and Gaiman's Four Bikers be tokens of one type. He closes with Russell's defense of philosophy's value: like Richard Mayhew's tale of London Below, a philosophical answer need not convince or be final to teach us 'what things may be.'
- ch. 25 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard, Michel Foucault — Existence Precedes Essence; Authenticity; Bad Faith; Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom) — Robert Tally Jr. reads The Graveyard Book as 'spectral existentialism': Bod's climax, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' is Sartre's existence precedes essence made literal, a self made rather than found, and the climactic claiming of the name enacts the self-ownership of the nursery-rhyme pauper 'who nobody owns.' Heidegger supplies the uncanny not-at-home-ness (unheimlich) of the graveyard, which Tally, citing Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' calls a heterotopia, while Silas the vampire embodies Lukacs's transcendental homelessness and Kierkegaardian anxiety is transmuted by Bod into the spectral gift of Fear he wields on his bullies. The identity-leeching ghouls named after the Duke of Westminster and the 33rd President are the avatars of bad faith, and the Jacks' attempt to dodge the prophecy fulfills it like Oedipus's, showing that Bod's fate, too, is self-made.

- ch. 9 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "1 Primal and Spontaneous Neil Young’s Aesthetics of Authenticity" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson, Friedrich Nietzsche, Walter Benjamin, Immanuel Kant — Authenticity; The Apollonian and the Dionysian; The Aura of the Artwork; Self-Reliance — Forest argues that Neil Young's habit of keeping early, flawed takes with Crazy Horse ("audio verite") embodies an aesthetic of authenticity as primal spontaneity. He reads Young through Emerson's self-reliance and trust in first impressions, Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian split (Harvest vs. Tonight's the Night, Young's onstage abandon on "Like a Hurricane"), Benjamin's loss of aura in mechanical reproduction, and Collingwood's art/craft distinction, contending that the "garage band" imperfections of jams like "Down by the River" let fans identify with the band's expressive, un-repeatable moment.
- ch. 11 "2 Neil Young and Creativity" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Arthur Schopenhauer, Friedrich Nietzsche — Pragmatism; Authenticity — Berger surveys Young's repeated claim that he does not intentionally compose but "receives" songs, comparing himself to a radio station or microphone and echoing Schubert's "I remember it." He illuminates this with C.S. Peirce's categories of firstness (feeling), secondness (reaction) and thirdness (thought/signs), arguing that Young's refusal to "judge" lyrics like "Tell Me Why" or "Cowgirl in the Sand" protects the originary feeling, and that songs communicate feeling through Peircean icons and metaphors rather than deliberate rational design.
- ch. 12 "3 Lawsuits, Master Narratives, and Artistic Commodification" **·** Theodor Adorno, Karl Marx — The Culture Industry; Commodity Fetishism — Mitchell examines Young's Geffen-era lawsuit (sued in 1983 for "uncharacteristic" music like Trans and Everybody's Rockin') and the competing rebel/misunderstood-artist/lost-in-the-video-era narratives around it. Using Heilbroner on capitalism's commodification of rebellious art and Mark Fisher's "capitalist realism" and pre-corporation of dissent (Cobain as spectacle), he argues that Young himself actively authored the "rocker-turned-folkie" and anti-commercial persona, so that even his gestures of resistance to the music business were absorbed as marketable integrity.
- ch. 13 "4 Extended Mind and the Music of Trans" **·** Andy Clark, David Chalmers, Daniel Dennett — The Extended Mind; Authenticity — Umbaugh reads Young's synthesizer/Vocoder album Trans, written amid efforts to communicate with his quadriplegic son Ben ("Transformer Man"), alongside Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis and its Parity Principle. He uses examples (Otto's notebook, bartenders' glassware, navigation, Dennett on the elderly) to argue cognition couples with external scaffolding, and parallels the "unnatural" reception of Trans (like the homophobic anti-disco backlash) with resistance to extended cognition, concluding both Trans and the extended mind are authentic once the "natural/artificial" boundary is questioned.
- ch. 14 "5 Neil Young Lover of Sun, Moon and Cars" **·** Henry David Thoreau, Aldo Leopold, John Dewey — Pragmatism; The Land Ethic; Walden (deliberate living); Anthropocentrism — Anderson traces Young's environmentalism from the hippie-romantic nature worship of "After the Gold Rush" and Greendale toward a pragmatic "middle way" that reconciles his love of nature with his love of cars and recording technology (the Lincvolt project, Storytone). Drawing on Thoreau, Muir and Leopold's land ethic while rejecting the fixed prescriptions of Singer and Regan, he presents Young as an experimentalist "meliorist" who owns his own complicity in CO2 abuse and urges informed, practical, self-aware action rather than utopian or deontological solutions.
- ch. 15 "6 Neil Young and American Indians Politics, Lyrics, and Authenticity" **·** Michel de Montaigne — Objectification; Authenticity — Hester critiques Young's treatment of American Indians, arguing "Cortez the Killer" idealizes the Aztecs into Montaigne-style "noble savages," makes their sacrifices seem voluntary, and ultimately centers Young's own lost-love lament rather than the conquest's real victims. He shows "Pocahontas" objectifies and commodifies a Native woman (the "thousand pelts" line, Young's cavalier interview remarks) as cultural appropriation and "playing Indian," yet notes Young's genuine activism (Honor the Treaties) leaves fans wanting to credit his good intentions.
- ch. 16 "7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young" **·** John Locke, David Hume, Thomas Hobbes, Daniel Dennett, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Bundle Theory of Self — Sizer analyzes how memory shapes Young's songwriting: childhood trauma (polio, his parents' divorce, Omemee) fueling "Sugar Mountain," "Helpless" and "I Am a Child"; the "use and lose" pattern of collaborators and the ghost of Danny Whitten in Crazy Horse; and his late-life dread of memory loss watching his father's dementia. He frames this with Hobbes and Hume on memory-as-imagery, Wittgenstein's associative memory, and Locke's memory theory of personal identity (with Dennett on writing as a means to reconstruct and preserve the self).
- ch. 17 "8 Images of Women in the Music and Life of Neil Young" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Mary Wollstonecraft, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, William James — Objectification; The Male Gaze; Feminism — McKenna uses Sarah Lucia Hoagland's feminist analysis of "heterosexualism" to argue that Young's songs ("Cinnamon Girl," "A Man Needs a Maid," "Unknown Legend," and the femicide of "Down by the River") portray women as objects to be desired, possessed, used and harmed, positioning them as helpmates (like Rousseau's Sophie, against which Wollstonecraft argued). She extends this to Young's own "backgrounding" of the women in his life (Pegi, Carrie Snodgress) in Waging Heavy Peace, comparing him to William James's reliance on his wife Alice.
- ch. 18 "9 Neil Young’s Search for the Simple Life" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Aristotle, Henry David Thoreau, Sigmund Freud, Epicurus — Bad Faith; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Walden (deliberate living); Existentialism — Watson and Riches reinterpret "A Man Needs a Maid" not as simple misogyny but as Young's ambivalent inner conflict between craving companionship and fearing the pain of intimacy. They read his pursuit of the "simple life" ("Heart of Gold," avoidance of reading) through Epicurean simplicity, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Bowlby/Freudian avoidant attachment and cognitive dissonance, and Sartre's "bad faith" as self-deception, set against Thoreau's chosen solitude and Aristotle's claim that the non-social being is "beast or god."
- ch. 19 "10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care" **·** Carol Gilligan, Jane Addams, Nel Noddings, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — The Ethics of Care; Deontology; Utilitarianism — Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.

- ch. 21 "Contributors" *(notes)*

## Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield

- ch. 1 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*

- ch. 9 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The volume's introduction, 'Learning from the Insiders.' It introduces Orange Is the New Black (Piper Kerman's book and the Netflix series about Piper's time in Litchfield) and previews each contributor's topic: other minds, manipulation, the Prisoner's Dilemma, religion, existentialism, race, Crazy Eyes as Don Quixote, prisoners' moral obligations, Nietzsche on a trans woman, Aristotle on friendship, Bentham's panopticon, and Foucault on punishment. It frames the show as ripe for philosophy on punishment, moral obligation, existential themes, and race, gender, identity, and sexuality without itself applying any single theory.
- ch. 10 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Bad Faith; Authenticity — Hoyt argues the show's core lesson is dropping the little lies we tell ourselves: Bennett calls his crush on Daya 'love' to excuse framing Mendez, Pornstache is a man performing a blustering guard (Sartrean bad faith), and Larry and Polly's 'love just happened' dodges responsibility for betrayal. Piper's arc (the Colt 45 scene in '40 Oz. of Furlough') shows the payoff of authenticity, while Healy's Safe Place is a fantasy that cannot will a change of worldview. Using Wittgenstein's aspect-seeing from Philosophical Investigations, he shows how characters and viewers miss ethically significant meanings, like Taystee's shower 'compliment' as intimidation and Piper's convenient blindness to Soso's humanity when selling her for a blanket.
- ch. 12 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Philosophy of Love — Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.
- ch. 13 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch — DiEdoardo, a trans criminal-defense lawyer, reads Sophia Burset through Nietzsche: her 'why of life' (bringing her body into line with her gender identity) lets her endure the 'how' of misgendering by Figueroa, Red, and her wife Crystal, plus a sentencing disparity she compares to Piper's lighter drug deal. Burset's rational appeals ('Lesbian Request Denied,' her WAC run) fail, confirming Nietzsche's disdain for dialectics, but in 'A Whole Other Hole' she stops asking and acts, teaching the inmates vulval anatomy until Taystee's 'she's right' marks her acceptance. She is the 'creator' who breaks the tables of values, migrating from freak to woman with unique knowledge.
- ch. 15 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Carveth examines African-American portrayal on the show through Piper, Taystee, and Sophia: Piper's whiteness wins Healy's favoritism and makes her complicit in keeping the inmates powerless ('we understand each other, don't we?'), while Taystee's parole violation shows Litchfield as the only place she fits. Using Lippmann's account of media stereotypes, he credits the show with multidimensional characters of color but faults it for a 'white voice': Black women's incarceration is framed as bad choices and culture of poverty, and only Piper's SHU suffering is shown while Black and Latina women cycle through it. The series critiques the prison system yet stops short of showing the structural forces that leave its inmates no options.
- ch. 16 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; The Panopticon (surveillance); The Hedonic Calculus; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Ketcham greets Piper Kerman at the prison door with Bentham's ghost: the state's utility calculation of her drug money laundering, the rat's discounted sentence, and the design of the panopticon, whose one-way inspection tower was meant to make surveillance cheap, obedience automatic, and prisoners productive and even saved. He contrasts that reform vision with the reality reconstructed from the book, where punishment falls on everyone, including families paying commissary prices and denied visits, and Danbury's 'vocational training' amounts to changing light bulbs. Bentham's own principle that 'punishment is an evil' is turned against a system that warehouses rather than rehabilitates.
- ch. 18 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Authenticity; Existentialism — Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.
- ch. 19 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Michel Foucault — Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Panopticon (surveillance); Power/Knowledge — Stephenson and Waller start from disliking bland, marketable Piper and use Foucault's Discipline and Punish to argue that Litchfield is a microcosm of State power: arbitrary unwritten rules, counts, strip searches, and constant surveillance train prisoners into docile, compliant participants in capitalism, with specialist wardens, psychologists, and lawyers molding the abnormal into the normal. Prisoners specialize too (Red's kitchen, Nicky's ear, Vee's drugs) to survive, and specialization hides the surveillance. The show itself embodies the mechanism, making viewers aware they too live under the Panopticon, though deviants like Crazy Eyes and her standing pee keep open the possibility of refusing State values.
- ch. 21 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Niccolò Machiavelli — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Autonomy of the Will; The Unexamined Life; The Ends Justify the Means — Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.
- ch. 22 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** John Rawls — Justice as Fairness; The Ethics of Care — Robison-Greene argues Rawlsian ideal theory breaks down at Litchfield: Soso's hunger strike gets only cosmetic concessions from Caputo, Sophia's WAC human-rights platform loses to Taystee's realism, and Piper learns the council 'is basically bullshit,' showing how idealization made by the powerful ignores the lived facts of Mendoza's abusive marriage, Jimmy's 'compassionate' death sentence, and Sophia's denied hormones. Against taking a 'moral holiday' in prison, she proposes care ethics, with role-based duties sensitive to actual circumstances, as the morality that fits life inside, and suggests non-ideal theory may fit the outside world too.
- ch. 24 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, Karl Marx — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; The Ethics of Ambiguity; The Meaning of Life — Walker contrasts Pennsatucky's Christian fundamentalism with Piper's secular humanism (Kurtz's six features) in their 'Fool Me Once' confrontation. With no God, Sartre's existence precedes essence makes Piper condemned to create her own meaning: owning her crime to her mother and confessing the Pennsatucky prank, while Red and Vee play Sartre's cafe waiter, reducing themselves to chef and dealer, and Pennsatucky's 'defender of the unborn' persona is de Beauvoir's sub-man sheltering behind ready-made values. Marx's opium-of-the-people analogy explains why comforting, unverifiable belief can block the authentic, responsible pursuit of a meaningful life.
- ch. 25 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — Archibald casts Crazy Eyes as the show's Don Quixote, read through Descartes's Meditations: like Descartes ridding himself of conditioned false beliefs, Suzanne slaps her head to 'reset' and question everything, and like Quixote she blames an inner evil enchanter when her noble illusions collapse. Her rationalist imagination (chivalry, poetry, Piper as her Dulcinea) produces false beliefs that hurt, above all her devoted service to the manipulative Vee, yet the same faculty creates the beauty, coping, and nobility that make an ugly prison survivable, so truth may not be all that matters.
- ch. 27 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Embodiment (the lived body) — Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.
- ch. 28 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Susan Wolf — Meaning in Life; Dharma; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Duffy applies Susan Wolf's formula (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) to Red's cooking, Poussey's friendship, and Taystee's library work, arguing these women meet the conditions yet still cannot live meaningful lives because Litchfield hands out 'chickens': WAC, the mock job fair, and the yard chicken are illusions of meaning designed to keep inmates quiet, as Healy admits with his bath-before-dinner analogy. Only projects that change the prison's conditions themselves, Piper's newsletter sting and Soso's hunger strike, are genuinely meaningful, and the yogic dharma of non-attachment (Yoga Jones's mandala advice) is a survival tool, not a substitute. She closes that guards too can find meaning, and have an obligation, in rehabilitating rather than punishing.
- ch. 30 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Elsby and Luzecky use Nicomachean Ethics VIII to sort Litchfield's bonds: Red's kitchen empire runs on friendships of utility that dissolve when her pipeline closes, race pre-assigns everyone's default friends, and Vee, who sleeps with RJ before having him killed, is incapable of friendship in any sense. The chapter locates genuine Aristotelian friendship only in Red's concern that Nicky stay off heroin (wishing her good for her own sake) and reads Red's sparing of Vee, held by a plastic bag, as respect without care, the recognition of a kindred quality that distinguishes Red from her evil counterpart.
- ch. 31 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Ethical Egoism — Greene reconstructs the Prisoner's Dilemma with Pennsatucky and Vee in separate interrogation rooms, then maps a variant onto 'Thirsty Bird': whatever Alex does, Piper is better off testifying against Kubra, yet mutual silence was the group-rational outcome the two pact on the van ride. Alex defects anyway, leaving Piper with perjury and no leniency, and Greene argues Piper should have done the 'rational' thing, since Balik's revenge is only a threat while extra time in Litchfield is a certain harm and Alex has always been willing to screw her. The episode shows why honor among the self-interested fails without trust.
- ch. 32 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' appendix, 'Sugar and Spice and Some Things Not So Nice!,' argues that part of the show's success is our cultural obsession with women-in-prison stories, from the film Caged to tabloid celebrity mugshots. It then catalogues famous imprisoned women from history and today: Marie Antoinette and Eleanor of Aquitaine under house arrest, Elizabeth Bathory and Joan of Arc in castle towers, the Salem witches, Patty Hearst, Billie Holiday and Martha Stewart at Alderson, Pussy Riot in Russian penal colonies, Aileen Wuornos, and the Tower of London's Anne Boleyn and Anne Askew. The survey supplies the real history behind the women-in-prison genre that Litchfield reworks, with no single philosopher or theory applied.
- ch. 33 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 34 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(notes)*

- ch. 9 "Leda Thinkin’ to Us . ." *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction retells Sarah Manning's situation: a broke grifter on the run from her drug-dealing ex, she watches her double Beth kill herself on the train platform and steals her identity, which earns her shootings, kidnapping, torture, and the loss of her daughter. It jokes that Sarah's real mistake was not reading this book first, listing its topics — the metaphysics of cloning, personal identity, sisterhood, family, the absurd, Buddhism, feminism, epistemology — as the Mill-style "higher pleasures" that would have prepared her, and ushers the reader on to Chapter 1.
- ch. 10 "Part I “How many of us are there ”" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. Fearfully and Wonderfully Made" **·** Derek Parfit — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Argues that Project Leda and Castor are a textbook case of Parfit's non-identity problem and its "Implausible Conclusion": Neolution knowingly built the clones barren by design and doomed to fatal illness, yet since none of them could have existed otherwise, and their lives remain worth living, it appears the clones were not harmed — the same paradox as Sarah conceiving Kira young and disadvantaged. After surveying Boonin's conclusion that every escape route from the paradox fails and Benatar's antinatalist extreme, the chapter adopts Rivka Weinberg's solution that existence is a condition rather than a conferred good, so the wrong lies in knowingly making a person a means to eugenic ends. The Leda dance party at the end of Season Two, where each clone dances in her own style, shows the book's verdict: the clones' lives are worth living on their own terms, exactly as they fight to live them.
- ch. 12 "2. Go Ask Alison" **·** John Stuart Mill — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Treats Project Leda's monitors as data gatherers in a botched social-scientific experiment, contrasting the Mill/Durkheim prediction paradigm (social science modeled on physics, seeking causes and regularities) with Max Weber's interpretive paradigm that seeks motives and understanding from the inside. Donnie's ignorance of the experiment and deep involvement in Alison's life skew his reports; Daniel and the clone-raised Rachel, who thinks of clones as property, ruin Rachel's role as the experiment's control group; and Delphine's love for Cosima makes her report selectively. The chapter concludes that Leda fails as science under both paradigms while trampling the informed-consent ethics owed to human subjects — the same project that got Alison's neighbor Aynsley killed.
- ch. 13 "3. When Clone Club Looks for Answers" **·** Aristotle, Epicurus — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Maps two ancient accounts of happiness onto the two clones we meet first. Cosima is the Aristotelian: like her fellow biologist Aristotle she holds that knowing truth for its own sake is essential to human flourishing, so she demands Sarah's briefcase ("the answers are in the briefcase"), studies a murdered sister's autopsy, and accepts Leekie's offer of unfettered research even inside Dyad. Alison is the Epicurean: happiness is the removal of pain and protection from threat, so she wants nothing to do with the C-word, hunts her monitor only to restore her safety, and signs Leekie's contract for the promise that her family will be left alone.
- ch. 14 "4. Who Owns Clones" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Natural Rights — Takes the message Cosima decodes in the clones' DNA — "This organism and derivative genetic material is restricted intellectual property" — and asks whether Dyad can legally and morally own the Clone Club. The chapter walks through US patent law and the Supreme Court's Myriad Genetics decision (naturally occurring DNA unpatentable, synthetic cDNA patentable) and argues that because the Leda and Castor clones were genetically engineered, their modified sequences could fall under the synthetic exception, making ownership legally possible. Morally, though, it sides with self-ownership: people own the products of their labor but not people, so patenting clones would recreate the wrongs of slavery, down to who controls clone marriages and clone offspring.
- ch. 15 "Part II “If we’re genetically identical, do you get that little patch of dry skin between your eyebrows ”" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "5. The Human Being in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction" **·** Walter Benjamin, Hannah Arendt — The Aura of the Artwork; Authenticity — Extends Walter Benjamin's analysis of art under mechanical reproduction to human cloning: as photography and film stripped artworks of their "aura" (their unique link to an origin) while democratizing art, cloning strips human beings of Hannah Arendt's "natality" — our connection to a unique beginning — while democratizing human nature itself. The chapter argues this is liberation, not loss: Sarah is as human as Felix or Kira, denying the clones' humanity would strip the naturally born of their own freedom ("Either Sarah and her sisters are human, or no one is"), and Tony Sawicki's chosen trans identity shows that once natality stops being destiny, authenticity and autonomy become possible for the first time. The only truly immoral path is Leda and Castor's — treating the bioengineered as property, as Rachel was raised to treat herself.
- ch. 17 "6. One Clone from Another" **·** John Locke, The Buddha, David Hume, Aristotle, René Descartes — Personal Identity; Non-Self (anatman); Personal Identity (memory theory) — Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.
- ch. 18 "7. I Am and Am Not You" **·** Edmund Husserl, Søren Kierkegaard — Phenomenology; Embodiment (the lived body); Personal Identity — Reads the opening scene phenomenologically: when Sarah sees her face on Beth, her identity does not merely change genetically but unravels generatively, since her birth, ancestry, and place in world-history are all thrown into question. Using Husserl's lived-body (the absolute "here" of experience), his static/genetic/generative levels of analysis, the homeworld/alienworld distinction (Clone Club solidifies its identity against the Castor "brothers," until Helena cradles the dying Rudy), and Husserl's co-originality of I and world, the chapter presents identity as intersubjective, constituted by shared projects like Sarah's fight for Kira and the Clone Club's tribe-rituals. Kierkegaard's "life must be lived forwards but understood backwards" is broadened: to understand identity we must look before our own birth and beyond our death, into the lifeworld we inherit and pass on.
- ch. 19 "Part III “You want to grow a tail, that’s your business.”" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "8. Laughing in the Face of the Absurd" **·** Albert Camus, Simone de Beauvoir, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; The Ethics of Ambiguity; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Argues that watching Beth die on the platform is Sarah's existential awakening — the absurd realization that "it is no longer true that everyone has their own face" — analyzed through Camus's absurd (the impossible and the contradictory), Sartre's nausea at inhuman humans, and Beauvoir's "subman" who never wakes from the mechanical life. Sarah must repeatedly witness "her own" death (Beth, Katja, Jennifer, the Helsinki clones), which robs death and life of settled meaning, yet she refuses nihilism: exercising the radical freedom Sartre says grounds all values, she fights Dyad on behalf of everyone's freedom, implicitly choosing it for all humanity. Like Camus's Sisyphus, whose rock is his thing, her struggle is her thing — and the Season Two clone dance party is her laughing in the face of the absurd.
- ch. 21 "9. Variation under Ethics" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; The Harm Principle; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Weighs the clones' bodily autonomy against the special obligations they owe one another, since genetic sisters can harm each other as no strangers can: Helena's murder of Katja nearly pins a killing on Sarah, and Vic's drug-world drags danger into Alison's suburb. The chapter builds a clone-specific cousin of Kant's categorical imperative — "act only and always in a way that you would want your clone to act" — to argue that the clones' liberty may be legitimately more restricted than ours: Alison's public drunkenness endangers sisters who can be mistaken for her, clones arguably must stay in Clone Club and share medical information like Cosima's illness, and hard cases (Beth's suicide leaving cases dangling, the brain-cut-open Castor clone begging Helena to kill him) all turn on balancing autonomy against what we owe others.
- ch. 22 "10. How Can Clones Disagree" *(no index entry yet)* — Uses the clones to test whether rational disagreement between epistemic peers with identical evidence is possible. Helena's convent indoctrination places her beyond peerhood, and Rachel's vastly superior inside information voids shared evidence, so neither of those clashes counts — but the Sarah–Cosima argument over approaching Delphine does: they are peers on the monitor question, they share all the relevant evidence about Paul and Delphine, and the unshareable "private evidence" (Sarah's knowledge of what fooling Paul felt like) turns out to be mere feeling, not evidence, as the blindfolded free-throw example shows. The clones therefore vindicate the possibility of rational disagreement.
- ch. 23 "Part IV “You know I never would’ve got in if you’d said we were going to suburbia.”" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "11. Leda, Castor, and Their Families" **·** Heteronormativity; Feminism; Objectification — Shows how the clones queer the normative family: clones as such are "biological outlaws" (via Stephanie Turner's reading of Ripley in Alien), Siobhan turns out to be the genetic half-sister of the clones cloned from her own mother Kendall, and the chosen family — Felix the "brother sestra," Kira's aunties, Helena's dream baby shower — repeatedly rebuilds kinship outside blood and marriage. Against this stands the stripping of reproductive agency: the infertility sequence written into the Leda clones, Coady's weaponized sterilizing virus, and above all Helena, whose eggs are harvested and implanted by Henrik and Gracie's father without consent. The chapter's conclusion is that Orphan Black's blood families are abusive and controlling while the non-normative chosen families of Clone Club are where love and consent actually live.
- ch. 25 "12. Not Why but Who" **·** Sigmund Freud, Jacques Lacan — The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real; Feminism — Reads the mothers of Orphan Black through Freud and Lacan: Dr. Coady is the "phallic mother" at the center of the Castor clones' Oedipal drama (Rudy's kiss, the DNA trophies brought home to Mom), Tomas is Helena's abusive false father, Rachel is the child of a shattered Oedipal triangle, and the Symbolic Order that makes men active rational subjects and women passive reproductive objects is mirrored in the defects — neurological for the male clones, reproductive for the female. The chapter then brings in Luce Irigaray to show the show rewriting these stereotypes: the clones' spectrum of personalities and their constant impersonations destabilize fixed gender categories, and the many equally "real" mothers (Mrs. S., Amelia, Alison, Kendall) burst the woman-equals-womb equation. Beth's counsel to the delirious Sarah — "Stop asking 'Why?' and start asking 'Who?'" — becomes the feminist move from mechanism to women as active subjects.
- ch. 26 "13. Sisterhood’s Back in Orphan Black" **·** Feminism; Intersectionality — Recounts the rise and fall of second-wave sisterhood — the dream of a unified female voice that erased differences of race, class, sexuality, and nation until the 1980s backlash killed it — and argues Orphan Black resurrects a corrected version through Rosi Braidotti's posthumanism. The clones, disposable bodies of biogenetic capitalism, build a sisterhood that celebrates difference (grunge Sarah, dreads-and-lab-coat Cosima, suburban Alison, savage Helena) rather than enforcing sameness, and that welcomes the Others the Seventies excluded — gay Felix, Black Art, Hindu Raj — while white Western men like Paul remain the surveillance agents of the backlash. Through posthumanism's dissolution of fixed human identity, the chapter claims, feminism's old ideal returns both transformed and inclusive.
- ch. 27 "14. Re Production" **·** Aristotle, Simone de Beauvoir — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Woman as the Other; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); One Is Not Born a Woman — Framed as leaked Project memoranda, the chapter argues Projects Leda and Castor embody philosophy's male-rational/female-reproductive dichotomy: Aristotle's function argument defined the human good (eudaimonia) through rationality while relegating women to reproduction, and the clones' engineered diseases literalize the split — fatal illness of the reproductive organs in the Leda clones, of the brain in the Castor. Simone de Beauvoir's Second Sex supplies the critique: "woman" treated as synonymous with womb, the Other denied the rich self-definition granted men, visible in Leda's passive unmonitored clones versus Castor's self-aware, active brothers. Combining a redeemed Aristotle (practical wisdom shows virtuous potential is not set by biological sex) with Beauvoir's free, independent woman, the chapter concludes both reproductive and rational autonomy must be restored to the clones of both sexes.
- ch. 28 "Part V “You just broke the first rule of Clone Club.”" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "15. The C-Word" **·** David Hume, Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant — The Naturalistic Fallacy; Is–Ought Problem; Master and Slave Morality; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Works through the ethics of cloning and genetic selection, starting with the objection that such technologies are "unnatural": that reasoning commits the naturalistic fallacy, since following Hume you can't get an ought from an is, and human ingenuity (roads, eyeglasses, IVF) is itself part of nature. Using Nietzsche's Genealogy account of master morality — good as the noble traits of intelligence, beauty, and strength — the chapter asks whether parents would then be obliged to engineer better children, while warning where trait-selection slides: Nazi eugenics, racist trait-lists (both Leda and Castor are white and conventionally attractive), and "abilism" against the deaf. It concludes that cloning itself is not evil: Projects Leda and Castor are immoral not because they clone but because they treat clones as mere means to an end, in Kant's sense, and trample their autonomy.
- ch. 30 "16. Is Sarah Manning Responsible for What She Does" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Uses the genetically identical Leda clones against genetic determinism: Helena seems excused and Cosima responsible despite identical genes, so upbringing must explain the difference. But appealing to background triggers Galen Strawson's Basic Argument — no one is ultimately responsible for who they are, so no one is ultimately responsible for what they do — which the authors escape through Peter Strawson's reactive attitudes (our disgust at Helena softening to pity once her abuse is known, our judgment of Donnie shifting from malice to gullibility) and John Martin Fischer's two conditions: an agent is responsible when she is responsive to reasons that would move well-adjusted rational people and takes ownership of the psychology that produces her action. Helena's Prolethean programming exempts her; Cosima, Alison, and a marginally reformed Sarah remain responsible for what they do.
- ch. 31 "17. Dialog with the Buddha" **·** The Buddha — Karma and Rebirth; Non-Self (anatman); The Four Noble Truths; Impermanence (anicca) — A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.
- ch. 32 "A Brief History of Cloning" **·** Personal Identity — A history of cloning in science and popular culture, from Driesch's 1885 sea-urchin split and the tadpole nuclear-transfer work of Briggs, King, and Gurdon, through Rorvik's In His Image hoax, to Dolly, Polly, Ditto and Neti, and Mitalipov's human embryonic stem cells. On the fiction side it tracks how early stories (Sleeper, Four Sided Triangle, The World of Null-A, Invasion of the Body Snatchers) assumed a clone is literally the same person as the original, with the same age, memories, and desires — a metaphysical mistake, since a clone is a new person whose own experiences make her someone else — while later work (The Boys from Brazil, Jurassic Park, The Island, Never Let Me Go, Moon) got the science roughly right and moved on to the ethics, exactly where Orphan Black, with its careful Leda and Castor biology, lands.
