## Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture

- ch. 1 "Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Table of Contents" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 6 "NOTES" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Allegory of the Cave; The Culture Industry — William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.
- ch. 7 "I - PHILOSOPHY AND POPULAR CULTURE" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "NOTES" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Aristotle, René Descartes — The Ethics of Ambiguity; Existentialism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.
- ch. 9 "NOTES" **·** Plato, Theodor Adorno, Walter Benjamin — Allegory of the Cave; The Culture Industry; The Aura of the Artwork — Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).
- ch. 10 "NOTES" *(no index entry yet)* — Theodore Gracyk analyzes artistic allusion in mass art, arguing (against Carrier and partly with Carroll) that accessibility does not preclude esoteric interpretive richness. His signature case is that The Matrix's red/blue pill scene overtly alludes to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland yet covertly alludes to Lewis Carroll's Sylvie and Bruno lockets, foreshadowing Neo as a Christ figure who must 'love all.' Drawing on Paul Grice's conversational implicature and Austin's illocutionary/perlocutionary speech-act theory, he argues allusion (Alien/Star Wars, Randy Newman's 'I Love L.A.', the Deliverance banjo in The Simpsons) is intentional and normatively constrains which associations transfer from source to alluding text.
- ch. 11 "NOTES" **·** Plato — Noel Carroll examines how popular fictions bind audiences emotionally through their relation to characters, starting from Plato's claim in the Republic that the popular arts pander to the emotions (pity and fear). He rejects both 'identification' (we rarely share characters' states—we fear for lovers who feel bliss, feel joy when the villain is foiled) and the fashionable 'simulation' theory as comprehensive accounts, arguing instead that sympathy—a pro-attitude directed at morally endorsable protagonists like Maximus in Gladiator—is the real 'tie that binds,' supplemented by involuntary 'mirror reflexes' (mimicking a screaming face in horror films, tapping to Riverdance).
- ch. 12 "NOTES" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo, G.E. Moore — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Theory of Forms — Ted Cohen denies there is any sound argument from 'X is better than Y' to 'it is better to like X,' using Bach vs. Elvis vs. Milton Babbitt on complexity to show the criterion collapses. He reframes art around 'communities of appreciation'—citing Augustine's claim that a people is defined by what it loves in common—and reports (via a blues club in Memphis and the Marriage of Figaro) that what all appreciators of a work share is 'nothing' but their love of it, a Goodman-style nominalism. He challenges Kant's insistence that genuine aesthetic judgments claim universality, arguing real appreciative communities are less-than-universal overlapping circles.
- ch. 13 "NOTES" **·** G.E. Moore, Theodor Adorno, Immanuel Kant, G.W.F. Hegel, John Dewey, Aristotle — The Culture Industry; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Pragmatism — Richard Shusterman defends the entertainment value of popular art from a pragmatist ('meliorist') stance, tracing entertainment's genealogy through Plato, Aristotle, Montaigne, Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Adorno—whose 'culture industry' opposes pleasure to cognition. Using rap (KRS-One's 'Edutainment', Public Enemy, Ice-T) and T.S. Eliot's 'superior amusement,' he argues knowledge and enjoyment are compatible. He rejects Hannah Arendt's contrast of imperishable art vs. life-serving entertainment, and critiques G.E. Moore's Principia Ethica 'method of absolute isolation' for intrinsic value, replacing it with a Deweyan transactional account in which even intrinsic values are relational and temporal.
- ch. 14 "II - INTERPRETATION AND POPULAR ART FORMS" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 15 "NOTES" **·** Aristotle, Adam Smith — The Invisible Hand; The Four Causes — Cantor argues that TV shows like The Simpsons and The X-Files can be genuine art despite multiple authorship, contingency, and commercial pressure, using the Lone Gunmen's audience-driven revival and Scully's pregnancy-forced abduction plot as evidence of a 'feedback' rather than 'perfect plan' model of creation. He rejects the Romantic/New Critical ideal of the solitary genius producing organic form and reframes popular culture through Hayek's spontaneous order, drawing directly on Adam Smith's self-regulating markets (the invisible hand) and Darwinian selection. Aristotle's Poetics supplies the target organic-form doctrine—that every part serves the whole—which Cantor says wrongly theorizes contingency out of art.
- ch. 16 "NOTES" **·** Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Gracia examines six Dracula films (Murnau, Browning, Morrisey, Herzog, Badham, Coppola) and asks how they relate to Stoker's novel, tracing the count's evolution from Murnau's rat-like horror to Coppola's tragic romantic knight who dies for love. He rejects the topical, essentialist, and family-resemblance accounts of the films' relation to the book and proposes instead that they are 'relational interpretations'—works in their own right whose primary aim is to link Stoker's story to an outside agenda (sex, humor, sympathy, heroism) rather than to explicate the novel. The argument is a piece of interpretation theory, distinguishing work-oriented from relational interpretation to explain why popular adaptations legitimately diverge from their source.
- ch. 17 "NOTES" **·** Socrates, Aristotle, John Searle — Socratic Method (elenchus); Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism); Biological Naturalism / Intentionality — Matthews argues that certain children's books are 'subversive' in a Socratic sense: they problematize concepts adults assume they command, challenging adult epistemic authority the way Socrates exposed the pretended knowledge of Athens' elite. Morris the Moose raises Aristotelian questions of natural kinds and essence-versus-accident; Leese Webster probes the concept of art; The Shrinking of Treehorn destabilizes 'normal' child development; Frog and Toad's 'The Garden' dramatizes the post hoc, ergo propter hoc fallacy about causation. In the Ozma of Oz Tik-Tok discussion, nine-year-old Paul reconstructs an argument that only brains think, which Matthews aligns with Searle's claim in The Mystery of Consciousness that consciousness is caused by specific neurobiological processes; he explicitly distinguishes his subversive stories from those promoting Pyrrhonian skepticism or Protagorean relativism.
- ch. 18 "NOTES" **·** Theodor Adorno — The Culture Industry; The Categorical Imperative — South reads Batman, Batgirl, and Catwoman comics through J. M. Bernstein's Adorno-derived account of the 'damaged life' lived under Weberian rationalization and the disenchantment of the world. The Joker's 'one bad day' in The Killing Joke embodies 'affective skepticism'—the split between rational universal norms and agent-specific motivation—while the debate between moral internalism and externalism (which he ties to Kant-style abstract justification) expresses the hurt of a disenchanted world where justifying and motivating reasons no longer converge. Barbara Gordon's 'because I can,' Bruce Wayne's vow, and Selina Kyle's turn toward 'basic human dignity' exemplify Bernstein's 'fugitive ethics,' fragile promises that restore authority outside juridico-legal channels and produce genuine happiness in damaged lives.
- ch. 19 "NOTES" **·** René Descartes, Aristotle — The Cogito; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Baur reads Don McLean's 'American Pie' as an enactment of how a culture can criticize itself from within, decoding its Buddy Holly, Dylan, Rolling Stones (Altamont), and Manson/Beatles allusions while insisting the song's meaning lies in simultaneous multiple meanings, not one-to-one correspondence. He argues McLean rejects any 'foundationalist' Archimedean point for critique—paralleling the standard objection that Descartes' cogito illicitly borrows the concept of finite substance from the tradition it claims to doubt—so the 'girl who sang the blues' shows that seeking a purer external origin only deepens disenchantment. Baur concludes with an Aristotelian point that cultural self-critique follows the model of the prudential sciences (phronesis) rather than techne: one reforms a tradition only by participating in it and exposing its internal contradictions.
- ch. 20 "NOTES" **·** William James, John Dewey, W.V.O. Quine, Walter Benjamin — The Will to Believe; The Web of Belief; The Aura of the Artwork — Hare treats mass photography—from the daguerreotype through digital cameras, Abu Ghraib snapshots, and diagnostic imaging—as making everyone a practicing epistemologist caught between two folk tenets: the photo as mirror of reality and as manipulation of reality. Defending photography as a genuine causal 'mode of seeing' (a prosthetic like telescopes), he proposes 'flexible realism,' adjusting Dewey's warranted assertibility and virtue-epistemology standards to context, and invokes William James's defense of beneficial 'overbeliefs' when National Geographic images strengthen confidence in one's own culture. Reading the Fallujah lead-pipe photo debate between editors Sullivan and Kushner, he uses Quine's recalcitrant-experience and web-of-belief holism—extended by Morton White's 'holistic pragmatism'—to show moral, epistemic, sensory, and emotional claims are tested together, and frames photography's democratization via Walter Benjamin's mechanical reproduction and loss of aura.
- ch. 21 "About the Editors and Contributors" *(notes)*

## Philosophy in The Twilight Zone

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Dare to Enter the Zone" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — The Absurd; The Unexamined Life — Hooke and Rivera's editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone dramatizes the Nietzschean disappointment of the epigraph from Twilight of the Idols—that we seek great human beings and find only 'the apes of their ideal.' They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnated Socrates, a gadfly whose episodes ('Time Enough at Last,' 'The Hunt,' the eternal-youth trade-in) stage the gap between our ideals of love, justice, and truth and the treacherous, self-deluding creatures we actually are, so that viewers laugh at absurd twist endings because we are the species most deserving to be laughed at.
- ch. 8 "First Dimension Facing the Zone" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. Lost in Time" **·** David Lewis — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Free Will vs Determinism — Rard uses David Lewis's definition of time travel—a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the gap between departure and arrival—to show that 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' suspended-animation heist is NOT time travel, while 'Last Flight' (Terry returning to save Mackaye) is, complete with a self-consistent causal loop. She then applies Lewis's argument that mundane events always thwart attempts to change the past to 'No Time Like the Past,' where Paul Driscoll is repeatedly distracted from killing Hitler and even accidentally causes the schoolhouse fire he meant to prevent, illustrating that the past is unalterable but interactable.
- ch. 10 "2. Where Is the Twilight Zone" **·** René Descartes, Sigmund Freud — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Unconscious — Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of surrealist philosophy (Breton, Dalí) that provokes the Freudian 'uncanny.' He traces a line from Descartes—whose cogito and 'clear and distinct' rational mind produced the mind–body problem that lets surrealists destabilize waking reality—through psychoanalysis to Breton's 'point' where real and imagined cease to be contradictions. Episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing), 'The Mirror' (Dalí's paranoiac-critical method), 'Shadow Play,' 'The Shelter,' and 'The Lonely' unleash the imagination unbound by reason and provoke the uncanny in viewers.
- ch. 11 "3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis" **·** Martin Heidegger — The Question Concerning Technology; Authenticity — Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a meditation on our ambivalent dependence on technology and other people. Henry Bemis experiences the bank, his marriage, and finally the post-nuclear wasteland as successive 'cages' where time belongs to others; his misanthropic wish for a timeless world to himself is granted only for his glasses to shatter, revealing his short-sighted fantasy of exempting himself from the technological system on which even his vision depends. Pichanick concludes the episode demands not another pair of glasses but a philosophical clarity about our limits and interdependence.
- ch. 12 "4. Faces from Another Dimension" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Alan Turing — The Face of the Other; The Turing Test — Hooke, drawing on Levinas and his translator Alphonso Lingis, treats the face as the site where trust in a stranger is risked. The Twilight Zone weaponizes our trust in familiar (actors') faces: death wears Robert Redford's face in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Satan is the avuncular Pip in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the Kanamits' gentle faces mask a cookbook in 'To Serve Man.' He invokes the Turing test for Corry and Alicia's love in 'The Lonely,' and finds the most truthful face of love in 'The Trade-Ins,' where the aged couple cannot bear each other's altered faces after rejuvenation.
- ch. 13 "Second Dimension Beyond the Boundaries of You and Me" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "5. True Love or Artificial Love" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Peter Singer — The Pragmatic Method; Philosophy of Love — Klayman analyzes whether James Corry's love for the robot Alicia in 'The Lonely' is true love, using C.S. Lewis's four loves (charity, affection, friendship, Eros) and their three qualities (gift-, need-, appreciative-love), plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim to define 'truly loving' by its practical effects. He argues true love falls within Eros and requires a reciprocating individual, invoking Peter Singer's speciesism to reject a human-only requirement; concluding Corry showed only appreciative-love (not gift- or need-love) and that his bond was really companionship—Corry became fictional (Walton) to have something to believe in.
- ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" **·** John Locke, Immanuel Kant, Peter Singer, Tom Regan, Aristotle — Personal Identity (memory theory); Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Personal Identity — Karavitis arranges thirteen Twilight Zone android/machine episodes on a moral spectrum from simple machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'I Sing the Body Electric,' 'The Lateness of the Hour') to fully synthetic humans ('The Trade-Ins'). Using personhood, moral-agent/moral-patient distinctions, Aristotle's and Kant's views on animals, Singer and Regan on degrees not kinds, and Locke's memory theory of identity, he argues that if body-swapped Holts remain persons then scratch-built androids are persons too—so the destroyed androids were murdered, and evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Lay contrasts Locke's memory theory of personal identity with Parfit's psychological-continuity view across several episodes. Locke's factive-memory account explains 'The After Hours' (Marsha the mannequin) and 'Person or Persons Unknown' (David Gurney's non-factive memories), but fails for 'The Lateness of the Hour' (android Jana has installed beliefs, not memories) and especially 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You,' where post-Transformation Marilyn keeps all her memories yet is a different person. Using a Reid-flavored chain of episodes, Lay argues Parfit gets it right: a whole overlapping network of mental states, not memory alone, individuates the self.
- ch. 17 "8. What Are You Hearing" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Theory of Forms; Aristotle on the Soul — Wissner analyzes how the musical scores of dream/imagination episodes signal states of being, framing music through Plato (music as mimetic yet man-made and 'unreal,' functioning as image-evoking signs) and Aristotle (music forms images of character and, via ethos, can alter minds and moods). She shows how electronic instruments, reverberation, whole-tone and repeated melodies mark dream versus reality in 'Perchance to Dream,' 'A Stop at Willoughby,' 'Twenty-Two,' 'Shadow Play,' and 'The Midnight Sun,' arguing the scores answer whether characters are dreaming, awake, imagining, alive, or dead through contextual musical signs.
- ch. 18 "9. Machines Who Care" **·** Martin Heidegger — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); The Question Concerning Technology — Weiss examines 'robots that care' through 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric,' invoking Sherry Turkle's 'relational artifacts' and current debates (PARO, Alexa, Coeckelbergh, the Sparrows) about outsourcing companionship and care to machines. He notes Alicia becomes a relational artifact the moment she weeps, and that both she and the electric grandma are gendered, boxed, assembly-line products designed to fill human loneliness that a consumer culture itself produced. The essay asks whether we want a society where care and love are purchased off an assembly line—fable or nightmare.
- ch. 19 "Third Dimension That Wondrous Land Called Truth" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" **·** David Hume — Bundle Theory of Self; Personal Identity; Philosophical Skepticism — Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.
- ch. 21 "11. The Truth about Lying" **·** David Hume, Immanuel Kant, Blaise Pascal, René Descartes — On Miracles; Pascal's Wager — Fallis treats the Twilight Zone as a workbook in the philosophy of testimony (the ethics and epistemology of communication). Truth-tellers get dismissed as insane ('Nightmare at 20,000 Feet') while liars come to bad ends even when believed ('The Four of Us Are Dying'); Kant's reticence offers a third option to truth-telling and lying. On receiving testimony, he uses Hume on evaluating witnesses and disbelieving reports of miracles, then argues the show endorses Pascal's Wager—believe crazy testimony just in case—citing 'The Last Rites of Jeff Myrtlebank' and 'Mr. Garrity and the Graves,' plus Descartes's deceiving demon for the show's alien and devil deceivers.
- ch. 22 "Fourth Dimension As Vast as Space and Timeless as Infinity" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep" **·** Utopia and Dystopia; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Jones argues the Twilight Zone is not really 'somewhere else': Serling's narration insists on a remote realm, but episodes like 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'Eye of the Beholder' take place in recognizable America. He claims the show performs a 'double distancing'—framing mundane, uncomfortable truths (we're selfish, easily manipulated, not special, mortal) as strange by locating them elsewhere and delivering them via impossible catalysts (gremlins, the Devil). 'The Shelter,' with no supernatural cause and a Cold War fallout-shelter premise Kennedy actually urged, breaks the pattern, forcing viewers to see that the Twilight Zone is the room they sit in.
- ch. 24 "13. No Place like a Non-Place" **·** Authenticity; Existentialism — Pagnoni Berns, Juvé, and Aguilar apply Marc Augé's concept of the 'non-place'—transit spaces (roads, airports, ships, hotels, malls) of anonymity and 'supermodernity' that confer no identity—to the show's empty landscapes. Postwar gender and identity crises play out in 'Passage on the Lady Anne' (slowness versus speed), 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'The Passersby' (the road as a non-place where dead women refuse their fate), 'Will the Real Martian Please Step Up?', 'Nightmare at 20,000 Feet,' 'The Parallel,' 'The After Hours,' and 'The Four of Us Are Dying,' where identification briefly pierces anonymity, often fatally.
- ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" **·** David Lewis, Karl Popper, Nick Bostrom — Possible Worlds; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Falsificationism — Morgan surveys the physics and philosophy behind the show's 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions and parallel universes ('Little Girl Lost'), time as Einstein's fourth dimension and relativistic time dilation ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), the Grandfather Paradox and the self-consistency of time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics ('The Parallel'), and the cosmological multiverse. He closes with Popper's falsification criterion, arguing that unobservable other universes may be, like the show itself, forever 'a dimension of mind.'
- ch. 26 "Fifth Dimension Our Twisted Imaginings" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — The Stages on Life's Way; Despair (sickness unto death); The Meaning of Life — Karavitis groups twist-ending episodes into nostalgia, time-travel, and second-chance types and reads them through Kierkegaard's Either/Or distinction between the aesthetic and ethical modes of life. Living aesthetically—chasing present gratification—leads to despair, as in 'A Nice Place to Visit' (Rocky's boring 'heaven' is Hell) and 'A Game of Pool' (Jesse wins only an eternity in Limbo). Living ethically—taking responsibility and moving forward—earns a real second chance, as when 'Printer's Devil' editor Winter reclaims his soul; life must be understood backward but lived forward.
- ch. 28 "16. The Pleasure of the Twist" **·** Thomas Kuhn — Paradigm Shifts; Scientific Realism vs Anti-Realism — Scales argues that Twilight Zone twist endings mirror Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions: seeded anomalies accumulate until a 'paradigm shift' makes us reinterpret everything, as in 'To Serve Man' ('It's a cookbook!'), 'The Lateness of the Hour,' and 'The Hitch-Hiker.' He ties Kuhn's theory-ladenness of observation (the anomalous playing-card experiment) to Paul Churchland's connectionist, prototype-based bottom-up neurophilosophy, concluding the pleasure of the twist is the dopamine reward for deploying a new prototype—the same jolt we get from a joke or a genuine insight.
- ch. 29 "The Dimension that Can’t Be Named or Numbered" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" **·** Hannah Arendt — The Banality of Evil; The Problem of Evil; Totalitarianism — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' and 'He's Alive' against the Eichmann trial and Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, framing Serling's concern as Susan Neiman's 'problem of evil.' The earlier episode's SS captain Lutze (driven insane by his victims' ghosts at Dachau) matches the grotesque-monster Eichmann of the film Operation Eichmann, while 'He's Alive' (Vollmer as a frightened man seduced by Hitler's ghost) foreshadows Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, empathy-less doer. He contrasts both with Hogan's Heroes, which Serling condemned for trivializing Nazi atrocity.
- ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Vuckovich analyzes 'Still Valley,' where Confederate Sergeant Paradine can win the Civil War using a witchcraft handbook that freezes Union troops but only by renouncing God. He reads Paradine's temptation through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges myth in Plato's Republic (the committed unjust man who outdoes enemies without scruple) and Aristotle's friendships of shared pleasure (Paradine and the witchman Teague bonded by hatred of the enemy). Paradine burns the handbook rather than damn the Confederacy, preserving a core principle of fairness even at the cost of an easy victory—winning isn't everything.
- ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" **·** Theodor Adorno — The Culture Industry; One-Dimensional Man — Busk reads 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' through Horkheimer and Adorno's 'culture industry' and a philosophical account of subjectivity as active, critical agency. Marilyn's forced 'Transformation' into a standardized model (with banned books, 'Instant Smile,' and 'super soccer') dramatizes how commodified mass culture produces conformist, mannequin-like subjects who cannot resist—linking it to 'The After Hours,' where Marsha is literally a department-store mannequin. Yet Marilyn's and Marsha's very existence, like Adorno's theory, is a faint hopeful sign that critical subjectivity survives.
- ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" **·** Hannah Arendt, Aristotle, Jean Baudrillard — Totalitarianism; The Banality of Evil; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Altmann traces totalitarianism from The Twilight Zone into Black Mirror. 'He's Alive' shows Vollmer wielding Aristotle's rhetoric to grow a Nazi movement; 'Number 12' shows Umberto Eco's fascist 'fear of difference'; 'Deaths-Head Revisited' illustrates Arendt's banality of evil in Lutze's 'just following orders.' He then argues Black Mirror episodes ('The Waldo Moment,' 'Fifteen Million Merits') realize Guy Debord's 'society of the spectacle' and hyper-capitalism, where politics becomes entertainment and even resistance is commodified—a totalitarianism that needs no tanks.
- ch. 34 "21. That Unnamed Zone We Call Freedom" **·** John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Michel Foucault, Friedrich Nietzsche — Justice as Fairness; The Minimal State; Two Concepts of Liberty — Hooke reads Serling's ambivalence toward the State through the liberal–libertarian debate between Rawls's A Theory of Justice (equal rights and the difference principle) and Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (the minimal state, wary of a central authority regulating personal life). 'The Obsolete Man' (the condemned librarian Wordsworth laughing before the Chancellor), 'Eye of the Beholder' ('The State is not God'), and 'The Shelter' dramatize the shepherd-paradox (via Foucault) and the danger of any state that crushes human dignity; freedom, like the Nietzschean laughter Wordsworth aims at power, cannot be defined but is known in experience.

## Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Pink Floyd and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Pink Floyd From Pompeii to Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Thomas Nagel — Theory of Forms; What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — George Reisch's introduction reads the 1971 Live at Pompeii film, with the band playing to no audience inside a circular stone amphitheatre, as an ironic anticipation of The Wall, tracing how Waters's fury at stadium crowds (culminating in the 1977 Montreal spitting incident that spawned the wall concept) had not yet arrived. It frames the band's post-Barrett move from psychedelic whimsy to minimal formalism as philosophical stripping-away: Barrett wrote like an Aristotle fascinated by odd particulars ('Lucifer Sam,' 'The Gnome'), whose puzzlement at his impenetrable cat prefigures Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, while Waters pursued Plato's monolithic 'forms' of time, money, and madness. On this reading Dark Side's closing 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon' indicts Being itself, making life essentially and permanently tragic, a circular trap signaled by The Wall's interlocking 'we came in?' and 'Isn't this where...'
- ch. 6 "Pink Floyd in Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Does Johnny Rotten Still Hate Pink Floyd" **·** Authenticity; The Culture Industry — Reisch argues that Johnny Rotten's 'I hate Pink Floyd' T-shirt was a provocation aimed at the band everyone loved, since Pink Floyd was the exception to late-1970s corporate blandness rather than a symptom of it. Tracing the band from Syd Barrett's disintegration (the ever-changing 'Have You Got It Yet?', his unrecognizable 1975 walk-in at the Wish You Were Here sessions) through the Dark Side triumph and the Waters/Gilmour split, he contends that Pink Floyd 'was punk long before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols.' Where punk used two-minute power chords, Pink Floyd meticulously sharpened an ax to grind: 'Have a Cigar' and 'Welcome to the Machine' dissect the industry machine that cages and commodifies artists, and the whole project attacks the inauthenticity, alienation, and tragedy of modern life.
- ch. 8 "“A New Broom Sweeps Clean, but an Old Broom Knows Every Corner”" **·** Buddhism — Callis interweaves a memoir of the teenage boyfriend who played her Dark Side and later killed himself with an account of Easy Star Records' 2003 reggae remake, Dub Side of the Moon, arguing that the album's themes of time, money, materialism, and madness translate naturally into Rasta reasoning. Nyabinghi drumming, singjay toasting, and bong-bubble effects re-read 'Money' (the cash register replaced by a lighter firing the chalice) and 'Time' (Ranking Joe's 'Time is the master') through Rasta rejection of Babylon, anti-capitalist subsistence, and 'soon come' patience, which she glosses with the Buddhist principle that things happen in their own time. The reggae setting, she concludes, weaves all this pain and madness, from Barrett's collapse to her own ghosts, into something more optimistic than the original ever sounded.
- ch. 9 "Feelings of an Almost Human Nature" **·** Aristotle — Mroz rereads Alan Parker's film The Wall twenty-five years after it left her speechless, arguing it works on the viewer like Jungian lucid dreaming, a conversation between the brain's holistic image-making and linear verbal halves (via Shlain), and that its uroboros structure (the '...we came in?' / 'Isn't this where...' loop) replaces Aristotle's linear plot curve with something closer to Campbell's Hero's Journey, in which the audience's identification rises and the true 'return' happens after the film ends. She complains that most of the film's symbols are over-explicit, since the Judge is literally a talking asshole and the flowers that couple and then maul each other need no interpretation, leaving the viewer nothing to do; the one sequence that earns identification is Young Pink nursing the sick rat that dies anyway. The Trial's 'tear down the wall' becomes the moment the trauma-built self could finally be exposed, leaving the children in the ruins ambiguously alone.
- ch. 10 "Caring Dogs Watching Flying Pigs" **·** Adam Smith, Karl Marx — The Invisible Hand; Ideology and False Consciousness; Utopia and Dystopia — Croskery reads Animals as a beast fable in the tradition of Orwell's Animal Farm that opens with a thought experiment ('If you didn't care what happened to me / And I didn't care for you') and portrays a world without empathy across three corruptible institutions. 'Dogs' dramatizes a malfunctioning marketplace where Adam Smith's invisible-hand justification fails, since success requires lying to those you must trust and ends with the sad old man 'dragged down by the stone'; 'Pigs (3 Different Ones)' targets state corruption from Mary Whitehouse's censorship crusade to war-waging and regulatory capture; and 'Sheep' depicts Marxist false consciousness, the pastoral illusion hiding the slaughterhouse, capped by the Twenty-Third Psalm parody that 'converteth me to lamb cutlets.' The chapter concludes that libertarian, statist, and traditionalist errors each idolize one institution, and that Waters's closing 'Pigs on the Wing' points to the delicate balance of market, state, and community that political philosophy must strike.
- ch. 11 "Thematic Synchronicity" **·** Thomas Kuhn — Paradigm Shifts — Jones asks what the famous Dark Side of the Rainbow synchronization (album plus The Wizard of Oz, started on the third MGM lion roar) could mean given that the band denies designing it. He catalogs vivid syncs ('Time''s chimes as Miss Gulch bicycles past, 'Money''s cash register entering Munchkinland, 'Us and Them''s 'black and blue' over the Witch and Dorothy), then rejects both the Waters-conspiracy model and Jung's acausal 'synchronicity' as pseudoscience, proposing instead Conrad's apophenia and Kuhn's point that suspecting patterns others miss is the lifeblood of discovery. His resolution is 'thematic synchronicity': both works stage the struggle between security and transcendence, Dorothy's 'Over the Rainbow' against 'Eclipse''s 'all you touch and all you see is all your life will ever be,' so the coincidences feel objective because they are subjectively real to everyone.
- ch. 12 "In the End, It’s Only Round and Round (and Round)" **·** Eternal Recurrence — Steiff argues Pink Floyd's music is cinematic in itself: like film it unfolds in time and uses foreshadowing ('Speak to Me'), dynamic contrast, and Kuleshov-effect juxtaposition, which explains why the Wizard of Oz mashup creates any meaning at all, though she finds that mashup a novelty compared to 'Echoes' over the ending of Kubrick's 2001. The heart of the chapter is circularity: the heartbeat that both opens and closes Dark Side, The Wall's interlocking 'isn't this where / we came in,' and the fish bowl of 'Wish You Were Here' make the listener see, not merely be told, that life is a maze of metaphysical necessity, doomed to repeat the same round. Compared to Waters's doggerel 'Free-Four,' which says the same thing about death, Dark Side's forty-three-minute loop lets you live a microcosmic life, and that shown-rather-than-said quality gave a lonely listener the dark hope of knowing he was not alone.
- ch. 13 "Alienation (Several Different Ones)" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "We Don’t Need No Indoctrination" **·** Karl Marx, Martin Heidegger, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Bertrand Russell — Alienation; Being-Toward-Death; Thrownness (Geworfenheit); Authenticity — Detmer argues the four classic albums from Dark Side to The Wall form a unified meditation on alienation, from others, work, nature, and oneself, and reads Waters's stated 'political and philosophical' aims through the existentialists. 'Breathe''s rabbit digging one hole after another illustrates Marx's alienated labor (the worker 'only feels himself freely active in his animal functions'), echoed by Russell on industrialism's life against instinct and Camus on the day the 'why' arises; 'Time''s missed starting gun dramatizes our thrown condition and Heidegger's claim that only facing mortality head-on cures the inauthenticity of living as 'they' do, while Gilmour's improvised solos model the spontaneity such authenticity requires. 'Money' is a satire of greed confirmed by 'Dogs,' whose self-rationalizing climbers end 'dragged down by the stone,' and 'Us and Them' attacks artificial divisions (soldiers manipulated by map-movers, racism's 'black and blue,' the old man who dies 'for the want of the price of tea and a slice'). 'Another Brick in the Wall (Part 2)' indicts indoctrination, being told what to think, rather than education itself, making independent critical thought the road to the Sartrean autonomy and responsibility the chapter urges.
- ch. 15 "Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone" **·** Albert Camus, Plato, G.W.F. Hegel, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; Allegory of the Cave; Rebellion and Revolt — Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.
- ch. 16 "The Eclipse of Musical Alienation" **·** Theodor Adorno, Karl Marx — The Culture Industry; Alienation — Macan uses Adorno to measure Pink Floyd's career-long confrontation with alienation: after 'Echoes' fused metaphysical loneliness ('I am you and what I see is me') with an explicitly Marxist account of capitalist atomization and commodification, the early epics 'Interstellar Overdrive,' 'Careful with that Axe, Eugene,' 'Set the Controls,' and 'Echoes' unknowingly resurrected Stravinsky's primitivism, their LSD-shaped structures (dechronization, depersonalization, dynamization) modeling the ego's dissolution and reintegration through climactic 'breakthrough' passages of maximum alienation, just as Schoenberg's twelve-tone music 'points out the ills of society' by musically modeling them. Against Adorno's 'On Popular Music,' he argues the early Floyd audience sought challenge rather than reassurance, but that from Dark Side onward the increasingly conventional music, polished by producer Bob Ezrin on The Wall, began 'hearing for the listener,' so Waters's plainspoken social critique lost its transgressive force. The Adornian moral is that you cannot critique alienation through music that is no longer itself alienating.
- ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" **·** Martin Buber, Friedrich Nietzsche, The Buddha — I–Thou Relation; The Death of God; Buddhism — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- ch. 18 "Apples and Oranges Or Just Apples" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "To Join in with the Game" **·** John Locke, Immanuel Kant — Personal Identity (memory theory); Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Gracyk argues Waters is wrong that Pink Floyd ended when he quit in 1985: Waters's case rests on an illicit use of the identity of indiscernibles, since if losing Waters's lyrics destroys the band's identity, then losing Barrett's or Wright's, or adding 'Lucifer Sam,' would too, which proves too much. Borrowing Locke's distinction between the same man and the same person (the oak that remains the same oak through change; the unrecognized Syd in Abbey Road's Studio Three) and Kant's contrast between free and dependent beauty to explain how intentions change aesthetic evaluation, he defends actual intentionalism over hypothetical intentionalism: Hendrix really sings 'kiss the sky,' and interviews with Waters genuinely aid interpretation of Wish You Were Here. He then argues for collective agency, that groups can have intentions through members charged to act responsibly on the group's behalf, so no single member can disband a collective: Waters had a duty to leave, Gilmour, Mason, and Wright were entitled to continue the group's longstanding intention of making and performing original music, and the Echoes compilation is therefore an accurate portrait of the real Pink Floyd.
- ch. 20 "Absolutely Curtains" **·** Derek Parfit — Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — Michael Patton retells the Ship of Theseus (his 'Trump Princess' rebuilt part-by-part from spares, then duplicated from the salvaged parts) to ask whether Pink Floyd survived its upheavals: Bob Klose's pre-Piper exit, Syd Barrett's 1968 dismissal ('No, fuck it, let's not bother' on the drive to Southampton), Rick Wright's firing during The Wall, and Roger Waters's 1985 lawsuit to stop Gilmour and Mason using the name. Roster, stylistic ('Lucifer Sam' versus 'Money'), legal, and nominal criteria each fail, so he proposes an 'Officeholder View' of identity in which constituencies decide sameness — as when UFO Club's Joe Boyd saw a different Syd at the June 1967 show, while the author's locked-in brother Josh (like Bauby in The Diving Bell and the Butterfly) remained the same son and brother to his family. Parfit's claim that survival tracks memory and personality rather than body underwrites the 'death of a thousand cuts' scenario: the band's criteria, not Syd's own, ended the life of the person 'Syd Barrett', and he didn't get a vote.
- ch. 21 "Wondering and Dreaming. The Words Have Different Meanings" **·** René Descartes, Ludwig Wittgenstein, George Berkeley, John Locke — Philosophical Skepticism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); The Private Language Argument — Scott Calef argues that the causal theory of perception — the inflatable pig over Battersea reaches you only as an internal representation — breeds Cartesian skepticism: the dreaming argument, asylum inmates who don't know they're mad ('the lunatic is in my head'), the evil demon, and the modern brain-in-a-vat version behind The Matrix. Locke's unknowable substratum behind the Dark Side jacket's qualities and Berkeley's idealism deepen the veil of perception, with 'Julia Dream', Waters's 'If I go insane, please don't stick your wires in my brain', and Syd's 'Jugband Blues' self-diagnosis as Floyd illustrations. Against skepticism he deploys mutual corroboration ('It takes two to know'), J.L. Austin's point that waking experience is qualitatively unlike dreams ('A Pillow of Winds': 'the dream is gone'), and Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box private language argument (rebranded as Lucifer Sam's cat) — a purely private language is impossible, so skepticism expressed in language defeats itself, leaving the Barrett-era enigma to keep philosophy's original wonder alive.
- ch. 22 "Meet You on the Dark Side of the Moon" **·** Karl Marx, Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Parmenides, G.W.F. Hegel, Jacques Derrida — Alienation; Being and Changelessness; The Dialectic — Jere Surber frames Pink Floyd as musical heirs to Parmenides's 'path of Non-Being', then maps Marx's four alienations onto the catalog: self-alienation in 'Brain Damage' ('There's someone in my head, but it's not me'), alienation by things in 'Welcome to the Machine', alienation from other persons in 'Us and Them' and The Final Cut's war trauma, and alienation from species-being in Animals ('Dogs'). Existential absence follows: Sartre's café scene, where the whole ensemble arranges itself around the missing Pierre, parallels the absent Syd and the father killed in World War II behind The Wall ('Comfortably Numb': 'the child is grown, the dream is gone'), while Heidegger's withdrawal of Being accounts for the cosmic Angst of 'Eclipse' and Obscured by Clouds. A postmodern coda reads the band's mid-thought-breaking lyrics and Ummagumma sound experiments as Derridean différance woven through language and sound.
- ch. 23 "The Sun Is Eclipsed by the Moon" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Phenomenology; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Randall Auxier uses Sartre's Psychology of Imagination to explain what 'Brain Damage' and 'Eclipse' do to a listener: auditory images live in time (unlike the spatial visual image of the prism cover), so Waters's repeated 'The lunatic is on the grass' and the anticipated drum entrances seize the will through repetition and the vortex of attention, while musicians themselves escape through an expanded 'now' — the trap-door in time Gilmour knows too well. Sartre's four positional acts of the image (positing the object as non-existent, absent, existing elsewhere, or neutral) are then worked through examples: imaging the contingently absent song, the superstition around imagining a beloved as dead (mode 1), and the neutral mode (4) that Pink Floyd favors over both benevolent and malevolent negations. The dark conclusion: music like Metallica at Guantanamo cancels the will, but Pink Floyd uses neutrality to show that in annihilating the world you destroy above all yourself and remain responsible for the choice — the sun eclipsed by the moon.
- ch. 24 "The Art of Insanity Nietzsche, Barrett, and Beyond" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "You Legend, You Martyr" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Taoism (Daoism) — Erin Kealey reads Syd Barrett's 1967–68 collapse through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: Barrett 'surrendered his subjectivity in the Dionysian process' to make Piper's songs — 'Astronomy Domine', the wordless 'Interstellar Overdrive', 'Matilda Mother' where 'the words had different meaning' — and 'Chapter 24', written from an I Ching divination on change and return. 'Bike' teeters on psychosis as the room of musical tunes swallows the singer, and 'Jugband Blues' ('much obliged to you for making it clear that I'm not here') with the motionless Scarecrow foretells the catatonia that ended his tenure, after which the band pivoted from anarchic spontaneity to the meticulous Apollonian constructions of Dark Side through The Wall. Following Nietzsche, Kealey argues that the fall of this tragic hero — mourned in 'Shine on You Crazy Diamond' and mirrored in Pink's exploits in The Wall — affirms life, since art alone transfigures the horror of existence into something worth living.
- ch. 26 "“The Madcap Laughed at the Man on the Border”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Walter Benjamin, Arthur Schopenhauer — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; The Aura of the Artwork — Brandon Forbes reads The Madcap Laughs and Barrett between Nietzsche and Walter Benjamin: the melting-hair gig and the ever-shifting 'Have You Got It Yet?' show Barrett shedding Apollo's principium individuationis (borrowed from Schopenhauer's lone man steadying his boat among the waves) and submerging into the Dionysian dithyramb — 'Opel''s 'warm shallow waters', 'Octopus''s 'lost in the wood', 'It Is Obvious''s minds 'shot together'. He then applies Benjamin's 'Work of Art in the Age of Its Reproducibility': technological mass reproduction destroys the aura and authenticity (the unique 'sequin fan' of 'No Good Trying' versus a supermarket fan), yet the deliberately lo-fi tracks — audible page-turning on 'She Took a Long Cold Look', the false starts and broken 'yum, yummy, yum' of 'If It's in You' — re-introduce the aura in mass form, subverting the record industry's commodification of music much as the unplayable 'Have You Got It Yet?' refused to become a reproducible commodity.
- ch. 27 "Art, Madness, and Syd Barrett" **·** Michel Foucault, Jean-Paul Sartre — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Panopticon (surveillance) — George Reisch reads The Wall through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: madness is not a brain lesion but a historical construction — Renaissance unreason, classical confinement, then Tuke's and Pinel's psychiatric regime in which the madman must know 'he is watched, judged, and condemned' until judgment is internalized — which explains why Pink imprisons himself brick by brick and asks at 'The Trial', 'Have I been guilty all this time?' The fascist worms and skinhead riots of 'Waiting for the Worms' are the same crusade for uniformity that drove Pink mad — Foucault's 'moral city' where 'virtue is an affair of the state' — so fascism and insanity are versions of each other, with Sartre's 'Hell is other people' from No Exit as the framing thought. Both the album ('Outside the Wall': 'the bleeding hearts and artists make their stand') and Foucault end by defending art as the last channel of unreason, and Reisch argues Syd Barrett's unanswerable absence was exactly that interrupting void powering 'Echoes', Dark Side, Wish You Were Here, and The Final Cut.
- ch. 28 "Resignation and Exploration—I’ll Climb the Hill in My Own Way" **·** Karl Marx, Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — Alienation; The Myth of Sisyphus; The Unexamined Life — Steven Gimbel asks how to live with the 'pink' malaise of Waters's lyrics and tests five options: capitulation (Marx's four alienations via 'In the Flesh?', 'Have a Cigar', and 'Dogs'), medication ('Comfortably Numb' and the Prozac-ad mother as one of the 'neuro-chemically well-adjusted sheep'), re-creation of childhood (Nietzsche's child playing 'between the fences of past and future' against memory's 'it was' in 'Remember a Day'), and emancipation through LSD or romanticized madness ('See Emily Play', 'Brain Damage'), with Syd Barrett's vacant eyes as the fatal counterexample. What survives is Camus's Sisyphus — fully conscious of his futility yet 'superior to his fate', imagined happy — joined to 'Fearless''s 'I'll climb that hill in my own way' and the mutual care of 'Pigs on the Wing', closing on Socrates' unexamined life: the answer lies in the searching itself, so living pink means living.
- ch. 29 "Selected Pink Floyd Discography" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "Author Bios" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "Pink Floyd and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

- ch. 1 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Elizabeth Anscombe — Anthropocentrism — John Huss's introduction frames the franchise as mirroring successive revolutions: Taylor before the ape tribunal recalls Galileo's heresy trial, the Darwinian revolution that toppled humans from evolution's pinnacle is taken to its logical extreme from Boulle's 1963 novel on, and Rise of the Planet of the Apes stages a 'Molecular Revolution' whose wake-up call is addressed to 'human chauvinists' who forget we share the planet with other species. He reads the cover's interspecies erotica through the Sexual Revolution, quoting Elizabeth Anscombe on contraceptive intercourse and asking whether her argument can get us over the species line, and closes with President Morsi's Tahrir Square allegory of the films: 'We are human, we did do this to ourselves.'
- ch. 9 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 10 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, John Stuart Mill — The Extended Mind — Kristin Andrews uses Taylor's silent attempts to show Zira he has a mind - mouthing answers, wiggling his fingers when she mentions the Hopkins Manual Dexterity Test - to stage the problem of other minds, pushing against Descartes's claim that language is required for thought and Mill's argument from analogy, while Dr. Zaius can always redescribe it all as 'a definite gift for mimicry.' Drawing on her fieldwork with the orangutan Cecep (the leaf-wiping pantomime, guiding the frightened Aldrin home from the turtle scare), she argues against reducing mindreading to false-belief tasks and for knowing minds through shared interaction, inductive overhypotheses, and natural context. She ends with an extended-mind point - 'when you're in a cage, you act caged,' and we offload thinking onto our homes and tools - so lab studies can show what apes can do but never what they can't.
- ch. 12 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** W.V.O. Quine — Indeterminacy of Translation; Speciesism — Sara Waller argues the films show language operating as a tyranny that measures minds and withholds moral standing: Dodge mocking signing Caesar as a 'stupid monkey,' Zaius dismissing Taylor's speech as mimicry, 1894 literacy tests used to disenfranchise Black voters, and IQ tests whose vocabulary sections double-count language skill. She surveys the non-linguistic tests the apes face - the Hopkins dexterity test, the Wisconsin Multiphasic, Kohler's banana-and-boxes task ('Because I loathe bananas'), the Lucas Tower, Caesar's cookie-jar deception - and then deploys Quine's 'gavagai' inscrutability of reference to argue that speech cannot be the ultimate measure of intelligence or moral worth. Nova's hand over Taylor's mouth and Zira and Cornelius's 'be clever... be quiet' suggest that under oppression, silence is the smart play.
- ch. 13 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Daniel Dennett, René Descartes, Ludwig Wittgenstein, William of Ockham — The Intentional Stance; Second-Order Desires (personhood); Ockham's Razor — Don Fallis proposes deception rather than language as the personhood test: following Dennett, a deceiver must be a second-order intentional system who can want someone else to have a false belief, as when General Thade lies to Senator Sandar about Ari's kidnapping, Zira and Cornelius feign muteness before the Presidential Commission, and Caesar fakes his own electrocution in Conquest. The roles' reversal makes this a test for the films' mute humans too, while Descartes's beast machines, Wittgenstein on dogs that cannot simulate pain, and Lloyd Morgan's canon voice the skeptical reading of fake alarm calls and Koko's 'Cat did it.' Against them Fallis invokes Occam's Razor over Hare, Call and Tomasello's food-competition experiments: apes track who sees what, but they fail the misinformed false-belief version, so real apes may not be 'sneaky enough to be people.'
- ch. 14 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, Ludwig Wittgenstein, David Hume, Heraclitus — Anthropocentrism; Falsificationism — Bernard Rollin reads Dr. Zaius's tribunal as 'scientific ideology' in action - 'human see, human do' refuses to believe its own eyes, just as bishops refused to look through Galileo's telescope. He traces the ideology from Newton's 'hypotheses non fingo' through logical positivism's verifiability criterion (which validates the Hasslein Curve prediction while rendering 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven' meaningless) and Wittgenstein's point that 'killing is wrong' is not a fact of the universe, to the 'science is value-free' dogma that left animal pain untested and untreated - as he documents from his own campaign: the empty analgesic literature search, the 1985 federal legislation, and the pain physiologist whose dog research refutes his own denial. Zira's neurosurgery on mute humans repeats what Descartes's beast-machine doctrine licensed, and IASP's language requirement for pain collapses into a Cratylus-grade confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions ('You can't step into the same river once').
- ch. 16 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Michael Sandel — Virtue Ethics (arete); Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
- ch. 17 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Peter Singer, Jeremy Bentham, Plato, Martha Nussbaum, John Locke — Speciesism; Animal Liberation; Euthyphro Dilemma — Travis Timmerman argues the series dramatizes Singer's equal consideration of interests: Zira frees Taylor once he writes 'My name is Taylor' because like interests must count equally regardless of species, while Dr. Zaius's erasing the writing, lobotomizing Landon, and destroying the cave artifacts is pure speciesism in Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' sense. He rejects the crude 'humans are smarter' argument (it would strip severely cognitively disabled humans of standing) and Nussbaum's species-normal version (it would permit caging Zira and Cornelius since normal apes are mute), then deploys Plato's Euthyphro dilemma against Locke-style God-given rights: a deity bellowing that human interests outrank ape interests is arbitrary unless grounded in independent reasons. Since farming severely cognitively disabled humans is obviously wrong and species membership is morally irrelevant, it is equally wrong to factory-farm and experiment on animals - so, like Caesar in Battle for the Planet of the Apes, become vegetarian.
- ch. 19 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Peter Singer, Bernard Williams — Speciesism; The Ethics of Care — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry defends a 'moderate speciesism' built on relationships rather than individual capacities: Taylor's trial strips him of clothes, name, and speech - the symbols of ethical community - showing how institutional speciesism rationalizes domination behind the Sacred Scrolls' Declaration-of-Independence-style self-evidence. Against Singer's anti-speciesist challenge that any distinctively human capacity is shared by some animals or missing from some humans, he argues both camps wrongly pedestal intrinsic traits, and reads Taylor's love for the mute Nova together with the failed Project Nim as showing that within-species bonds of love, care, and family are genuinely and justifiably valuable without licensing mistreatment. Bernard Williams's 'The Human Prejudice' - should we surrender to superior invading aliens? - marks where impartial anti-speciesism leads, while Zaius's 'Man is evil' and the doomsday-bomb ending show extreme speciesism as self-fulfilling prophecy.
- ch. 20 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds — David Morgan separates the franchise's two kinds of time travel. Forward travel is physically respectable: special-relativistic time dilation (Taylor's six months against nearly 700 Earth years implies 99.99997 percent of light speed) and gravitational dilation near black holes, confirmed daily by muon lifetimes and GPS satellite corrections. Backward travel, as when Cornelius, Zira, and Milo flee the doomsday blast to 1973, invites the Grandfather Paradox - Hasslein killing the apes would erase the future they came from - but the films resolve it through a closed causal loop in which Hasslein's killings set Caesar's rebellion in motion. Morgan then reads the Aldo-versus-Caesar continuity clash between Escape and Conquest through Hasslein's freeway-of-time speech as a multiple-timelines model aligned with the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, which also lets fans file the Burton and Rise reboots as parallel-universe futures.
- ch. 22 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Free Will vs Determinism; The A-Series and B-Series of Time — Ralph Shain argues forward and backward time travel are categorically different: relativistic time dilation is conceptually harmless (in Boulle's novel Merou could not return to Soror for a thousand years), but Escape from the Planet of the Apes' backward jump is conceptually impossible because it treats the open future as fixed like the past - Hasslein's plan to kill baby Milo is the Grandfather Paradox, checked against presentist, possibilist, and eternalist ontologies of time. The real philosophical engine is Aristotle's sea-battle argument from the law of excluded middle: since Cornelius's story of the takeover is past for the apes and future for 1973 humans, the film's causal loop (Milo saved at the circus) enacts the fatalist conclusion that the ape takeover will necessarily occur. Hasslein's freeway image of time defeats itself - switching lanes means landing in the past of a different, parallel universe, so the apes' jump would be travel between worlds, not times.
- ch. 23 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Plato — Justice in the Republic; The Philosopher King; The Noble Lie; Tripartite Soul — Greg Littmann maps Ape City onto Plato's Republic class by class: orangutan rulers who legislate, censor, and propagandize; gorilla warriors who enforce; chimpanzee producers who do all the work - including, pointedly, the science Plato made no provision for; and humans as the 'barbarians' Plato says may be enslaved or exterminated. The overlaps are detailed: the Sacred Scrolls' first article of faith functions as the noble lie's myth of the metals, orangutan funerals promise heaven to keep gorillas unafraid of death, and Zaius's erasing of Taylor's dust-writing and blowing up of the archaeological cave enact the rulers' duty to supervise stories. But the films also refute Plato: hereditary orangutans show that power corrupts philosopher kings, Dr. Honorius's 'reason' is dogma serving the faith, the gelding threat that finally breaks Taylor cracks the tripartite-soul analogy of justice, and democracy's rough virtue is that it lets us remove rulers 'without sticking anybody with iron spears.'
- ch. 25 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Plato, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — Leslie Dale Feldman reads the 1968 film's blasted opening as Hobbes's state of nature - 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short' - with the Lawgiver's 'Beware the beast Man' scroll echoing Hobbes's three causes of war (competition, fear, glory) and Plato's Ring of Gyges explaining why even the 'just' man acts rightly only under compulsion, both grounding the social contract's origin story. She then casts Dr. Zaius as Alexis de Tocqueville's tyranny of the majority - erasing Taylor's writing, lobotomizing Landon, and sealing Cornelius's cave 'to spare them all the care of thinking' - with Rousseau's man 'born free; and everywhere he is in chains' behind it. The chapter also traces Rod Serling's Twilight Zone fingerprints (nuclear-war twist endings like 'Time Enough at Last,' the cave of 'The Old Man in the Cave,' Adam-and-Eve survivor pairs, the beauty reversals of 'Eye of the Beholder') and reads Taylor and Nova's westward ride through Turner's frontier thesis and Kennedy's New Frontier, holding Serling's Hobbesian pessimism and his hope in tension.
- ch. 26 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Existential Risk; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Michael Ruse reads the 1968 film as a study in forbidden knowledge: Dr. Zaius has sealed the cave of human artifacts because he knows a prior human civilization destroyed itself and fears the knowledge could cause a repetition. Weighing nuclear weapons, recombinant DNA, bird-flu research, and data-driven political manipulation, Ruse argues Zaius's censorship is both impossible and undesirable, since the search for knowledge is intrinsically valuable and containment only increases the need for research. The film's deeper lesson is evolutionary: intelligence and sociality co-evolved only to the level 'good enough,' so any species that acquires weapons of mass destruction will likely destroy itself, meaning the Planet of the Apes scenario would recur across the universe.
- ch. 27 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Harry Frankfurt — Second-Order Desires (personhood); Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life); Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Lori Gruen uses Taylor's cage and Caesar's confinement in Rise to examine real chimpanzee captivity in research labs and sanctuaries, asking whether captivity wrongs apes even when it causes no physical or psychological suffering. Against the view that autonomy requires language-grade self-endorsement, she argues chimpanzees are autonomous: they make choices, deceive (Tristan's false alarm call among the vervets), follow social norms, and set things right (Sheba returning Sarah's book), so denying them freedom is itself a wrong, as Caesar's 'Am I a pet?' moment shows. Since wild habitat is vanishing, she concludes the best we can do is captive care that respects apes' wild dignity and lets them come as close to feeling at home as captivity allows.
- ch. 29 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Hobbes, Plato, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Categorical Imperative; Ethical Egoism; The State of Nature — John Wilkins treats Caesar, who spares the neighbor he has beaten, as a Kantian exemplar whose reason lets him adopt the Categorical Imperative, contrasting him with the rational egoism of the film's human keepers and executives. He argues the film trades on the outdated Great Chain of Being, which Darwinian tree thinking dissolves: with no higher or lower species, only branching homologies, human nature must be continuous with ape nature, and talk of innate species essences must allow for statistical variation and dispositions rather than determination. Caesar's morality also needs more than reason, namely the primate dispositions of deference and empathy scaffolded by his human family, though Buck's instant moral conversion after enhancement shows the film is ambivalent about whether scaffolding alone explains it.
- ch. 30 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus); Paradigm Shifts — John Huss asks whether Andy Serkis deserved an Oscar nomination for playing Caesar through performance capture, and argues that 'What is acting?' is a Socratic-style definitional question (like stumping Euthyphro on piety) of the sort Wittgenstein diagnosed as a language confusion, since the definition of movie acting is in flux. Using the seeing-as debate, Kuhnian theory-ladenness of observation versus Fodor's Muller-Lyer point that belief does not dictate sight, he explains why animators and fans see such different things in the identical raw footage. He concludes, with James Franco, that acting is an emergent ensemble property of actors reacting to one another on a shared stage, which performance capture enables rather than threatens, and a coda notes PETA's hope that CG performers will end the use of animal actors.
- ch. 32 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, G.E. Moore, Plato — Language Games; Philosophical Skepticism; The Noble Lie — Tom McBride reads the film through Wittgenstein's On Certainty: Dr. Zaius's certainties (flight is impossible, humans come from the forests) are hinge or riverbed propositions that cannot be doubted within the ape form of life, so Taylor's true story sounds not false but insane, like claiming to have slept on the moon. Speaking and able to prompt empirical investigation, Taylor fractures a foundational principle where G.E. Moore, facing a 'wild tribe' playing a different language game, could only confess that things 'stand fast' with him; and Zaius's explicit origin myth, a parallel to Plato's Myth of the Metals, is flimsy precisely because rulers who must insist on rules are not potent and are reduced to destroying the cave evidence. The genre's appeal is Margaret Atwood's 'controlled hallucination': crazy doors that swing on safe hinges, rivers that still have stable beds.
- ch. 33 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Theodor Adorno, Charles Sanders Peirce — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Binary Oppositions — William McGinney argues Jerry Goldsmith's modernist score, with its twelve-tone themes, ostinati, cuica, slide whistle, and ram's horn, carries no inherent meaning but acquires it through learned associations: its dissonance recalls Cold War modernist concert music promoted as the high art of Western freedom, while its Stravinsky-like rhythms and 'primitive' timbres mark the apes as other and feed the film's deconstruction of the human-ape, advanced-primitive, civilized-barbaric oppositions. Because Taylor is given no heroic music, the score undercuts identification with him as an anti-hero, and its modernist associations implicate the technocratic, militarized West he represents in Earth's self-destruction. The chapter's machinery is the semiotic view of Kant, Adorno, Cage, Peirce, and Saussure: music modifies a film's images the way adjectives modify nouns.
- ch. 34 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 35 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes — The Cogito — Chad Timm reads Caesar's arc, from 'Am I a pet?' to 'What is Caesar?', through Lacan: the mirror stage fixes an alienating ideal-I (his reflection, the human children he watches), entry into sign language inducts him into the symbolic Other, and the over-stuffed signifier 'pet' confronts him with the real, precipitating an identity crisis that deepens when the shelter chimps also reject him. Against Descartes's cogito, an unconscious structured like language means the self can never fully know itself, and Zizek's ideological fantasy explains how the new master signifier Freedom quilts Caesar's ape liberation, with humans cast as the savage oppressive Other. His closing 'Caesar is home' completes the Zizekian Act, traversing the ideological fantasy and retroactively redefining the coordinates of his identity.
- ch. 36 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Charles W. Mills, Kwame Anthony Appiah — The Racial Contract; Epistemic Injustice — Jason Davis opens with Sammy Davis Jr. thanking the white producers for the best film ever made on black-white relations, and their cluelessness, to show that white privilege rests on an epistemology of ignorance, paralleled by the human enjoyment of ape slavery in Conquest. He reads the ape castes through the ontology of race: the films first stage race as biological realism and essentialism (warrior gorillas, chimpanzee scientists, orangutan priests), but Battle for the Planet of the Apes shows biology is not destiny, and human genetics (race accounts for about 0.012 percent of human variation) discredits biological racial realism altogether. Via Charles Mills's social ontology of race and Kwame Anthony Appiah's racial skepticism, the chapter treats ape racism as a mirror of anti-miscegenation-era America whose racial categories are social constructs, down to the dropped ape-human hybrid child.
- ch. 37 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger, René Descartes — Dasein (being-there); Authenticity — Shaun May uses Heidegger's being-in-the-world to mark off the human: Caesar correcting Charles's fork grip shows a grasp of the unspoken norms governing equipment, and the apes of the 1968 film, surgeons with scalpels and years of training, inhabit the same world of projects, skills, and tools that Heidegger says other animals lack. Language seals the difference: Taylor's syntax, Zaius's carefully ordered 'The Almighty created the ape in his own image,' and socially learned practices like pointing and map-reading stand against Nim Chimpsky's syntax-free signing and chimps' failure to understand pointing. Caesar's foresight in stealing the ALZ-113 before leading the escape extends this to Heideggerian temporality, and the ape uprising becomes a move toward authenticity, lives owned as a meaningful narrative whole.
- ch. 38 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 39 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** John Locke, Tom Regan — Anthropocentrism; Speciesism; Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life) — Norva Lo and Andrew Brennan set Richard Routley's 'last man' thought experiment beside Taylor's triggering of the doomsday bomb in Beneath the Planet of the Apes: both ask whether wiping out every living thing would be wrong once no humans remain to be harmed, which basic human chauvinism cannot condemn. The chapter argues the act is wrong from both sides: non-anthropocentrism counts the apes, mutants, and horses as intrinsically valuable beings, and even human-centered standards condemn it, since the talking apes and mutants are Locke's rational persons and Nova's people are biologically human, making Taylor's outburst 'you damned dirty ape' a form of speciesism. Taylor emerges not as simply mad or evil but as the Cold War logic of mutually assured destruction made flesh, a warning that excessive self-interest, personal or species-level, is itself the danger.
- ch. 40 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Friedrich Nietzsche — Anthropocentrism; Pragmatism; Deep Ecology — Eugene Halton retells human history as the fable of Peirce's 'degenerate monkey': a neotenous, instinct-weak blunderer (Homo errans) whose gift for abductive guessing and attunement to the intelligence of the wild was inverted by agriculture and civilization into Narcissistic self-mirroring, anthropocentric religion, and the worship of the machine. The telepathic, rubber-masked mutants of Beneath the Planet of the Apes who worship the Alpha-Omega bomb ('I reveal my Inmost Self unto my God!') become a prophecy of our own screen-mediated, empathy-poor life, from Facebook to Botox, in Huxley's pleasure-conditioning rather than Orwell's pain. Against this, the chapter holds up Armando's Franciscan empathy for Caesar and the hope of a 'planet of the regenerate monkeys' re-attuned to the community of wild life.
- ch. 41 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(notes)*
